title: The Fathers on 1 Corinthians
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: Paul’s phrase “through the will of God” means he was sent by Christ with the Father’s approval, since the Father wills and works through the Son.
comments.comment: “Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 1:1). The inspired Paul says that he has been sent by Christ, by the good pleasure of God the Father. For this, I think, is what “through the will of God” means (1 Corinthians 1:1). Since the Father’s willing and working are through the Son, we say that it is again through the Son that the saints have been appointed to their apostleship.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “through the will of God” means in Paul’s greeting.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By saying “in every place,” Paul shows the call reaches beyond Corinth, since the Law confined worship to Jerusalem but Gentile believers now worship everywhere, as the prophets foretold.
comments.comment:
“And Sosthenes the brother,” and so on (1 Corinthians 1:1). Paul makes it plain that the power of the preaching will benefit not only the Corinthians but also all who have been called in Christ to the sanctification that comes through faith, when he says, “to those sanctified in Christ in every place, theirs and ours” (1 Corinthians 1:2). For the Law did not command this to be done in every place; it commanded them to come to the divine temple itself in Jerusalem (Deuteronomy 12:13–14). It feared, as one would expect, how easily their minds could be carried away: if they were commanded to worship or sacrifice in every place, they might perhaps take the Law as a pretext for turning to more shameful things, and worship carved images, setting up temples and altars for themselves.

But now that we who come from the Gentiles have been called, through faith in Christ, into a close bond with God, and have been enriched with the security that comes through the Holy Spirit, we are commanded to worship, not all of us in Jerusalem, but in every place. This, then, was what was spoken through the prophets: “And they shall worship the Lord, each one from his own place” (Zephaniah 2:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says “in every place, theirs and ours.”
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The church is all who are sanctified and call on Christ’s name, Jew or Gentile, and Paul calls them God’s church yet assigns them to Christ.
comments.comment: So he writes, together with Sosthenes, to the church of God, which Christ presented to himself (Ephesians 5:27). And who were seen to be that church? All who have been sanctified and called through Christ to justification, and who call upon his name “in every place, theirs and ours” (1 Corinthians 1:2), that is, whether in the land of the Jews or in the cities and countries of the Gentiles. He proclaims Christ to be God by nature, and with him and through him he renders glory to God the Father. For he names the sanctified “the church of God,” and yet he assigns them to Christ, saying, “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul’s “together with all who call on the name” shows that calling on Christ is not yet the same as being the church, so believers should press on to the spotless church.
comments.comment: … if everyone were already the church, what need would there still be to add “together with all who call upon”? And if all alike were calling upon the Name, what need would there be for the letter not to be written only to all who call upon it, but beyond them also to the church of God? … only those who deserve praise ought to be styled “church,” while those who deserve blame are not yet apostates—they are still wrestling with sin—but are still calling upon him, and are not yet the church itself. So let us hurry on from mere calling upon him to rising up into the church that is spotless and without blemish.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul adds “together with all who call on the name” to “the church of God.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul crowns believers with grace and peace from both the Father and the Lord Jesus, who shares in giving heaven’s gifts and is himself the peace of all.
comments.comment: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 1:3). He crowns those who have believed with the grace that comes from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. For through him and in him all things come from God the Father. He is co-giver and co-provider, with the one who begot him, of the good things from above, and he distributes the gifts from heaven. He himself is the peace of all (Ephesians 2:14), and by the grace that comes from himself he makes radiant principalities, thrones and authorities (Colossians 1:16), and, to put it simply, every rational creature.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why grace and peace are said to come from both the Father and the Son.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Thanks to God is always right over what is praiseworthy, and Paul gives it as a father over his spiritual sons when they prosper.
comments.comment: “I thank my God always”: it is right to give thanks over the praiseworthy things he names, and not sometimes to thank and sometimes not, but always to thank. If I see someone sometimes doing well and sometimes sinning, I do not thank God concerning him always, but when he does well—and so also concerning myself. In whom, then, does the thanksgiving Paul offer find its ground? In his own hearers, of whom he has become a father according to God. Just as a father gives thanks over sons when they are healthy and when they prosper, so too, whenever a teacher sees his hearers boiling with the Spirit, rich in word and wisdom, worthy of praise, he thanks God always concerning them. Let us look, then, at the grace of those praised in Corinth, so that we may be eager for it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the word “always” in Paul’s thanksgiving.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul praises the Corinthians before rebuking them because the gathering was a mixture of just and unjust, so praise and rebuke each fit only part of it.
comments.comment: … neither do these praises suit sinners, nor do those rebukes suit the righteous alone—I mean the words “I appeal to you, brothers… that you all say the same things and that there be no divisions among you,” and whatever is like them. So the church was mixed, if one may even call “church” this whole blend of just and unjust. Still, those who were gathering were mixed; therefore, when the apostle was about to convict the gathering for sins done with wickedness, he first, of necessity, offers praise for those who come together well upon the same thing.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Being enriched “in every word and in all knowledge” means being able to explain any Scripture and defend the truth, since knowledge only knows while speech also interprets.
comments.comment: “That in everything you were enriched in him.” Blessed are those who are rich in everything and lack nothing that belongs to God, but practice every virtue and enjoy his gifts freely and richly—in every word and in all knowledge—so that they are at a loss over no Scripture, but seek and find everywhere; and when a text must be explained they can use every kind of discourse, both the so called continuous exposition and question and answer, and are ready to speak against every heresy, to stand with the dogma of the truth, and to fulfill what the apostle said: “Always ready to make a defense to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you.” So also “in all knowledge”: not only according to the Scriptures, but so that one may say, “For he himself gave me unfailing knowledge of the things that are,” and what follows from that. For knowledge shows knowing alone, while word also interprets what is known. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what being enriched in word and knowledge means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ’s testimony is confirmed in a person whose faith holds firm under trial, and it is also confirmed by the Scriptures and by the signs and powers that bore witness with him.
comments.comment: Christ is, if I may put it this way, the chief martyr [witness]; and though there are many witnesses to Christ through their death, he is the ruler of the martyrs. This testimony of Christ is firm in some, and in others it is not firm but shaken. For if faith about the testimony is such that from a true disposition one can say, “I am persuaded that neither death nor life” and what follows “will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord,” then the testimony is firm in such a person; but if we are not like that, and are shaken by what happens, the testimony of Christ has not yet been confirmed in us. And again we may take the saying another way: every Scripture that bears witness about Christ is a testimony of Christ; so it is good to be confirmed also in the testimony of Christ that comes from the Scriptures. And otherwise: look at the testimony of Christ—signs and wonders and various powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit according to his will also bore witness with him; and the testimony of Christ is firm in the saints.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “the testimony of Christ was confirmed among you” can mean.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The righteous person hopes not in this age but awaits Christ’s revealing, and no one yet has blamelessness, since it belongs to the day of the Lord.
comments.comment: “So that you are not lacking in any gift”: as there are many gifts, he will discuss them also later in the letter. “Awaiting the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ”: the righteous person does not have his hopes in this age, but while suffering and facing danger he awaits the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, what Christ Jesus reveals. “Who will also confirm you to the end”: who confirms? Christ Jesus, the Word, Wisdom; and the testimony that is being confirmed is not for a few days, but to the end. “Blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ”: until we arrive there, we do not yet have blamelessness; for we do not know what the coming day will bring forth, and even if someone seems to have blamelessness for the present, it is in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul’s phrases about waiting for the revealing and being blameless in the day of the Lord.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Believers should keep believing God, who is faithful and has made them fellow heirs with Christ.
comments.comment: “God is faithful, through whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord.” Origen: keep believing him always; for you were called so that we might simply be under Jesus. Great is what God grants the saints: we were called into fellowship with his Son; therefore heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what being called into fellowship with the Son involves.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: No divisions means agreeing with the church’s teaching and following its rules.
comments.comment: “and that there be no divisions among you.” Origen: the one who agrees in everything with the right word and the church’s dogma concerning Father and Son and Holy Spirit, and further concerning the economy [God’s plan of salvation] that touches us, concerning resurrection and judgment, and who also follows the church’s canons, is not in a schism.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by “no divisions among you.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul urges them to take their honor from Christ’s name and to be of one mind, since Christ is one and undivided and has joined believers into one soul.
comments.comment:
“But be joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment” (1 Corinthians 1:10). It was both necessary and wise to persuade them that they ought to take their honor from the Master’s name, as the Master himself says through one of the holy prophets: “But those who serve me shall be called by a new name, which shall be blessed upon the earth” (Isaiah 65:15–16). For we have been named Christians, and we are rich in the new name.

Some are rightly deprived of it: those who desert the right teaching of the Church and give themselves to deceiving spirits (1 Timothy 4:1) and to the wonder-mongering of certain unholy false teachers. They have taken those teachers’ name, and very fittingly, for they are not Christ’s. They have each taken a share in the blasphemy against him and have been split into differing opinions and judgments, although Christ called his own in peace.

It was needful also to persuade them that Christ himself is one and is not divided (1 Corinthians 1:13). So we are all one in Christ (Galatians 3:28), and for this we have been joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment, since he has bound us into one soul by a spiritual union, he who says of us to God the Father, “I desire that, as I and you are one, so they too in […]” (John 17:21–22).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Only the one who died for us and into whose name we were baptized should be called our own, so Paul’s questions show that believers belong to Christ alone.
comments.comment: “Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you?” (1 Corinthians 1:13). If someone else endured the cross for us, let us be called his. If perhaps we were baptized into someone else’s name, let him have us, and let us enroll him as Savior and Redeemer. But if “Christ died for our sins” (1 Corinthians 15:3), and with him alone we have been “buried through baptism into death” (Romans 6:4), then let him, he says, possess those who have been bought. For we have been saved through him and by him, who laid down his own life for us (1 John 3:16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the force of Paul’s two questions about Christ and Paul.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul thanks God that he baptized few because preaching is the greater task, and polished speech would keep the power of Christ from reaching the hearers’ souls.
comments.comment: “I thank God that I baptized none of you… for Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, not in wisdom of word, so that the cross of Christ might not be emptied.” Origen: preaching the gospel is greater than baptizing; and because Paul knew that some were set apart for baptizing, he thanks God for having a better lot than baptizing. … Origen again: there is need not so much of word as of power; therefore it is written, “The Lord will give a word to those who preach good news with great power,” the King of the powers of the Beloved. So Christ sent me not to baptize but to preach the gospel, not in wisdom of word, not in clarity of diction; for if I do that and want to hand on the word that way, the power of Christ does not reach the soul of the hearers, and I empty and tear down the grace of the power.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul’s being sent to preach rather than to baptize does not mean an apostle may not baptize, but he left it to local overseers so as not to spend preaching time on it.
comments.comment: “For Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel” (1 Corinthians 1:17). He was admittedly sent to proclaim Jesus to the Gentiles. But we say that it also belongs to the work of an apostle to baptize some, as the occasion and need require, if he so chooses. So that he would not seem to spend the time owed to preaching on other pursuits, he very rightly left this to be done at leisure by those in each region and by all who were appointed to oversight. He himself preached the gospel instead, since he had been entrusted with the ministry of the word and had searched out the mystery of Christ with great precision. Yet just as the inspired Stephen, though appointed a servant of tables, did not set aside the duty of teaching the mysteries (Acts 6:2–5), so too the inspired Paul, though appointed to preach the mystery of Christ, also met the need for baptism when the time came. Authority for both lay before him, and nothing prevented him from doing it if he chose.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by saying Christ did not send him to baptize.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The cross seems a scandal but is a great mystery: as pagans say a plague ends when one gives himself for all, so one died to end the plague of ignorance and ruin.
comments.comment: “For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.” Origen: the name of the cross seems a scandal; but if someone lends his ears to the word of God and to grace, he will see that this too is a great mystery. Even the pagans have handed down that often, when great plagues or floods or droughts came, these ceased when a person gave himself up for the common good. Why then is it surprising if, when the whole world was sick with error, one had to die for the true plague—to destroy the plague of ignorance and darkness and ruin? …
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear reason why Christ had to die, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ’s death was a public victory, since the cross is a trophy raised against Satan, and the one who knows its power boasts in it and is crucified to the world.
comments.comment: [Only a divine power was] able to take on dying for all, with a kind of public display, so that through that death a trophy might be raised against the devil. For those who triumph in the world are accustomed to set up trophies against the conquered in the manner of a cross. So the cross of Christ is a trophy against Satan; therefore he says, “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross”—for the one who has come to know what the power of the cross is: that I was freed from evils through that One who died to rescue me from death—“except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me and I to the world.” It is a great good that the world has been crucified to me; through what did this good come to me? Through the cross of Christ. It is a great good for me to be crucified to the world; for if I died to the world, I have been crucified to the world with Christ; but if I live in sins, I have not yet been counted worthy of the good that belongs to the cross. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in a vivid, clear image why the cross is the power of God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The gospel is foolishness to those proud of worldly wisdom, and Paul’s wise man, scribe and debater are the orators, schoolmasters and word-fighters who do not know the God who made the universe.
comments.comment:
“Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age?” (1 Corinthians 1:20). To those who pride themselves on worldly wisdom and do not accept the faith, clearly meaning faith in Christ, the gospel is foolishness. But it is not so with us; far from it. For we are convinced that it is the power of God (1 Corinthians 1:18), a way of salvation that leads to sanctification, and that by its abundant preaching it wisely guides us to the knowledge of the truth.

I for my part think that here he calls the orators “wise,” who by the cleverness of their speeches always wove persuasion into falsehood and strove to win for it the appearance of truth. By “scribes” I think he means the schoolmasters or grammarians, whose custom it was to labor over the writings of the poets and to explain them to the young. By “debaters” he means those who are used to fighting over words and who, supposedly with precision, put things to the test. Through the concepts they devise they pretend to seek the truth, that is, whatever seems, as far as possible, to stand beyond reproach on each question set before them. But they do not do it rightly at all; rather, they do it with utter carelessness. For they have not known the God of all, who without toil framed this whole universe by ineffable workings, and by a mere nod brought into being all things that were not. So the wisdom of the world has truly been made foolish (1 Corinthians 1:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains who Paul’s “wise man, scribe and debater” are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God destroys only seeming wisdom, as when a teacher of the truth shows to be folly the arguments a forceful opponent relied on, not the wisdom of the truly wise.
comments.comment: And if you want to understand “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise and set aside the discernment of the discerning,” picture for me someone very formidable in heretical arguments … who seeks with such force for the heretical case that not just anyone can stand against him; then picture someone competent according to the truth, whom God also made competent as a minister of a new covenant, showing all those things to be folly on which the deceived man relied. So he destroys their wisdom—not that of the truly wise, Isaiah, Jeremiah, or Solomon; he destroys seeming wisdom, not the true.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul’s phrase “in this age” matters: only worldly wisdom is made foolish, and believers must seem fools to people for trusting Christ crucified, the resurrection and judgment.
comments.comment: [On “the wisdom of the world”:] it is not the same to be wise and to be wise in this age; for without such an addition the word covers true wisdom. You will understand folly likewise: it is not the same to be a fool and to be a fool in this age; for without the addition “in this age” one is truly a fool. We who believe the words of wisdom are therefore commanded to become fools in this age; for so we seem to people when we believe in Christ Jesus crucified, and believe the resurrection of bodies, and believe that we shall live—not only that those now on earth will later be in the heavens, but that if we sin we shall be handed over to eternal fire.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says “wise in this age” and in what sense believers are fools.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul’s censure of worldly wisdom does not reject wise men: it targets teachings that put everything in matter and the senses, while the wisdom of God turns the soul toward things invisible.
comments.comment: But it is likely that what Paul wrote in the First Letter to the Corinthians, addressed as it was to Greeks who were greatly puffed up over Greek wisdom, has moved some to think that our teaching does not want wise men. Let anyone who thinks so hear this. When the word censures worthless men, it says that they are not wise about things intelligible, invisible and eternal, but that, having busied themselves with the things of sense alone and placing everything in these, they are wise men of the world. In the same way, since there are many doctrines, it says that those which plead for matter and bodies, and assert that all things that primarily exist are bodies and that there is nothing else besides them, whether called invisible or named incorporeal, are “the wisdom of the world,” which is brought to nothing and made foolish, and the wisdom of this age (1 Corinthians 1:20; 2:6). But those which carry the soul over from the affairs of this world to the blessedness that is with God and to what is called his kingdom, and which teach people to despise all things perceived by sense and seen, as being temporary, and to hasten toward things invisible and to look at the things that are not seen (2 Corinthians 4:18), these it says are “the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 2:7).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The world did not know Christ preached in the law and prophets, so God sent him to be crucified.
comments.comment: And how “in the wisdom of God the world did not know God through wisdom”? The wisdom of God is in law and prophets; the world did not know Christ preached in law and prophets. Therefore at the end of the ages he sent Jesus Christ to be crucified for the human race, so that by the folly of the preaching those who believed in Jesus Christ crucified might believe.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “in the wisdom of God the world did not know God through wisdom” means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul calls human understanding and eloquence “the wisdom of God” because God made them, and “the foolishness of the preaching” means the plain words of disciples unskilled in speech but rich in knowledge.
comments.comment: “For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe” (1 Corinthians 1:21). He calls even human understanding and eloquence, that is, the very bloom of style, “the wisdom of God,” to teach that God is the maker of the mind and the giver of good sense and eloquence, even if some have used them for ends they should not. By “the foolishness of the preaching” he means the plainness of the words. For the inspired disciples were unskilled in speech but rich in knowledge (2 Corinthians 11:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul words the verse as he does, and what “foolishness of the preaching” means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God ought to have been known through his wisdom, and since that failed he chose as a second course to save believers through the foolishness of the preaching, which only seems foolish at first sight.
comments.comment: Further, that even in the judgement of the Word it is far better to assent to doctrines with reason and wisdom than with bare faith, and that the Word willed this also because circumstances required it, so as not to leave human beings wholly without help, is shown by Paul, the true disciple of Jesus, when he says: “For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of the preaching to save those who believe” (1 Corinthians 1:21). These words clearly show that God ought to have been known in the wisdom of God; and since this did not happen so, God was pleased, as a second course, to save those who believe, not through foolishness without qualification, but through foolishness so far as the preaching goes. For Jesus Christ crucified, when he is preached, is at first sight the foolishness of the preaching; as Paul too, who was aware of this, says in the passage: “But we preach Jesus Christ crucified, to Jews a stumbling block and to Gentiles foolishness, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:23–24).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul’s statement that Jews ask for a sign is true, as when they demanded a sign of Christ for driving the traders out of the temple.
comments.comment: “For Jews ask for a sign, and Greeks seek wisdom” (1 Corinthians 1:22). Paul’s statement is true on both counts. Once, when Christ was driving out of the temple courts those who sold sheep and oxen, turtledoves and pigeons, and saying, “Do not make my Father’s house a house of trade” (John 2:14–16), they retorted, “What sign do you show us, since you do these things?” (John 2:18), and, “Who gave you this authority?” (Matthew 21:23). Some of the scribes also came to him, after a very great display of signs, and said with malice, “Teacher, we wish […]” (Matthew 12:38).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jews demanded signs while ignoring the words of the saints, and Greeks, who seek brilliant argument, thought the Word’s becoming man, a virgin birth and a resurrection to be foolishness.
comments.comment:
[Of the Jews who asked for signs:] So, counting the words of the saints as worth almost nothing, words through which they could well have learned that he was the Christ, they kept demanding signs from God. That is why the Savior said to those sent by John, “Go and tell John what you hear and see: the blind receive their sight, the lame walk,” and so on (Matthew 11:4–5).

The Greeks, for their part, seek brilliance of diction and argument, and they think even the way of the dispensation [God’s plan of salvation] in the flesh to be foolishness. They say, “Why was it necessary at all for the Word who is from God, being God by nature and able to accomplish whatever he purposes by will and nod, to become man and to endure death? How could a virgin give birth?” they say. “And how will what death has destroyed rise again?” But it is not at all surprising that they say such things: “For the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit, for they are foolishness to him” (1 Corinthians 2:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Jews and Greeks each asked for, and why Greeks found the gospel foolish.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Believing in Christ crucified gives power from God.
comments.comment: [On Christ crucified, the power of God:] we received power from believing in Jesus Christ crucified; and as far as we fall short in that faith, so far we fall short in the power of having in ourselves the things that come from God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ crucified is the power and wisdom of God, and the Word himself cannot be called God’s weakness or foolishness.
comments.comment:
But we preach Christ crucified and the following. It is evident that he says Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God according to the logic of the cross, as being superior; for the word of the cross is foolishness to those being destroyed, but to us being saved it is the power of God.

He demonstrates this more clearly after saying: to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, he brought Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God; because the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men. Who would dare say the Word God is the weakness of God, and the foolishness of God regarding the crucified Christ? God the Word is powerful as the Father, not a power as a part fulfilling the essence of the Father, and likewise wise …
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Christ is the power and wisdom of God, through whom the Father saved the world and by whom all things were made and are preserved.
comments.comment: But to us it is the power and wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). For through him God the Father has saved the whole world under heaven, as through the power that is naturally his and through his own ineffable wisdom. For the Son is the wisdom and power of God the Father, through whom all things were brought into being and, once made, are preserved.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that Christ is the power and wisdom of God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God’s works that seem weak or foolish are still beyond all human strength and wisdom.
comments.comment: And if anyone, he says, should choose to measure the power that is in God against the powers of men, he will certainly see that whatever among the divine works may seem to have been done as in weakness, and as it were not with the full power of its Maker, is beyond and better than all human strength. You will understand wisdom in exactly the same way: what seems to be foolish is wiser than men. Suppose someone wished to compare the small and least of created things with the size and beauty of the elements, I mean heaven and the sun and the other stars, and fire and water and the rest. The power and wisdom found in the small things would be very slight, and, judged by their inferiority at least, it might seem a [The text is damaged here.] sort of thing. Yet no one among us could become the maker even of things so [The text is damaged here.]. Truly, then, “the weakness of God is stronger than men, and the foolishness of God is wiser than men” (1 Corinthians 1:25). So the dispensation holds all wisdom, for Christ has reigned with understanding, in wisdom, over the whole world under heaven.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul adds “according to the flesh” because some are wise by the flesh and others by the Spirit.
comments.comment: And he added “according to the flesh” to “not many wise,” knowing there are differences among the wise: some wise according to flesh, some according to spirit; and wise according to flesh are those who have practiced only little phrases and dress up whatever is not truth as if it were truth …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul says few, not none, of the wise are called, and he means those wise, powerful and noble in the flesh, as opposed to those who are so by the Spirit, like Christ, the apostles and God’s children.
comments.comment:
Yet even so he did not shut the wise according to flesh out of the faith; for he did not say “No one wise according to the flesh comes to the word,” but that they are exceedingly few.

Powerful according to the flesh are those who hold the offices; according to the Spirit you will understand if you see how the Savior was not powerful according to the flesh—he was handed over and crucified from weakness—yet was powerful according to the Spirit, healing every disease and every illness in the people. So look at the apostles: how they were powerful according to the Spirit. One is powerful according to the Spirit also who lives according to the Spirit and by the Spirit puts to death the deeds of the body.

Likewise with the of noble birth: of noble birth according to the flesh are those from rich and famous fathers; according to the Spirit the of noble birth are the sons of God, of whom it is written, “As many as received him, he gave them authority to become children of God.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains the phrase “according to the flesh” for wise, powerful and noble.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God chose the foolish things of the world, meaning believers whom the world laughs at for their faith, and the world’s wise are shamed when simple Christians die rather than worship idols.
comments.comment: Whom then did God choose? Not simply the foolish, but with the addition “of the world”: we who believe are fools as far as the world is concerned. So they laugh and call us fools: “Christians say there is a resurrection of the dead, and that we live after death, and that Jesus whom the Jews crucified was born of a virgin,” and such things. Let them laugh and call us fools; for the soulish person does not receive the things of the Spirit—they are folly to him. So God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the wise—not simply the wise, but, by common construction, of the world: God chose the world’s foolish to shame the world’s wise; for truly the world’s wise are put to shame when they worship idols while the unlettered and simple die rather than commit idolatry.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who “the foolish things of the world” are and how they shame the wise.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God chose the simplest Christians, who live more purely than many philosophers, to shame those who boast of knowing God yet turn to statues.
comments.comment: God, I think, also saw the arrogance, or the contempt for others, of those who pride themselves on having known God and on having learned divine things from philosophy, yet who, like the most ignorant, turn to statues and their temples and the much-talked-of mysteries. And so he “chose the foolish things of the world” (1 Corinthians 1:27), the simplest among Christians, who live more temperately and more purely than many philosophers, “to put to shame the wise” (1 Corinthians 1:27), who are not ashamed to converse with lifeless things as with gods or images of gods.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By “the wise” Paul means, broadly, all who seem advanced in learning yet have fallen into godless polytheism.
comments.comment: “God chose the foolish things of the world to put the wise to shame” (1 Corinthians 1:27). By “the wise” he means, in a broad sense, all who seem to have advanced in learning but have fallen away into godless polytheism, since “claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man and birds and four-footed beasts and creeping things” (Romans 1:22–23).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The “low-born” and “things that are not” are those the world despises, and God chose them so that no one could boast of being chosen for noble birth.
comments.comment: “And God chose the of low birth of the world and the despised”—again with the addition “of the world.” For what is nobler than a soul that leaves the idols and says, “Our fathers acquired false idols, and there is none among them who brings rain”? So God chose the of low birth of the world but of noble birth of God; … “And the things that are not, to abolish the things that are”: he named “things that are not” the foolish, weak, of low birth, and despised of the world; “things that are,” the of noble birth of the world—for in the world they are somebody, and we are not, worn down by all and despised. Now God chose the things that are not to abolish the things that are, so that no flesh may boast and say, “I was chosen because I am of noble birth.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains who “the things that are not” are and why God chose them.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul says “flesh” and “before Him” to belittle human boasting, since credit that belongs to God was being given to men.
comments.comment: So that no flesh may boast before Him; that is, so that the achievement of the preaching is not written upon the advantages of those at home. But he said 'flesh' and not 'soul', belittling human boastings. And why 'before Him' and not 'before men'? Because the boasting upon our own advantages was set in opposition to the boasting upon God. For what was necessary to write upon God, they were writing upon men. Therefore he said 'before Him'; for boasting occurring before Him, He who sees all, was impious. …
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Christ became wisdom, righteousness and sanctification for believers so that to boast in him fulfills “let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”
comments.comment: “And from him you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption”: for this reason Christ is all these for us, so that what is written may come to pass—“Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.” For if the one who boasts in wisdom ought to boast, and Christ is the wisdom, clearly the one who boasts in Christ boasts; and likewise for the rest—I mean sanctification and righteousness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ is called wisdom, righteousness and sanctification.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since believers are of God and Christ became their wisdom, sanctification and redemption, any boasting should be in the Savior, not in their own advantages.
comments.comment: But of Him you are. … If therefore it is of Him, how shall we boast in our own advantages? But it is in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom and sanctification and redemption; not the wisdom of men saved—for it was wandering—but He Himself has become wisdom for us unto the knowledge of God; not the understanding of men snatched away, but Jesus having been crucified. Not men redeemed, so that the boasting may be from the Savior, not from the saved.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul calls Christ the testimony of God because the Father bore witness to him.
comments.comment: “Proclaiming to you the testimony of God” (1 Corinthians 2:1). He calls Christ the testimony of God, for God the Father bore witness to him, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “the testimony of God” refers to.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul avoided persuasive wisdom for fear they would be puffed up, and his weakness, fear and trembling came from persecution and showed his humility for their sake.
comments.comment: I was always afraid lest you be puffed up by outward training, since I did not use the persuasive wisdom. And in weakness, he says, the weakness from persecutions—for this is his custom to say everywhere—in weakness and in fear and in trembling, the weakness of those from whom I was persecuted. I demonstrated the fear and the trembling concerning you, I was all humble, so that you might be taught by this and not be puffed up. …
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul’s weakness and fear came from using modest teaching suited to infants, while the apostles’ signs and wonders, not eloquence, demonstrated that God was at work in them.
comments.comment:
“And I was with you in weakness and in fear,” and so on (1 Corinthians 2:3). Although I used such modest instruction, he says, I was very much afraid that my words, if they proved too lofty for the understanding you had, would do you no good but rather harm. For those who are infants in mind, a tender and gentle word would suit their learning, “but solid food is for the mature, for those who by practice have their senses trained to distinguish good and evil” (Hebrews 5:14). So my word to you, he says, came as in great weakness, and not with the full power of one who teaches the mysteries. Nor was it “in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2:4–5).

For to their preaching the apostles added signs from God as well. They made the deed itself a clear demonstration that one must believe that God was attested in them, through the Spirit and through the deeds themselves, since they used a certain ineffable and inexpressible power and working and performed their wonders with ease. The little myths of the Greeks would naturally need an eloquence to fight in their defense and, as it were, to cover up their ugliness. But for the divine preaching a plain and gentle word suffices, attested as it is by the power of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul came in weakness and what the “demonstration of the Spirit and of power” was.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The “demonstration of the Spirit and of power” is a proof more divine than Greek logic: of the Spirit through the prophecies, and of power through wondrous works.
comments.comment: We must say further that our teaching has a demonstration of its own, more divine than the Greek demonstration drawn from dialectic. This more divine demonstration the apostle calls a demonstration “of the Spirit and of power” (1 Corinthians 2:4): “of the Spirit” because of the prophecies, which are able to bring the reader to faith, above all in what concerns Christ; and “of power” because of the wondrous works of power. That these took place must be shown from many other things, and also from this, that traces of them are still preserved among those who live according to the purpose of our teaching.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “demonstration of the Spirit and of power” means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Had Jesus chosen men wise in the crowd’s opinion, his message would have looked like a philosophers’ school resting on polished words, so he used men whose success showed God’s power.
comments.comment: To this, then, I say that those who are able to examine the story of the apostles of Jesus with good sense and fairness can see that these men taught Christianity by divine power and succeeded in winning people over to the word of God. For what was in them and won over their hearers was not a power of speech or an ordered delivery shaped by the dialectical or rhetorical arts of the Greeks. It seems to me that if Jesus had chosen men who were wise in the opinion of the multitude and able to think and speak in a way that pleases crowds, and had used them as ministers of his teaching, he would with very good reason have been suspected of having been proclaimed by a method like that of philosophers who stand at the head of some school. Then the claim that the message is divine would no longer have shone out, since the message and the preaching would have rested on the persuasiveness of a wisdom that lies in the phrasing and arrangement of words (1 Corinthians 2:4); and “faith,” like the faith that the philosophers of the world have in their doctrines, would have been “in the wisdom of men” and not “in the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2:5).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Even true and persuasive words cannot reach a soul unless God gives the speaker power and grace, as the Psalm says of those who bring good news with great power.
comments.comment: “My word and my preaching were not in persuasive words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that our faith might not rest on the wisdom of men but on the power of God” (1 Corinthians 2:4–5). The divine word says that what is spoken, even if it is true in itself and most persuasive, is not enough to reach a human soul unless some power is also given from God to the speaker and grace blooms upon what is said; and this grace too does not come without God to those who speak to good effect. So the prophet says in the sixty-seventh Psalm (Psalm 68 in English Bibles): “The Lord will give a word to those who bring good news with great power” (Psalm 68:11).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul adds that he speaks wisdom among the perfect so no one thinks the faith has none: leading people into faith is one thing and unveiling God’s wisdom to the proven is another.
comments.comment: … lest someone say, “Then, since he brought the proofs of faith in power and in Spirit, he had no wisdom at all, but the mystery of piety is only to believe, and there is no promise of wisdom in it,” he adds, “Yet we speak wisdom among the perfect—wisdom not of this age nor of the rulers of this age who are being abolished.” For it is one thing to lead people into the faith, and another to unveil the wisdom of God. So we unfold God’s wisdom not to those being introduced, nor to beginners, nor to those who have not yet given proof of a sound life; but when someone, having exercised the senses as one ought toward distinguishing good and evil, becomes fit also to hear wisdom, then we speak wisdom among the perfect …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says he speaks wisdom only “among the perfect.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Sinners are first called to healing teachings, and only those who show they have been cleansed and live better are called on to the wisdom Paul speaks among the perfect.
comments.comment: To this [Celsus’s charge that Christians summon sinners] we reply that it is not the same thing to call those who are sick in soul to healing, and those who are healthy to the knowledge and understanding of diviner things. We know both of these. At the beginning, when we invite people to be healed, we urge sinners to come to the teachings that teach them not to sin, those without understanding to the teachings that produce understanding, children to rise in mind to manhood, and, in a word, the wretched to happiness, or, to use the more proper word, to blessedness. But when those among them who are making progress show that they have been cleansed by the Word and, as far as they can, have lived a better life, then we call them to our own rites of initiation, for “we speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Corinthians 2:6).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The apostles’ lowly speech plants true knowledge of the mysteries, and the rulers of this age who did not know Christ are the evil, hostile powers who spoke through the world’s wise men.
comments.comment: “Yet a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing” (1 Corinthians 2:6). The word of the holy teachers of the mysteries goes forth in lowly speech, yet it plants in us an unadulterated knowledge of the divine mysteries. It shows that Christ is wisdom, not through the fine speech of the world’s wise men, but as he is attested by his own nature. None of the rulers of this age knew him (1 Corinthians 2:8). These rulers are the evil and hostile powers, who have spoken through the wise men of the world.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who “the rulers of this age” are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The wisdom of this age includes poetry, rhetoric and speculation about the world, whereas the wisdom Paul speaks is sought after faith and a good life, and the rulers who crucified the Lord did not know it.
comments.comment: At the same time he [Paul] has made clear that the lessons circulating among others are not, in their origin, of humans but of invisible powers that are being abolished. And I would say that the poetic wisdom is of this age, and perhaps rhetoric too; and so is the wisdom that claims to speak about heaven and earth and the administration of the whole. So if we speak wisdom and say it among the perfect, we do not mean the wisdom of this age; for it is not through poems or through any such art. Origen: but we speak wisdom in a mystery—things unknown to the rulers of this age who work the wisdom of the wise of this world; and thus they did not know: they plotted against our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ and crucified him; for if they had known they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. Therefore wisdom must also be sought in the word—but after faith, after the way of life, according to what is written: “Desire wisdom; keep the commandments.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “the wisdom of this age” covers and how God’s wisdom is to be sought.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The rulers would not have crucified Christ had they known him, because his cross defeated them, and Satan did not know Jesus was God, as his temptation in the desert shows.
comments.comment:
“For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). The saying is very reasonable. For by his own cross Christ triumphed over the evil and hostile powers, nailing to the wood “the bond written against us” (Colossians 2:14–15). He drove Satan away from his tyranny over us, abolished the sin of the world, opened the gates of Hades to the spirits below, and pulled down the power of death. How, then, could the suffering on the cross be anything but hateful to the unclean demons? So they would not have crucified him, had they known for certain that he was the Redeemer and the Lord of glory.

That the crucifixion of Christ, carried out through the madness of the Jews, was the work of the devil’s savagery, the inspired John showed plainly when he said of Judas, “After the morsel, Satan entered into him” (John 13:27). Satan did not know that Jesus was God. For if he had known and been convinced of it, how could he have tempted him in the desert, saying, “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matthew 4:3)? And the Savior himself, as all agree, took care to escape the notice of the rulers of this age, so that, unnoticed, he might suffer, and by his own blood win for himself and for his own Father all that lies under heaven.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the rulers would not have crucified the Lord of glory had they known.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God prepared something greater for those who love him than for those who fear him, and because only the Spirit can search the depths of God, the Spirit must be in us for us to search them with him.
comments.comment: Scripture knows a difference between those who love God and those who fear God, and knows that those who love far surpass those who fear. Some things have been prepared also for those who fear; yet he prepared something greater for those who love than what was prepared for those who fear. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. There is a Spirit that can search everything; the human soul cannot search everything, but a better Spirit had to come to be in us, so that when that Spirit is in us searching everything—even the depths of God—and is mingled with us, we may search together with it everything and the depths of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the things God has prepared are for, and why the Spirit is needed to know them.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The depths of God are the hidden knowledge of Scripture that the Spirit reveals.
comments.comment: “Even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10). The depths of God are the hidden knowledge laid up in the sacred writings. The Spirit knows it and reveals it to the souls of the saints, and makes the mind within them a divine mind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “the depths of God” are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: As a man’s knowledge is one with the spirit in him, so the knowledge of the Father and the Spirit is one, and the Spirit does not search as one who is ignorant.
comments.comment: God and the Holy Spirit are two persons, but man and the spirit in him are not two persons, but one man. He says this because just as there is no disagreement of knowledge within a man, so also the knowledge of the Father and the Spirit is one; for this reason, the Spirit would not have inquired as if he were ignorant. Furthermore, regarding the man, the Spirit in him spoke, but regarding the Holy Spirit, he did not say 'the one in God' but 'the one from God.'
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: We cannot know what God has freely given us unless his Spirit teaches us, because human arts do not teach what the Spirit teaches, and a human teacher only sets starting points from which the learner draws at the same spring.
comments.comment: let us understand the things freely given us by God; for if the Spirit from God that teaches us is not in us, we cannot say that we know the things freely given us by God—for no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. “Which things we also speak,” he says, “not in words taught by human wisdom but in words taught by the Spirit,” and what follows. All the wisdoms of this world are words taught by humans, which one learns in each of the rational arts; but they do not teach the things taught by the Spirit; and you would not say that the teacher, taught by the Spirit about what he says, taught them. For the Spirit present in the one who seeks and searches the truth shines in, and so always, by the renewal of the mind, he finds what he has not learned from humans. Therefore the Savior says, “Do not seek a teacher on the earth; for one is your Teacher, the Father in the heavens,” or “one is your Guide, the Christ.” A human sets down a few things—say Paul teaching Timothy—and Timothy, taking starting points, comes himself to the spring where Paul came and draws, and Timothy becomes equal to Paul. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “words taught by the Spirit” means, with a clear picture of how a teacher passes it on.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: No one can know God’s things except through God’s Spirit, and Paul says believers received that Spirit so they might know and speak what God has freely given.
comments.comment: But as no one among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man within him, so no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. And if no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God, it is impossible for a man to know the things of God. Consider too how even this becomes possible. We, he says, received not the spirit of the world but the Spirit who is from God, that we might know the things freely given us by God — things we speak not in words taught by human wisdom but in words taught by the Spirit (1 Corinthians 2:12–13).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Comparing spiritual things with spiritual means setting one passage of Scripture beside another to uncover its mind, with the help of the same Spirit who gave the words.
comments.comment: “comparing spiritual things with spiritual”—by examining this wording with that wording and gathering like with like, the mind of Scripture is uncovered as it were. In this way I understand the things of God and become taught by the Spirit: not only by having learned the things of the Spirit that moved Isaiah, but also by having the same Spirit that shut and sealed Isaiah’s words; for unless the Spirit opens the prophets’ words, what is shut cannot be opened.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what “comparing spiritual things with spiritual” means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A later revelation interpreting an earlier one is how spiritual things are compared with spiritual.
comments.comment: We compare spiritual things to the spiritual because when the second revelation serves as an interpretation and a clarity of the former, those receiving the revelations compare the later things to the first, and finding the same, they receive a greater full-knowledge of the revealed truth.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Only someone truly wise in Christ can set out the connected sense of the prophets’ hidden words, by comparing spiritual things with spiritual and confirming each point from the Scriptures’ own usage.
comments.comment: Others too, who wish to examine Scripture and have sense, would be able to find its meaning. It is truly unclear in many places, but it is not, as Celsus says, “nothing.” Nor can any fool or sorcerer smooth it out, or make what was said his own in whatever way he likes. Only the one who is truly wise in Christ, and every such person, could set out the whole connected sense of what was spoken with concealment in the prophets, “comparing spiritual things with spiritual” (1 Corinthians 2:13) and establishing each thing he finds from the usage of the Scriptures.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The natural man has only inborn human understanding, because the Spirit has not enlightened his mind.
comments.comment: “The natural man” (1 Corinthians 2:14). The natural man is the one who lives according to the flesh and has not yet had his mind enlightened through the Spirit. He has only the inborn, human understanding which the Creator puts into the souls of all.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by “the natural man.”
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A soulish person fails to receive the things of the Spirit not by nature but for lack of preparation, and he becomes spiritual when he turns to piety and receives the Spirit.
comments.comment: And since he said these things, he necessarily adds that there are some people who do not receive the things of the Spirit of God—not because of nature, as the heterodox suppose, but because they have not prepared themselves. For the soulish person does not receive the things of the Spirit—he was soulish; but when he inclined toward piety and received the Spirit, he became spiritual. … And it is not so much that he has rejected what is said as that what is said has rejected him; for “wisdom will not enter a soul that devises evil, nor dwell in a body in debt to sin.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the soulish person does not receive the things of the Spirit.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God’s revelation is so deep that it seems foolish to the world’s wise, and the spiritual answer them not with reasonings but with the mind received from God and the strength of wonders.
comments.comment: Such is the depth of the spiritual revelation that it appears as foolishness to the wise of this world; in this way, the revelation of God is uncontainable to them. For, demonstrating power through the grace of the Holy Spirit, he reproves the clever man, not by cleverness but by the strength of wonders. The spiritual ones do not overturn reasonings with reasonings, but receiving the mind from God and the revelation from there, they discourse, so that the one opposing does not refute reasonings, but opposes the knowledge of God. Because of this he says: for who has known the mind of the Lord, who will instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ, which is the knowledge.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: A person becomes spiritual by walking by the Spirit and growing God’s gift, and he is recognized by the fruits of the Spirit, so where any of them is missing he is not yet spiritual.
comments.comment: “The spiritual person examines all things, yet he himself is examined by no one.” The one who no longer walks according to flesh but according to Spirit, and always by care grows it and kindles more the gift of God, prepares for himself to become spiritual; and having become so he is able to examine all things—the Greeks’, the barbarians’, the wise’, the senseless’; and no one can examine him because of the greatness of his understanding and of his reasonings. And if you want to recognize the spiritual person, “by their fruits you will know them.” What then are the fruits of the Spirit by which one must know who is spiritual? Hear the apostle: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self control”; where these are, there is the Spirit, and that one is spiritual; and where any of these is missing, that one is not yet spiritual.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the spiritual person is and how he is recognized.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The spiritual man judges everything yet is judged by no one, and natural men need such teachers because only those with the mind of Christ can prepare them to understand.
comments.comment: “But the spiritual man judges all things” (1 Corinthians 2:15). The spiritual man judges all things and, so to speak, sifts them finely with exact care, but he himself is judged by no one. That those called natural need spiritual teachers, by all means, for their benefit and training, Paul makes plain by adding, “For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him?” (1 Corinthians 2:16; Isaiah 40:13). It is as if he said: No one could instruct the natural man unless he had the mind of Christ. By “instruct” he means “prepare him to understand.” And who are those that have the mind of the Lord? He showed this himself when he went on, “But we have the mind of Christ” (1 Corinthians 2:16), that is, the Spirit who speaks in the saints, unveils mysteries to them, and makes the mind within them a divine mind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul’s statements about the spiritual man and the mind of Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The spiritual person can judge every word and is judged by no one because his thoughts are too deep to grasp, just as a child cannot scrutinize a man’s mind.
comments.comment: And the apostle sketched the spiritual when he said, The spiritual examines all things, yet he himself is examined by no one. Who is the one discerning all things but the one able to scrutinize and judge every word? And he is examined by no one, because the depth of his thoughts is not grasped. For the spiritual has the mind of the Lord. Just as a child cannot examine a man’s mind and scrutinize his thoughts—for the small child does not even follow a man’s thoughts at the start—so neither can the soulish know which things are God’s and which are not; this work belongs only to the spiritual.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the spiritual person is judged by no one, with a clear comparison.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul held back the more perfect teaching because the Corinthians were unsteady infants who could not yet take in mysteries.
comments.comment: “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as to spiritual men, but as to men of the flesh, as to infants in Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:1). It was not for want of a word strong enough to raise you to perfect knowledge that I was kept from speaking to you of the more perfect things. It was because you are infants in your condition and have an unsteady mind, one that has not yet advanced to the knowledge of the more perfect things and cannot yet take in mysteries.
comments.selected_reason: States plainly why Paul gave the Corinthians simple teaching.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Believers who are not yet spiritual need simpler teaching, called milk, while the more demanding lessons on conduct and on God are solid food.
comments.comment:
… of hearers some are perfect—the spiritual … and those who are not spiritual yet believe in Christ are, as the apostle says, infants in Christ and fleshly in Christ—for I hear “in Christ” as common to both. … So those not yet more perfect and not yet exercised in the sacred Scriptures need lesser lessons, which the apostle named milk: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able, but neither are you able even now.” … What then is not solid food? The more ethical teachings and whatever among ethical matters is weaker—said by way of concession, not by command, stewarded because of the hearers’ weakness. But whatever more perfect teaching among ethical matters belongs to eager and hardworking hearers—these I would call solid food among ethical teachings: teaching about perfect chastity, about virginity or temperance, about martyrdom; these are solid food. And solid food in mystical matters is teaching about Father and Son.

So also the law sometimes hands on solid food, sometimes lesser. For example we come to the word about the snakes that killed the sons of Israel because of murmuring: if we read more simply, we say, “Let us not murmur, as some of them murmured and were destroyed by the snakes.” But if the hearer can hear a mystical word, we say who the snakes are and who the snake hung upon the wood, and how one is saved by looking to that snake—and so with each spiritual Scripture.
comments.selected_reason: Explains milk and solid food in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Scripture elsewhere speaks of spiritual milk for infants and solid food for the perfect.
comments.comment: [Peter will show in his first] letter when he says, “Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk”; and in Hebrews also, “You have become ones who need milk and not solid food; for everyone who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, because they are infants; but solid food is for the perfect, who because of habit have their senses exercised toward distinguishing good and evil.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Teaching about conduct, with light commands such as honoring parents, is milk, while the proclamation of the divine doctrines is meat.
comments.comment: He still calls the teaching concerning ethics and the believing through signs 'milk' in a figurative sense, but the proclamation of the divine dogmas is 'meat'. Light commands can be milk, such as honoring father and mother, and not committing adultery, and the like, and 'come here, follow me'. Then, having said, 'You are fleshly, and walk according to man', he says that you honor things in man and do not seek the things of God.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Jealousy and strife are among the lesser sins, and they mark a person as fleshly, living by ordinary human standards rather than by God's.
comments.comment: … among human sins the lesser ones are jealousy and strife. If someone is in fornication, such a person is no longer fleshly but worse than fleshly. … I think there is a difference between fleshly and earthy: “As we bore the image of the earthy,” he says, “let us also bear the image of the heavenly.” So if you sin unto death, you are not fleshly but earthy; but if you sin, yet not unto death, you are not wholly earthy nor fallen away from the grace of Christ, but then you are fleshly. And of our walks, one is according to a human, another according to God. If we walk as most humans do, we walk according to a human; but if according to “Let your light shine before humans,” we differ from the many and do not walk according to a human. So the life is clear to the one who can see what is according to a human and what according to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by fleshly and walking according to a human.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who boast of belonging to Paul or Apollos live in a merely human way, and those who lean toward a sinner fall even lower.
comments.comment: For whenever someone says, “I am of Paul,” “I am of Apollos,” “I am of Cephas”—let us also attend to these. We shall see that sometimes we are not even humans but worse than humans. For the one who then said “I am of Apollos” was speaking of a learned and holy and blessed man; the one who said “I am of Paul,” of a sacred and blessed apostle. But sometimes leanings arise not like the leaning toward Paul or Apollos, but someone leans toward a sinner and sometimes toward a heterodox person. So if those are humans and walk according to flesh who say “I am of Apollos” and “I of Paul,” whenever you say you belong to someone lesser, clearly you are no longer even a human but worse than human; and perhaps it will be said to you, “Brood of vipers.”
comments.selected_reason: Shows why party loyalty to teachers falls below even human standards.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Planting is the beginning of faith, acknowledging God as Lord of all, and watering is the teaching that nourishes the believer's mind.
comments.comment: “I planted” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Paul planted, Apollos watered, and God called them to growth. What, then, is the planting, if not what belongs to the beginning of faith: to acknowledge and to say that God is the Lord of all? And what is the watering, if not the sowing and pouring in, as it were, of the words that come from teaching, which nourish the believer’s mind to strength so that it may also prove fruitful?
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear, simple meaning for planting and watering.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul planted and Apollos watered only alongside God and Christ, who plant and water first, so we must bear fruit.
comments.comment: … if Paul planted, he planted together with God who plants first of all; if Apollos watered, he watered together with Christ who waters first of all; for God plants—therefore it is written, “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted,” and again, “My Father is the farmer.” So let us bear fruit lest we be cut down like the barren fig tree. For every tree not producing good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.
comments.selected_reason: Shows that the human workers share in God's own work.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul speaks first of farming and then of building, and he names the faith and its proclamation as the foundation.
comments.comment: The things spoken to him were as if concerning agriculture, and the others as if concerning building. He himself said he has planted and has given the beginning and has laid the foundation of God. He exhorts those building after him at the foundation, so that they do not work the building in vain. And he calls the foundation the faith and the proclamation.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Growth from Christ is the Spirit's strengthening, given in proportion to each person's eagerness.
comments.comment: And what is the growth that comes from Christ, if not the strengthening given through the Spirit and the rising up “to a mature man” (Ephesians 4:13), granted in proportion to each one’s diligence and eagerness?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because Christ redeemed believers with his blood, they belong to him alone, even though others serve as their ministers and teachers.
comments.comment: “You are God’s field, God’s building” (1 Corinthians 3:9). Since Christ redeemed us with his precious blood (1 Peter 1:19), having endured the death of the flesh, we surely belong to him who bought us, and to no others, even if some have become for us ministers, reconcilers, mediators, and teachers of the mysteries of the grace that comes from him. That is why we are named after no others, but after Christ alone, who is also our Lord.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why believers are God's, not their teachers'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul, as a wise master builder, founded the church in Corinth, where no one had been before, and others build upon it.
comments.comment: … since we are not only a field but also God’s building, I seek the master builder of the building and those who work with him. Understanding this the apostle says, “According to the grace given me, as a wise master builder I laid a foundation”; for Paul established the church in Corinth that before the apostle was in no way present. And since there were divisions among them he says that, grace having been given him by God, as a wise master builder he laid the foundation, and another builds upon it …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who laid the foundation and who builds on it.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul calls Christ the foundation because he called believers God's house, and he boasts of being first among the Corinthians' teachers.
comments.comment: “Like a wise master builder I laid a foundation” (1 Corinthians 3:10). Since he called believers the house of God, he fittingly names Christ the foundation. There had been many teachers among the Corinthians, but Paul boasts that he was the first of them all, a kind of firstfruits among those who preached to them the mystery of Christ. Christ is the unshakable foundation. He holds up those who are built upon him and shows them to be temples, fitted together with one another through faith (Ephesians 2:21) and brought together into one mind by the grace of the Holy Spirit. Of this foundation God the Father spoke through the prophet: “Behold, I lay in the foundations of Zion a costly stone, a precious cornerstone, in her foundations; and whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame” (Isaiah 28:16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the building image and Paul's part in it.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul is a wise master builder because he preached where Christ was not yet named, and his letters serve as architectural laws for the church.
comments.comment: So if you want to see that Paul is a wise master builder, hear him: “From Jerusalem and as far as Illyricum I have fulfilled the gospel of God, making it my ambition to preach the gospel not where Christ was named, so that I might not build upon another’s foundation.” And he not only laid a foundation as a wise master builder, but also wrote, as it were, architectural books—how the master builder must build a house, what sort the overseer must be, and elders and deacons and the rest of the church’s fullness; for all these were as it were architectural laws.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Others may build on the foundation Paul laid but cannot lay another, and whoever refuses Christ builds on sand and will fall.
comments.comment: So Paul says, and very rightly, that he himself laid the foundation, and that others can work on it and build upon it, but can no longer lay another beside the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3:11). … If anyone, then, denies the foundation and refuses the rock, he does not build on it but on the sand (Matthew 7:24–27), and so he will very easily be shaken down. For what Christ does not hold up will surely be moved, since it has no firm footing.
comments.selected_reason: Makes the force of 'no other foundation' clear.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Once Christ was preached the foundation was laid for good, so no one can lay another, and teachers build on it with gold, silver and precious stone, or with wood, hay and straw.
comments.comment: From the time my Lord Jesus Christ sojourned, this foundation has been preached into the world; and the apostles laid this foundation in Judea, and among the nations the apostle of the nations and his fellow worker Barnabas—“for they gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, that we to the nations and they to the circumcision.” So once Jesus Christ the Word of God has been preached and this foundation laid, no one can lay another foundation besides Jesus Christ; and those who build upon it, if they are orthodox through everlasting doctrines and divine thoughts and good words and holy deeds, build upon the foundation gold, silver, precious stone. For gold has often been kept, taken for mind and thoughts; if I speak well, I build silver; if I interpret as I ought and urge hearers well toward a way of life, I build precious stones. … Yet as many of those who teach Jesus Christ have missed the truth, they have built upon the foundation wood, hay, straw; and I would say that of those from the heresies the more blasphemous are wood, those who sinned less in teaching are hay, and those with thin and, so to speak, lesser faults are straw.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is the foundation of the faith, and whoever teaches on him builds either with the purity of gold or with the weakness of grass.
comments.comment:
Christ is not called the foundation of the creation, as the Arians falsely contend, but of the faith; for Christ was proclaimed, and every building happens upon him as the foundation. While some are teaching one faith and proclaiming the evangelical life, for us it is to make ourselves either precious stones or wood or grass or a reed.

… The one teaching proclaims Christ and gives his commands; therefore it is to be separated either by gold because of purity, or by grass because of weakness.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala
