comments.capsule: Each believer builds on Christ the foundation: good thoughts are gold, pure words silver, good deeds precious stone, and sins are wood, hay and straw.
comments.comment: Come, let us also see it according to the letter. What will be said touches each of us; each of us, having received the word of the gospel, received Jesus Christ as foundation, so that in all he does and says and thinks he may build upon this foundation. So if we think and intend good things, we build gold; if speaking purely we say every word spoken in a holy way, we build as silver; if every deed we do is good, we build as precious stone—and God judges the worth and quality of the stones. Yet if I sin after the foundation, my great sins will be wood, the lesser hay, and the still lesser straw. …
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear picture of what the gold and the straw stand for.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A teacher must build carefully, since bringing worthless souls into the church adds wood, hay and straw, and the fire will test every work.
comments.comment: For this also speaks to me, so that I may not build carelessly, knowing that the work I build—what sort it is—the fire itself will test on that day. And I take care lest, building, I build wood, hay, straw. For if I bring worthless souls uncritically into the church, I have brought to the good foundation Christ Jesus wood, and others hay, and others straw; just as again, if some shine out from the building, and shine so much that some are found analogous to what is written about Jerusalem and the temple—chosen stones and crystal stone and sapphire stones and whatever stones are named there—clearly I have built precious stones upon the foundation. … And since God’s temple and building must also have gold, as the temple Solomon built is a symbol of a temple having much gold and silver, if another comes being built up and is found more precious than silver, he would be gold. … But I fear lest through me wood and hay and straw enter, and wretched I (even if otherwise judged worthy of salvation—since it is written, “yet he himself will be saved, but so as through fire”) be saved in this way as one who became a cause, by not holding the grace nor building well, of filling the building with wood, hay, straw, which the word of God does not want; for the fire will test what sort each one’s work is.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God, as fire, consumes wickedness, and wood, hay and straw are figures for the deeds of the wicked, so the fire that tests them is not a material fire.
comments.comment: So when he is said to be “a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy 4:24), we ask what it is fitting for God to consume. And we say that God, as fire, consumes wickedness and the deeds that spring from it, which are figuratively called “wood” and “hay” and “straw.” For the wicked man is said to “build” “wood” and “hay” and “straw” upon the rational foundation already laid (1 Corinthians 3:10–12). Now if anyone can show that the writer meant these words otherwise, and can present the wicked man as building “wood” or “hay” or “straw” in a bodily sense, then clearly the fire too will be understood as material and perceptible. But if the works of the wicked man are plainly spoken of figuratively when they are called “wood” or “hay” or “straw,” how is it not obvious at once what kind of fire is meant, by which such “wood” is to be consumed? For he says: “The fire itself will test what sort of work each one has done. If anyone’s work that he has built upon it remains, he will receive a reward; if anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss” (1 Corinthians 3:13–15). And what work burned up could be meant in these words, if not everything done out of wickedness?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The church is God's temple made of living stones, and each stone must fit with the rest in one mind so that the building holds together.
comments.comment:
If you want to learn what the true temple of God is, seek living stones, cleanly quarried, set in place by the Word, standing four-square, with nothing unstable or rolling. For even if holy stones roll on the earth, the stonecutters do not let them keep rolling to the end. So you, as living stones, are being built into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.

And with the Apostle it is said that all of us are one temple, each of us a stone of the temple. So he speaks in Ephesians: “So then you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow-citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone, in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord, in whom you also are being built together into a dwelling of God in the Spirit.”

So no stone must be ill-fitted to the building. For if two of you agree on earth about any matter they ask, it will be done for them by my Father in heaven—how much more, then, if all the stones agree in one harmony and all share one heart and one soul, will their prayer be able and strong? It is good, then, that we all say the same thing, that we may be fitted together in the same mind and the same judgment; for so you are a building fitted together into a holy temple in the Lord.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the temple image in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Each person is a temple of God to the degree he has God's glory in himself, but no one with a spirit of sin can be one.
comments.comment: And in another sense each of us can be a temple by himself. For if a temple is what has God’s glory, everyone who has God’s glory in himself is in that respect God’s temple. One has more glory or less who makes the name of the Father in heaven glorified by his deeds; therefore it is written, “Those who glorify me I will glorify.” Then we will most of all be God’s temple if we prepare ourselves to receive the Spirit of God. Yet no one who has a spirit of some sin can be God’s temple, because the Spirit of God alone dwells where he judges it right to dwell.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear second sense of the temple.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who trust outside wisdom instead of the indwelling Teacher destroy the temple of God, which is the faith.
comments.comment:
Again, he turns to those who trust in their own wisdom. For while he calls the believers the temple of God, he also says that one destroys the temple of God. He will declare the following to those who trust in words. If anyone thinks to be wise in this present age, let him become a fool. For why then does the one trusting in external wisdom destroy the temple? If you are a temple of God, you owe it to have one who teaches and reveals; but if, having left the Inhabitant, you have used your own understanding, you no longer make a temple, but you destroy it.

… Therefore, those receiving a different teaching from external wisdom, these have destroyed their own reasoning, corrupting the faith, which is the temple of the Spirit. Consequently, God threatens that these will be destroyed, because having abandoned the indwelling Teacher, they wandered regarding external wisdom, which is sufficient to provide a supply of deception.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Anyone who sins ruins God's temple, anyone who puts a stumbling-block before the church does so, and the fornicator does so most of all.
comments.comment: “If anyone ruins God’s temple, God will ruin him.” As far as each person can, even if he is a stone, he ruins God’s temple when he sins; and anyone who puts a stumbling-block before the church also ruins God’s temple. Still more properly the one who fornicates ruins God’s temple, since your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, which you have from God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to ruin God's temple.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's destroying the one who destroys the temple is a testing, and the loss in view is a punishment, which is also called corruption.
comments.comment: 'if anyone destroys the temple of God, God destroys him' (1 Cor 3:17). God destroys by testing. And just as the name of loss is taken in two ways regarding the soul, we say both that the sinner suffers loss and that the one being punished suffers loss: 'fear him' (Matt 10:28) who 'is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.' Here, loss is a punishment, which is also called corruption.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Becoming a fool in this age, as the world calls it, is how a person becomes truly wise, since the world's wisdom is folly with God.
comments.comment: But because the Corinthians were proud of the world’s wisdom, he says to them, “If anyone among you thinks he is wise”—not “if anyone is wise,” but “thinks he is wise among you”—“in this age let him become a fool.” He did not say simply “a fool,” but “in this age,” as people call us fools relative to this age. So let him become a fool in this age, that by becoming a fool to this age he may become truly wise; for the wisdom of this world is folly with God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says 'in this age'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: There is a human wisdom, called the wisdom of the world, which is foolishness with God, and a divine wisdom that God gives to those fit to receive it.
comments.comment: … there is a divine wisdom and a human one. The human is what we call “the wisdom of the world,” which is “foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3:19). But the divine, which differs from the human, if it is indeed divine, comes by the grace of God, who gives it to those who have made themselves fit to receive it, and above all to those who know how each wisdom differs from the other …
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear distinction between worldly and divine wisdom.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Greek and barbarian philosophy is folly wherever it disagrees with Christ's teaching, and the Lord catches the wise through Paul and shows their reasonings to be futile.
comments.comment:
And when you examine all Greek and barbarian philosophy simply, you will say that wherever it disagrees with Christ’s teaching it is folly. For it is written, “He catches the wise in their craftiness.”

I say it is no great thing if God, as God, catches the wise in their craftiness—but rather in Paul, who says, “For though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh; for the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly but powerful with God for the tearing down of strongholds, tearing down reasonings and every height raised against the knowledge of God.” To understand this more clearly, picture Paul arriving in Athens and seeking opportunity among those he meets, so that some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers even clash with him; then by Christ’s grace he was catching hold of them and exposing their sophisms. Here I take “the wise” to mean the sophists—whoever spins entangled sophisms and does not teach truth.

And again: “The Lord knows the reasonings of the wise, that they are futile.” It is no wonder if the Lord, by himself, knows that the reasonings of the wise are futile. But I want the Lord, come to be in me, to know that the reasonings of the wise are futile. For if Christ comes to be in me, he can set beside me how the reasonings of this world’s wise are futile, and how God’s wisdom alone shines, conquering and trampling every seeming wisdom.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how God catches the wise, with the example of Paul.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Everything is ours: death as our dying to sin, the present as gathering, hearing Scripture and praying, and the future once the present becomes ours.
comments.comment: The one who can renounce all human beings and become wholly worthy of the boast that is in Christ does not boast in a human being. How, then, is death mine? So that I may die to sin; so that I may say, “If we died with him, we will also live with him.” For the other death—by which the sinning soul itself will die—is not mine. Present things too are ours: that we gather in the present age, hear the holy Scriptures, pray. And the future: when the perfect comes, then what is in part will be done away. And it is not possible to come to the future unless the present first becomes mine.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'all things are yours' item by item.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: All things belong to the faithful, who know the God who made them, and not even an obol to the unfaithful, who hold what they hold like a robber.
comments.comment: “All things are yours.” Among the Greeks a saying of this sort is admired: “All things belong to the wise, and nothing to the worthless.” But the word of God first taught that all things belong to the holy. Of the faithful, then, he says, the whole world of goods; of the unfaithful, not even an obol. For the unfaithful holds what he holds as a robber: not knowing how to use these things, nor knowing the God who made them, nor hearing the one who says, “Mine is the silver and mine the gold,” he does not hold them as his own.
comments.selected_reason: Makes the claim that all things are the believer's concrete.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A servant of Christ may serve in a common ministry, but a steward of God's mysteries must know them and prepare each hearer before speaking.
comments.comment: The one who has not crossed over in the word to the grasp of the mysteries hidden in Scripture can be a servant of Christ, but cannot be a steward of God’s mysteries. For the steward has what is administered and knows the mysteries of God. Perhaps, then, the servant of Christ is understood according to the more common ministry, while the steward of God’s mysteries is understood according to the management that concerns the mysteries once known—so that he does not toss them about at random, nor hand them over unexamined, but first cleanses, prepares, and draws away from the world the one who is about to hear supra-worldly lessons, and only then speaks them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between servants and stewards.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A clear conscience does not prove Paul justified, because he may have overlooked some ignorance, and only God's judgment settles it.
comments.comment: “I do not consider myself my own conscience, but not in this have I been justified” (cf. 1 Cor 4:4). For it enters into me to overlook something of the ignorances, and I have not been justified because of that. And as far as I think I have no conscience against myself, I think I am without responsibility. But it is not my judgment that shows me having been justified, but the judgment of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Do not avenge or judge now: at his coming the Lord will reveal the hidden things and the hearts, and the faithful will have praise from God.
comments.comment: He exhorts not to be eager to avenge oneself, nor to judge those who seem to have sinned, nor to be troubled by the faces of mortals who are currently deceiving (1 Cor 4:4–5). For the Lord himself, at his coming, will shine light on the hidden things of the ungodly in the darkness, and will reveal the purposes of the hearts of the orderly and God-fearing ones who act with moderation and without self-will, even though they are currently acting in secret; to these, he says that praise shall come from God (1 Cor 4:5).
comments.selected_reason: Plain summary of what Paul asks and why.
comments.author: Eusebius of Emesa

comments.capsule: Church judges may remove someone for the church's good, but no one may anticipate God's judgment, which no one can measure because hearts and reasonings are hidden.
comments.comment:
So do the Scriptures have contradictions, and must we both judge and not judge under the same sense of judgment? If those entrusted to judge those inside do not judge those inside, the church is about to become, instead of God’s church, a synagogue of evildoers. Then, with those inside being judged, how is “Do not judge, that you may not be judged” true?

We say, then: those entrusted to judge those inside are not so senseless that, when judging those inside, they claim, “We are judging God’s judgment.” Rather, they make the judgment with a view to the stewardship of what benefits the church. If it benefits that this person be put out of the assembly, having judged that, they do it. And again they will take their stand toward what benefits—not judging God’s judgment, but the judgment given them. For the judgment that God judges in Christ it is impossible for us to judge; we neither search hearts nor know with what reasonings each person’s deeds were done. The hidden things the judges according to the Gospel leave to the Lord God; the manifest things, as it is said, “to you and to your children.” Whatever has reached them and is known among them, these they judge.

So never anticipating God’s judgment let us say, “So-and-so is lost,” or, blessing, “So-and-so is saved.” For we do not know how to measure and compare deeds with deeds, or reasonings, or thoughts.
comments.selected_reason: Answers how not judging before the time fits with judging in the church.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The hidden things of darkness may be our sins and the purposes of the hearts our good deeds, since we sin in darkness but do good with counsel.
comments.comment: Of two things named, there ought to be a difference between them: some he called hidden things of darkness, others purposes of hearts. See, then, whether our sins are hidden things of darkness, and our brave deeds purposes of the hearts. For whatever we do well we do with counsel; but whatever we sin, we sin being in darkness. … For we must all be made manifest before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what was done through the body, whether good or worthless.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul speaks only of praise from God because blame for wrongdoing comes from the devil, not from God.
comments.comment: Someone who investigates everything might ask: why did he not say, “And then praise or blame will come to each from God,” but only “the praise”? One will explain it this way: he attached the more favorable word to God, keeping silent about the rest as not fitting him. But I will dare to say that God praises and accepts the good, while our evils the father of evils—the devil—does; and praise from God comes to the saints, while blame for those who have done blameworthy things comes from the devil. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says only praise will come from God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul's words about himself and Apollos warn every generation not to split over teachers as divided theater crowds split over performances.
comments.comment: These things are written in a transfer shaped to the circumstances then—not so that we may know them only about Paul and Apollos, but so that in every generation, seeing what happens analogously to these things, we may take care lest we too fall into such things and, as in theaters that split over performances, we split over teachers.
comments.selected_reason: Applies Paul's warning in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Anyone who tries to rise beyond what is written before fulfilling it will not understand it, just as one cannot climb a ladder without the lower steps.
comments.comment: But let us see the line, “So that in us you may learn, ‘Not beyond what is written.’” If someone with a lesser habit, before fulfilling what is written, wants to ascend to what is beyond what is written, he will not even understand what is written. For just as it is not possible to climb a ladder except by going the way from the lower steps according to one’s ability, so also with the divine lessons.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear picture of what 'not beyond what is written' means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul asks 'Already you are filled?' because someone who leans on one teacher is not helped by all, and he says 'without us' to include himself with the other teachers.
comments.comment: Since, then, “being filled” suggests that when there are more teachers—Paul teaching, and Cephas, and Apollos—one who leans to one is not helped by all, therefore he says to the Corinthians, “Already you are filled?” Following this is “Already you have become rich?”—as in, “Have you gathered the wealth from Paul’s lessons and no longer need those from Apollos or from Cephas?” Or do you despise all, as stuffed and rich in every word and all knowledge? And following also: “Without us you have begun to reign?” For as far as you could you cut me off from the kingdom—and yourselves too—leaning to one from among the rest. And he does not say “without me” but “without us,” so as to include and make it common; “and would that you did reign, so that we might also reign with you.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains the sense of 'filled' and 'without us'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The lesser reach the promise sooner and the more perfect later, so that the teachers and hearers arrive at the perfect kingdom together.
comments.comment: At once, perhaps, he also suggests a mystery at this place. For the lesser come more quickly into the promise, while the more perfect receive the promises later. And I will show this from Scripture: those allotted under Moses first received the promise; those allotted under Joshua later. And of all the righteous it is said, “These all, having been attested through faith, did not receive the promise, God having foreseen something better concerning us, so that they would not be perfected apart from us.” Therefore he says, “Without us you have begun to reign? And would that you did reign, so that we might also reign with you.” For when you the disciples and hearers reign, then it is necessary that we also arrive at the perfect kingdom of God and the Lord Jesus.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The higher a person's place in truth, the lower he makes himself out of humility, as Paul did when he called himself least of the saints.
comments.comment: The more one claims the true and heavenly first places, so much the more, from humility, he becomes last of all human beings. I think the Apostle meant something like this when he said, “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given.” Not that in holiness he was less than all the saints—for he neither thought this, nor if he said it would he speak truly—but among all believers he made himself lower, becoming gentle in the midst of all, as a nurse cherishes her own children.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul describes the apostles as last.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The apostles chose to be last but needed God's grace to be shown last, and those who live most fully as Christians are most exposed to death.
comments.comment:
Since, then, the apostles practiced being last by their own choice—and for every good practice, unless God witnesses and fills the practitioner’s will, the good end does not follow through the practitioner—therefore perhaps the Apostle said, “For I think God has exhibited us apostles last, as sentenced to death.” For even if I, he says, and the apostles have acted so that we become last, we still needed exhibition and grace from God to be perfected in being last to the world. And “I think” is as elsewhere he said, “I think I too have the Spirit of God.”

Fitting also for those exhibited last by God is becoming first with God; for it is true that the last become first. Fitting also for them is being sentenced to death. For the more perfectly one lives as a Christian, so much more is he death-bound. When does he not risk danger—reproving the sinner who is often stronger in life and able to punish, visiting places where Christ was not named, and laying a foundation strange and disturbing to hearers? Truly Paul said, “I die daily—by your boast which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Sentenced to death can mean carrying about Jesus' dying in the body, or being conformed to Christ's death by always dying to the world.
comments.comment: But as I search the word, “sentenced to death” can be taken two ways: one the way already said, by which one must always carry about the dying of Jesus in the body; another, the righteous is death-bound, being conformed to the death of Christ, always dying to the world. So it is fitting that God exhibit the apostles of Christ as both last and sentenced to death.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Angels hurry to watch a human being in flesh wrestle against the principalities.
comments.comment: Then one must see “because we have become a spectacle to the world and to angels and to human beings.” If Paul contends and Peter, the angels of God hurry to this new spectacle to see a human being clothed in flesh wrestling against the principalities …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul was a new spectacle to people and to the angels who rejoice over a sinner repenting.
comments.comment: [A human being wrestles] against the authorities, against the world-rulers of this world, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. And human beings also came to see a new spectacle—a herald and teacher of a new word. Thus Paul was a spectacle of all on earth and of the angels who rejoice over one sinner repenting.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul calls himself a fool for Christ, and says 'you are wise in Christ' ironically to urge the Corinthians to become wise in Christ.
comments.comment: Then such a one, as last in the world, rebukes the puffed up and says to them, “We are fools for Christ.” For Paul, giving me a command and saying, “If anyone among you thinks he is wise in this age, let him become a fool, that he may become wise,” much more himself kept becoming a fool in this world. For how was he not a fool in this world—announcing the crucified one and the resurrection of the dead and the things about the coming age, and persuading people to despise the present life? Then with irony: “You are wise in Christ.” For they were not truly wise in Christ; but saying this ironically he urged them to become wise in Christ. “You are honored, but we are dishonored”—he no longer added “you are honored in Christ.” For if you see many who seem to believe holding worldly ranks, say to them, if you yourself are humble in the world, “You are honored, but we are dishonored; we are weak, but you are strong.” For nothing is weaker than a true Christian as toward this world.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the irony in Paul's contrasts.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A father is the one who first sowed Christianity in a soul, and a guardian is the one who afterward receives the child and leads him.
comments.comment: No man is put under a guardian unless he is a child and incomplete. And he would not write these things to the Ephesians but to the Corinthians, to whom he says, “I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able. But neither are you able even now, for you are still fleshly.” And: “I could not speak to you as to spiritual people but as to fleshly, as to infants in Christ.” Still this too must be noted: if we need a guardian, the one entrusted must give the pattern—the word, the life—to our good order. So a father is the one who first sowed Christianity in a soul; a guardian is the one after him who receives the child and leads him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between a guardian and a father.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul urges the Corinthians to imitate his moderation and suffering, and sends Timothy to remind them, not teach them, since they had seen his virtue themselves.
comments.comment: “I urge you, then, brothers, become imitators of me.” That is: as I practice moderation, practice it; as I suffer, suffer; boast from sufferings, not from gifts. … “For this reason I sent you Timothy, who is my beloved child and faithful in Christ, who will remind you of my ways in Christ, as I teach everywhere in every church.” He showed both his disposition toward them by sending Timothy, and his affection for Timothy by naming him beloved child; and his other virtue by calling him faithful in the Lord. This one, he says, will recount my deeds; for he calls deeds “ways.” These he did not say “he will teach,” but that “he will remind.” The word charges them with forgetfulness; for they had been eyewitnesses of apostolic virtue. He added that he is accustomed to bring this teaching to all the churches.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what imitating Paul means and why Timothy is sent.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Foreseeing the offender's repentance, Paul says 'some' and does not name him, so he is not known to everyone.
comments.comment: Having charged all in common, against the one who fornicated he then issues the vote. … “Some are arrogant, as though I were not coming to you.” Foreseeing his repentance, the divine Paul does not set the name, lest he become known to all human beings, but indefinitely said “some.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Some in Corinth thought they needed no teachers and that Paul stayed away from fear of arguing with them, but he will come.
comments.comment: “Some have become puffed up, as though I were not coming to you” (1 Corinthians 4:18). There were some in Corinth who thought themselves sufficient and in no need of teachers, and who thought they surpassed Paul in the wisdom of worldly eloquence. For this reason they were puffed up to the point of contempt and rose up against the others, though they themselves were not blameless in their lives. Paul means: Since some have become puffed up while I am away, and think that I stay away because I am afraid to come and face them in argument, which is not so, I will come, if God wills and permits.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the puffed up were and what Paul answers.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul promised to come but modestly added 'if the Lord wills', as we must always say.
comments.comment: “But I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills” (1 Corinthians 4:19). He promised to come, yet not without condition. As was fitting, he modestly added the needful words, “if the Lord wills.” For we must think and speak in this way, and in no other.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Brilliant pagan speech holds nothing good, while Scripture's simple speech gives profit, and the kingdom's power is the Spirit's working in the apostles and a holy life in us.
comments.comment: “And I will find out not the talk of those who are puffed up, but their power” (1 Corinthians 4:19). What is the use of brilliant speech that holds nothing good, such as the speech of the pagan Greeks? But the speech of the inspired Scripture is simple and ordinary, yet it gives rich profit and carries one splendidly to the true knowledge of him who is God by nature. It also makes people diligent in every admirable work. And when this has come about, a person may be enriched with the grace of the gifts given through the Spirit, a grace worth receiving. “For the kingdom of heaven is not in word but in power” (1 Corinthians 4:20). As for “in power,” if it is said of the holy apostles themselves, you will understand it as the strength and working that comes through the Spirit, by which they also work wonders. But if it is said of us, you will take it to mean the power of a holy and sincere life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the contrast between talk and power.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By talk Paul means fluent speech and by power what is from God, since the kingdom is where the word has power to drive sin out of souls.
comments.comment: By “talk” he means fluency of speech, as elsewhere, “even if unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge”; by “power,” that from God. For when the word is from God it has power; therefore it is written, “The Lord will give a word to those who evangelize with much power.” And trusting more in power, the apostles visited the churches and cities than in talk. For it is not that if someone phrases well he thereby has the kingdom of God; but where there is power in words, there is the kingdom of God—which also drives out the sin reigning in souls and prepares God’s kingdom to come within us.
comments.selected_reason: Explains talk and power in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The rod means a wise rebuke and gentleness means passing over the matter in silence, but rebuke was better because it cuts the sin off at once.
comments.comment: Paul says: Do you wish me to bring a wise rebuke upon those who have sinned, as with a rod? Or shall I deal with you in a spirit of gentleness, as in love, and pass the matter by in silence (1 Corinthians 4:21)? But rebuke was better for them, for it would cut off at once the dreadful sin, the slackness, and the very attempt at such lawlessness. Of this the inspired Scripture also spoke concerning the people of Israel, through the voice of Joel: “A son and his father went in to the same girl, so as to profane the name of their God” (Amos 2:7).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the choice between the rod and love.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul had likely heard Greek tales like that of Theseus, who killed his son over the stepmother, and others the poets mocked on like charges.
comments.comment: He says that such fornication is not heard of even among the Gentiles (1 Corinthians 5:1). For he had heard somewhere, we may suppose, of Theseus, who was roused to fury against his own son, cursed him, and even killed him, after the stepmother had set him against the boy; and of certain others whom the poets in their fine verse mocked on similar charges.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Such things are heard among the Corinthians as are not even found among the Gentiles, so they should mourn instead of boasting.
comments.comment:
He does not allow one to be moved by glory without reason, and he brings forward the cause of the wrath, because not only fornication, but such things are heard among you as are not even among the Gentiles. …

It is necessary to mourn over him because he has not even dared to make fornication common to others. For this mourning either separated the fornicator, who remained in fornication, or it separated the impropriety itself and brought the man back, so that the spirit might be saved.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul was a prophet as well as an apostle, so he can be present in spirit, with the power of Jesus present too.
comments.comment: [Paul says he is present in spirit.] Such was Elisha. Even when he was not present in the body, he went along with Gehazi in the spirit and said to him: “Was not my heart with you when he took the two talents of silver and the garments from Naaman the Syrian?” (2 Kings 5:26). … Did Elisha then have this gift, while Paul, the apostle of Christ who was zealous for the greater gifts—and above all that he might prophesy—did not have such a gift? I declare, and I speak with confidence, that Paul was not only an apostle but also a prophet. … Having this gift, then, even if he was absent in the body, wherever he wished he was present in the spirit; for he was not alone present in the spirit, but the power of Jesus was also present.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by being absent in body but present in spirit, with a clear Old Testament parallel.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul could have condemned the man alone, but he wants the Corinthians to agree with him so that they are built up.
comments.comment: He did not say 'not having worked' but 'having worked it out,' even so that by this it might appear that, having used much endurance, he worked out the evil, and was not snatched away by sin, so that he might have a defense. Indeed, the apostle alone was sufficient to condemn him, but he wants the Corinthians to be in agreement with him, so that he might thus build up, being separated from the fellowship of the lawless, especially those nurtured in instruction.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Handing a man over to Satan means handing him over to the hardships of life, so that his spirit may be saved.
comments.comment:
He does not do this as one subjecting him to the authority of Satan—for if he were inflating this by doing so, he would be puffing up Satan—but because we have become accustomed to assigning all the difficult things of life to Satan, such as diseases, sorrows, griefs, and other trials, just as the apostle himself says: 'A thorn of Satan was given to me, so that he might lash me.' In this very way, he now commands him to hand him over to Satan, which is to say, to the difficulties of life.

He delivers him to the harms of life; for this is for the destruction of the flesh, not for the destruction of the soul, so that, being awakened by the things happening to the body, he might repent and the spirit within him, which is the gift, might be saved.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what 'deliver to Satan' means and why Paul does it.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Handing the fornicator over for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved, shows the power Paul was given from above.
comments.comment: “To deliver such a man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh” (1 Corinthians 5:5). By handing over the fornicator to the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved, Paul showed what is meant by “The kingdom of heaven is not in word but in power” (1 Corinthians 4:20). For this is a clear sign of the marvelous authority given to him from above. For our Lord Jesus Christ has honored the saints.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The man is expelled so that others are not led on to sin.
comments.comment: … you see that they were boasting over him, not paying attention to the impropriety of the fall, but being puffed up by his conceit. … He commands him to be expelled, so that the others, joining with him in sinning, might not be incited shamelessly.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul calls sin old leaven, and the unleavened bread of the Jews stands for new men not leavened with the sins of the old man.
comments.comment: … he calls sin an old leaven, with which the old man was leavened together. He moves the type to the truth; for the unleavened things among the Jews, not having been leavened with old leaven, represent the new men, not having been leavened with the sins of the old man. The lamb being sacrificed among the Jews revealed the passion and the cross as a mystery of the economy [God's plan of salvation].
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Keeping the feast means putting off the old man and searching oneself for leaven, as the Jews search their houses.
comments.comment: The one who has put off the old man with his deeds and has nothing of the old leaven in himself, but has made a new lump according to Christ Jesus, has kept the feast of unleavened bread. … Teaching about these things the apostle says: “Clean out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened.” … Something of this sort happens among the Jews: when the day of unleavened bread dawns, they clean out all old leaven, searching every place of the house lest leaven be found there. In the same way you also examine the storehouses within yourself lest leaven be there somewhere, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened. Since in Corinth some were holy and others were not such but sinners—as we said earlier in the preface of the letter—on account of the praiseworthy ones he says “as you are unleavened.” For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Seeing that according to the law of Moses the Passover comes first and the lamb is slain, and then after the lamb they eat unleavened bread, for this reason he said: Already the Passover has been sacrificed—Christ. Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth—sincerity according to the way of life, truth according to knowledge; for in both the true unleavened bread is characterized.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the picture behind Paul's words: clearing out leaven as a model for cleansing one's own life.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The feast calls for a life with no old leaven mixed in.
comments.comment: … he admonished in this way, as if he were saying: not in an evil and bad life, but in a life not having mixture with that old leaven; for this is in unleavened bread, sincerity and truth.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Some think Paul wrote an earlier letter that is lost, and that here he explains that he did not mean the immoral of the world.
comments.comment: Some have supposed from this saying that before the former letter to the Corinthians another letter had been written by the apostle which is not now preserved; and that he wrote to them not to associate with the sexually immoral, so far as the present wording goes. But having heard that the Corinthians were disturbed, thinking he meant they must not associate even with the immoral of the world—which is impossible, for one who lives in the world cannot avoid dealing with Gentile coworkers, traders, and others of that sort—he clarifies, they say, what had then been left out: I do not mean the immoral of this world, but those who are named brothers yet are not honorable.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul's earlier instruction meant and why he clarifies it.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Others say the letter meant is this one, and that the immoral inside the church are far worse than outsiders.
comments.comment: [Those who deny a lost earlier letter say that Paul's words refer to] this letter itself: that in this letter I wrote that you should not associate with the sexually immoral—and by “immoral” I mean these, not those. The apostle seems by comparison of fornicators to say that those among us who are immoral are far worse. For the outsider who fornicates does not destroy a temple of God, does not make the members of Christ members of a prostitute, and does not leaven the whole lump.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul wrote in this letter, and he does not forbid contact with outsiders, which would hinder the preaching.
comments.comment: … he wrote not in another letter, but in this one. Because of this, he does not forbid those outside from eating, since if he were turning away all such people, the preaching would be hindered; for all such people, as it is said, are among the Gentiles whom it happened to benefit from the fellowship of those having believed. He therefore shows to strike those at home who sin, and to exhort those who have been rebuked.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The church has immoral, greedy and idolatrous people as well as the world, and Paul calls such a one brother in name only.
comments.comment: And not at all with the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy, or robbers, or idolaters. Just as there are fornicators of the world and fornicators called to Christ, so also there are greedy people of this world and of the church. Let us therefore guard against greed even in the smallest matters; for it too is yoked to the sin of fornication. And third he names certain robbers, when they seize what belongs to their neighbors. And there are also some idolaters among us besides the idolaters of this world—those who want to teach that idolatry is a matter of indifference. This sin is found especially among those in military service. They say: Necessity is laid on me; the army requires this; I risk my head if I do not sacrifice or, dressed in white, offer frankincense according to the customs of the world’s army—and such a one still calls himself a Christian. With such a one, he says, do not even eat. And the denier of God in a time of persecution is also an idolater among us. So he says: I wrote to such a one who is not yet out of the world not to associate, since otherwise you would need to go out of the world. But now I have written to you not to associate if anyone is named a brother. Well does he no longer call such a one a brother, but a brother only as far as the name.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between sinners of the world and sinners who bear the name of brother.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul counts the reviler with the fornicator, the greedy and the idolater, so the mouth must be kept clean.
comments.comment: These evils many of us can know in ourselves that we do not have. But at what follows I fear for myself as well, lest somehow I be liable to the other sins. For he says: or a reviler or a drunkard or a robber—with such a one do not even eat. With how great evils he numbered the reviler together with the fornicator, the greedy, and the idolater! Therefore the reviler too is already an enemy of the church. For this reason we hear the Lord saying: “Bless those who curse you” (Luke 6:28), and the apostle saying: “When reviled, we bless” (1 Corinthians 4:12); for a reviler will not inherit the kingdom of God. We must therefore keep the mouth clean.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The church judges those inside, but each person must first remove the wicked one from himself.
comments.comment: He has permitted all of us to judge those inside who sin. We ourselves bring the sin up to the bishop, that such a one may be cast out of the church by law. And you will remove the wicked person from among yourselves. From these too remove the wicked one; but seek lest, while wishing to remove the wicked from outside, you have the wicked one within yourself. Therefore do everything to remove the wicked from yourself; for when that one has gone out, Christ Jesus will dwell in you.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The command to remove the wicked is from Moses, so the practice is not new and frees the church as from a plague.
comments.comment: 'to purge the evil one from among yourselves' is a voice of Moses, which Paul repeats. He remembers a saying in the old text, showing that not only are they benefited as if being freed from some plague, but such a thing is not a novelty; rather, it also seemed good to the Lawgiver to cut off such people.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Saints are the sanctified, and the unrighteous have not yet believed.
comments.comment: He [Paul] calls saints those who have been sanctified in the Spirit, and unrighteous those who have not yet believed, since they are all too ready to go after any evil whatever.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The saints will judge the world by the dignity of their lives, leaving the world with no plea before God's judgment.
comments.comment: They will judge it, not by sitting in every case as judges on the bench, for “there is one Lawgiver and Judge” (James 4:12), but by the dignity of their life and their readiness to obey in everything. By this they all but pass sentence on the sin of the world, because the people of the world did not become their imitators. … For we are all of one nature: we have all been given the earth for a mother and live in these perishable bodies. But if some of us have become lovers of God and good, what plea will be left to help, before the divine judgment seat, those who chose an inglorious and accursed life? For though they could have been honored equally with the others, they went of their own will after every kind of outrage.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms how the saints judge the world.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By angels Paul means the fallen ones, who will be condemned by the saints, so the saints cannot be unworthy of petty courts.
comments.comment: For who would dare to say that you are unworthy of such petty courts (1 Corinthians 6:2), you who judge the world by the brightness of your life? Then he adds a reason for what he has said, and confirms the force of his argument by setting the greater case beside it. By angels here he does not mean the holy angels, but rather the apostates, who did not keep their own first rank (Jude 6). Though they were from above and not weighed down with bodies made from earth, they will be condemned by the saints in the same way as the world, through the goodness of the saints, and stand accused of every kind of shameful deed. If, then, the saints are better than angels, how could they be unworthy of the smallest courts, those that deal with worldly affairs?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Judging worldly matters is a small thing for upright believers, who are better suited to judge spiritual teaching.
comments.comment: To judge the matters of this life is a very small thing, worth nothing to those in the church who are truly upright. We have been taught this, too, by the Lord. For someone came to him and said, “Teacher, tell my brother to divide the inheritance with me.” But he said to him, “Man, who made me a judge or divider over you?” (Luke 12:13–14). It would better suit the wiser members of the church to judge spiritual things, and to test with skill the teaching about the faith. This is counted among the good gifts given from above and through the Spirit; for to some is given a word of wisdom and a word of knowledge, and to others the discerning of spirits (1 Corinthians 12:8–10).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: If a believer needs a judge he should seek a wise one, and Paul shames the Corinthians for having no wise man to decide between brothers.
comments.comment: For the one who follows the Word, if he needs a judge, should seek a wise one, that he may be admonished by the wisdom of the wise man who brings him words that build up. Therefore seat those who are despised in the church. I say this to your shame. … Is it so, that there is not among you anyone wise who will be able to decide between his brother? He charges the Corinthian church that, though seated in the middle of Greece, they had no true wise men, although he had said earlier that many among them profess wisdom—on whose account he also said: “He catches the wise in their craftiness” (1 Corinthians 3:19). … But some are wise of this age, and others wise according to God. Paul knew those former ones …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To go to law with a brother is already a defeat, and the one who is wronged and does not repay has won.
comments.comment: We have rulers of the church to whom we ought to bring our judgments, that we may not be laughed at in the courts of the nations. … Already it is altogether a defeat for you that you have lawsuits with one another. Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded? (1 Corinthians 6:7). … Let us withdraw from the judgments of Gentile tribunals, from having lawsuits and disputes. For the one who has lawsuits with his brother is already defeated, and the one who is wronged has conquered; the one beaten and reviled who does not repay the one doing these things has conquered, for he keeps the command that says: Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be defrauded? But you wrong and defraud, and that your brothers. Everyone who does these things sins; and the more honorable the person wronged, the heavier the sin. For if someone wrongs the blessed one, he wrongs Christ in effect and defrauds Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says it is better to be wronged than to go to law with a brother.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The unrighteous do not inherit the kingdom because the kingdom is in Christ, who is righteousness, and no excuse or appeal to God's mercy will serve.
comments.comment: If the kingdom of God is in Christ, and Christ is righteousness, the righteous inherits the kingdom of God in Christ who is righteousness; and accordingly the one in the opposite state does not inherit the kingdom of God. Do not be deceived: neither the sexually immoral… Let no one deceive you with persuasive words: “God is merciful, kind, and loving toward humankind; he forgives sins.” We must all be manifested before the judgment seat of Christ, that each may receive the things done through the body, whether good or bad (2 Corinthians 5:10). Let no one make excuses: I was young; I was unmarried; before taking a wife I committed fornication. Why then did you not take a wife? Do you not believe that if anyone destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him? Do you take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? The one who fornicates acts impiously toward the God of all.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the unrighteous do not inherit the kingdom, and answers the excuse that God is merciful.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The kingdom of God must be pure from all sins, and the lists of sinners include the lesser sins of theft, dishonest trade and reviling.
comments.comment: Do not be deceived, then: neither the sexually immoral nor idolaters will inherit the kingdom of God; and so neither adulterers. The one who fornicates destroys the temple of God; the adulterer, in addition, also sins against the husband. Neither adulterers, then; nor the soft / effeminate. We exhort you also, children, to keep your own season pure and not to be defiled with such womanish pollution. Nor will men who lie with men inherit the kingdom of God; and may it be far from the church that even one such be found. Then he descends also to sins that seem lesser, saying: nor thieves. This sin of theft nearly all who serve in the army commit, not content with their wages, as the gospel taught, but shaking people down and bringing false charges. And those who lie in business are thieves, not inheriting the kingdom of God; and so also those who overreach in business are greedy; and others are drunkards; and he says revilers also do not inherit the kingdom of God. Therefore let sin reign over no one; for the kingdom of God must be pure from all sins and stumblings, that God may reign.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul had the right to do many things yet did not use it, since to be mastered by a thing is to be under its authority.
comments.comment: Therefore it was permitted to the apostle to do all these things [to eat and drink, and to take along a wife] … yet examining them with a view to his own advantage and to the ordering of the church he saw that it is permitted—if he does it, he will not sin—yet he does better by not using the right. … And again: every virgin is permitted to marry; but the good and noble woman abstains from marriage not as if marriage were forbidden, but having raised the right higher and wishing to be pure in body and spirit she remains a virgin. … “All things are lawful for me, but I will not be mastered by anyone.” The saying has something higher: for if our wrestling is not against blood and flesh but against the rulers, against the authorities (Ephesians 6:12), when the authority masters me I have been mastered by it; but if I conquer every authority, I will not be mastered by anyone.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by 'all things are lawful' yet 'I will not be mastered'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: One should stand above what is permitted.
comments.comment: One must stand above the things over which one has received authority—things which, even if we do them, we will not sin.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The body was made first to be a temple of the Lord and not for intercourse, and marriage is granted because of weakness.
comments.comment: Do not think that just as the stomach came to be for foods and foods for the stomach, so also the body came to be for intercourse. … If you wish to learn the primary reason why it came to be, listen: that it may be a temple for the Lord, and that the soul, being holy and blessed, may become, as it were by serving, a priest of the Holy Spirit within you. … I say these things not as marking off marriage; for I know that if anyone is not continent he ought to marry; for it is better to marry than to burn (1 Corinthians 7:9). … Yet even if the matter is conceded, it is not primarily but because of weakness. For what is primary is to live in chastity and purity and to have leisure for prayer. For of the one already raised with Christ and made conformed to his resurrection and to the newness of life, the body ought to belong to nothing except the Lord.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by saying the body is for the Lord, not for sexual immorality.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Bodies are members of Christ when Christ, not our own soul, moves them, so we move everything by his word.
comments.comment: Human bodies are instruments of the soul; and when the soul rules, the body serves and is used for whatever the soul wishes. But the Word especially wills that our bodies no longer be energized by our own soul but by Christ himself; therefore Paul says: “I no longer live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). They become members of Christ, then, when we move everything according to his word.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means for bodies to be members of Christ.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because we are members of Christ, falling into pleasure is a sin against him, handing his members to a prostitute.
comments.comment: If, then, he is “the head of the body, the church” (Colossians 1:18), we are its members, each one in particular. So whenever we fall into unseemly pleasures, then, precisely then, we will sin against him whose members we have become. For we will be, as it were, handing over what is his to fornicators: his members are defiled by sin and are made members of a prostitute (1 Corinthians 6:15). For just as the man who is joined to a woman will be one body with her, so also the one who is bound to God spiritually will be one spirit with him (1 Corinthians 6:16–17). … For we have become “partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4), and we have been joined to him and made holy through the Spirit in Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why sexual sin is a sin against Christ, whose members we are.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Other sins are not said to be against the body, but sins of seed sin against the body from which they arise.
comments.comment: Someone will ask whether every sin is outside the body. For someone will say: Drunkenness is a sin; taking oneself out of life by hanging or by a cliff is a sin; is this sin also outside the body? But one must hear fairly how this was said. We will take a starting point for understanding the place from Leviticus; for there it is said that from the flow his body has wasted. Since therefore the constitution of the body is from seeds, for this reason the one who sins according to the outflow of seeds sins against his own body; and this sin arises from those things from which also the beginning of the body’s constitution comes.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The murderer, the reviler and the greedy man wrong others, but the fornicator wrongs his own body.
comments.comment:
Someone might say: “Tell me, how will the murderer carry out his murder? Is it not by bloodshed? And if someone chooses to find fault with others, is it not with his tongue that he is such a man? What offense, then, could be committed other than through the body? Will the bearer of the Spirit, then, turn out after all to have spoken falsely?” By no means! For he speaks in Christ (compare 2 Corinthians 2:17), and Christ is the truth (John 14:6); so he will be truthful.

Suppose we look into the matter this way: if someone happens to choose to be perverse in his ways, he will surely be so toward others and not toward himself. The murderer will kill not himself but others; the reviler will insult not himself but others; the greedy man will wrong not himself but others; and in each outrageous deed that is done you will find the same course. In this sense, then, “every sin is outside the body, but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body.” For he will be caught wronging his very own body …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why fornication is a sin against one's own body.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Bodies that stay members of Christ share in his glory, and a defiled body is deprived of it.
comments.comment: The members of our body, if through purity they have remained members of Christ, will surely share in the life and glory that come from him; for “he will transform the body of our lowliness to be conformed to the body of his glory” (Philippians 3:21). But if they should become members of a prostitute, how could they receive that transformation and the spiritual splendor of being conformed to him? For when earthly bodies have been raised at the time of the resurrection, “the righteous will shine like the sun” (Matthew 13:43). The ungodly, the profane, and those who have lived outrageously will indeed be raised, yet they will not go on to live the glorious life; they remain without any share in glory. For they will rise not “in judgment, nor in the council of the righteous” (Psalm 1:5), but for penalty and punishment, for they will go down into the outer darkness (compare Matthew 25:30). For how can what is being punished be in glory?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Only sexual sin is called corruption, so it alone is against the body, and since Christ's blood ransomed us we must glorify God in an incorrupt body.
comments.comment: In addition, then, however many sins we commit—even if we commit murders—yet if we remain uncorrupted and have not tasted the corruption that belongs to intercourse, we are not said to have been corrupted by having murdered. But since both incorruption and corruption concern the nature that is without taste of sexual pleasure—for we say “the virgin was corrupted,” and again “the young man is uncorrupted,” or “he was corrupted”—every sin that a person commits is outside the body (1 Corinthians 6:18). Since therefore a ransom was given for you, the blood of Christ, and he took you from the authority of the devil, glorify God in your body, that your body may become worthy of blessedness as of those who have loved incorruption, as also the apostle says: the grace of God be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ in incorruption (Ephesians 6:24).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The body is a temple of the Spirit and not one's own, so sin against it is impiety toward Father, Son and Spirit.
comments.comment: Well did he, anticipating an objection and guarding against it, say: You are not your own. For someone will say: I sin against my own body; I have authority over my own body. … We act impiously toward the Holy Spirit, and through him toward Father and Son in whom we have been baptized, if we commit fornication—toward Christ when we make the members of Christ members of a prostitute; …
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'you are not your own' as the answer to the claim of authority over one's own body.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We are temples of God, bought with Christ's blood, and so we should offer our bodies to him in self-control.
comments.comment:
And we have been bought at a price (1 Corinthians 6:20), since Christ, the Savior of us all, laid down his own life for us (compare 1 John 3:16). We are, then, temples of the living God (2 Corinthians 6:16); for Christ makes his dwelling in us through the Holy Spirit, and in his own nature he has also the Father and God, from whom he came forth in essence. For he himself said, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him” (John 14:23).

So let foul-smelling pleasure be far from our minds, as from a temple of God, and let the sweet fragrance of self-control rise up instead, like incense. Let us present “our bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God, our reasonable worship” (Romans 12:1). For we were bought “not with perishable things, with silver or gold, but with precious blood” (1 Peter 1:18–19), as it is written. Let us therefore serve him who bought us; let us present ourselves to him for obedience (Romans 6:16), “and our members as instruments of righteousness to God” (Romans 6:13). For it is written, “The body is not for fornication but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body” (1 Corinthians 6:13). So when we keep the members of the body free of the defilement that comes from love of the flesh, then the Lord too will be for the body; for he dwells among the holy, being holy by nature, as God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'bought at a price' and 'temple' as a call to serve the one who bought us.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ paid the price of his own blood for all, yet does not force the unwilling to serve him.
comments.comment: Consider God's love for humanity. We, before we pay the price, ask those who are being sold, and when we learn that they are willing, then we pay the price. But Christ did not do this. He paid the price for all of us—his precious blood. For it says, “You were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 6:20). Yet even so he does not force those who are unwilling to serve him. If you are not grateful, he says, and do not wish of your own accord to have his lordship inscribed upon you, I do not compel or force you.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Paul praises the wish to live chastely yet does not abolish marriage, so each spouse must reckon the other's good.
comments.comment: People who sin, speaking generally, sin in two ways: by falling short of the commandments or by going beyond them. For when we do not live from knowledge and, not knowing the measures of righteousness, we slip, and sometimes by overshooting the rule in the fancy of doing something better we fall away from what is set before us. The proper weight, then—which is neither large nor small but commensurate—is to know how one ought to live. You have been bound with a wife: you make one large weight; you do not care for the wife but say: I am able to practice continence and live more purely. But see that your wife is being destroyed, unable to bear your purity, for whom Christ died. Something of this sort happened in Corinth, and there was disorder in the households of the brothers, husbands in one place and wives in another trying to practice continence and rising up against one another. So those in Corinth wrote a letter to the apostle about this, and to that letter the apostle writes back what has been written above. He neither stretched the word about chastity so as to abolish the word about marriage, nor, preferring marriage, abolished the word about virginity, as a good steward; but throughout the whole discourse he somehow keeps his wish and exhorts to purity; and having conceded condescension, he again exhorts to practice chastity; and having exhorted to practice chastity, he again brings them to the need to condescend to the weakness of the weaker. He began not from the lesser things—for that would not have been fitting—but from the more perfect matters, saying: Now concerning the things about which you wrote to me, it is good for a man not to touch a woman—as if: I praise you for having wished to live chastely, those who withdrew from mixture with the wife; but reckon not only your own interest but also the wife’s. For love does not seek its own (1 Corinthians 13:5). Therefore because of the cases of sexual immorality let each have his own wife, and each her own husband.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says both that it is good not to touch a woman and that each should have a spouse.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul gave husband and wife the same authority over one another's bodies, so neither may think himself above the other.
comments.comment: [Paul made this provision] to heal human weakness and to arrange the matters in those places most becomingly; therefore he said a due is owed from the husband and to the husband from the wife. Then, lest he shame those in marriage as being slaves of one another who must not come to the exercise of purity without agreement, he says: The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise also the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife. … The husband therefore has authority over the wife’s body, and having authority, if he wishes, let him not use the authority; … Does the wife then have authority over the husband’s body and is she unable not to use the authority? The word “likewise” set twice gives us to understand that the husband must not think that in the matters of marriage he excels the wife; there is likeness and equality for those married toward one another.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the word 'likewise' in Paul's teaching: husband and wife stand equal.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A husband's continence without his wife's agreement is not pure, since it may lead her to fall.
comments.comment: Not because of his own fornication should the stronger keep his own wife, but lest somehow the wife fornicate because of the husband’s continence, and the husband because of the wife’s. For it is more choiceworthy that the two be saved while found in the works of marriage than that on the pretext of the one the other fall from the hope that is in Christ. For how will he also be saved who is liable for the death of the wife? The husband’s solemnity is not pure, then, when the exercise does not arise from the wife’s agreement for both to have leisure for prayers according to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul requires agreement between husband and wife in abstaining.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prayer of the pure differs from prayer after intercourse, so spouses abstain for a time for prayer.
comments.comment: You both ought to know that prayer from a man’s and a woman’s purity is not the same as prayer from intercourse. For if Greeks sometimes practice chastity before idols, how much more you who pray to the God of all? It is good, then, to condescend because of weakness, and to hold back because of prayers. Moses also purifies the people and says for three days not to approach a woman, that by having purified beforehand they may become hearers of God (Exodus 19:15). And in the Kingdoms, when Abathar or Ahimelech the priest wishes to set holy bread before David fleeing Saul’s plot, what does he say except: If the young men are clean from a woman?—not from a strange woman but from a wife (1 Samuel 21:4–5). Then, that someone may receive the bread of the Presence, he ought to be clean from a woman; but that he may receive the greater breads than the Presence, over which the name of God and of Christ and of the Holy Spirit has been invoked, how much more ought someone to be cleaner, that he may truly receive the breads unto salvation and not unto judgment?
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul allows abstaining by agreement for a time, for the sake of prayer.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To deprive one's spouse is to withhold what is owed, and sometimes the debt to God presses first.
comments.comment: Many think “deprive” is said only of gold or silver or something of that sort; but the apostle clearly named deprivation also concerning those in marriages who practice chastity unseasonably and without agreement. Once for all, simply, the one who does not render what is owed deprives the one to whom he owes by not rendering the due. Sometimes a person is shut in so that he cannot render two dues at once; therefore it is written that he may render the necessary due. What I mean will be clear thus: it is not possible both to render prayers to God as one ought and for the married man to render the due to the wife; therefore if the debt toward God presses, one must deprive the other. Hear him saying: Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may have leisure for prayer and be together again—as if prayer sent up is not pure even for those who have come together, even if they have come together lawfully. … And one must be wholly pure also from one’s own wife in a time of prayer and fasting.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul loosens the rule because of weakness and tightens it again, and marriage is a gift when it is kept in agreement.
comments.comment: Everywhere he loosens the word because of weakness, and again tightens it to turn the hearers. I wish all people to be as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that (1 Corinthians 7:7). Marriage breathes of gift when the measures are kept—those of agreement. And one can truly say of some that for this one marriage is a gift, when there is no disorder, when there is all peace, all agreement.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'concession' and the 'gift' Paul speaks of.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since each has his own gift from God, marriage is also a gift, and one God gives both chastity and marriage.
comments.comment: Those from Marcion also use this saying, and without sense they forbid marriage, saying that chastity is a command of the other god whom they invented beside the Creator. Yet from the saying itself one can prove to them that they forbid marriage badly, and badly divide the Godhead. For if there is a gift to one in this way and to another in that, marriage also is a gift; if marriage is a gift, marriage the gift is badly forbidden; if the one in this way and the other in that are from God, it is clear that one God is the giver of chastity and the giver of marriage, and one is the God of the law and of the gospel, whom the prophets first proclaimed and later Christ Jesus.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Gifts beyond what the law required were freewill offerings, and marriage is allowed but celibacy is the greater thing.
comments.comment: These freewill offerings were the things beyond what the law required, given as the fruits of a good and God-loving generosity. It was not permitted to neglect the sacrifices ordained in the law, but God counted worthy of praise those who added to them gifts of their own, from their own free choice. We say that something of this kind has been arranged now as well. For Christ did not forbid anyone who so chooses to take part in the union the law allows; but nothing would keep us from achieving the greater thing, if we are eager to lay claim to glory as our final portion.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The unmarried state is a second good, and remarriage is better than burning though it is not the first good.
comments.comment: This is a second good; for there is another good first before this: it is good for a man not to touch a woman. … What second good? It is good for them if they remain as I also am; but if they are not continent, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn. … Better, then, to marry a second marriage—for he does not mean the first here, as is clear from the wording “to burn.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's 'it is good' and 'better to marry than to burn'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Remarriage is not forbidden, but when something is better than burning it is not in itself good.
comments.comment: Some among us teach beyond what is written; and thinking they are doing something, when they ought to exhort to single marriage without laying a snare on those who cannot, they do not do this, but impose necessity and wish not to gather the twice-married nor to share with them as with those who have transgressed, not respecting even the apostle’s voices. For the one who says to the unmarried and the widows, if they are not continent let them marry, openly permitted after the first marriage, after a woman has been widowed, to marry—while blaming the one who marries and the one who is married; for he said: If they are not continent, let them marry. See whether not being continent is not already an accusation—as when it is said to Christian people: Better to marry than to burn—he naming as burning the desire of the flesh not quenched by the Word but mastering the sinner’s soul. We therefore, taught by the apostle, do not forbid remarriage; for by comparison with burning, remarriage is more choiceworthy. Yet when something is thought better by comparison with evils, that thing is clearly not good.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Where there was no divine law Paul says 'I say', and where Christ commanded he says 'not I but the Lord', since the gospel measures its commandment to human nature.
comments.comment:
The people of Israel were found to be very fickle and easily carried away toward anything at all that pleased them. For this very reason they were rightly barred by the law from giving rulings of their own. For of the commandments it says, “To them nothing may be added, and from them nothing may be taken away” (Deuteronomy 4:2; compare Deuteronomy 4:2). But those who brought in the decrees of the Gospel had minds set firmly on the good and had Christ himself speaking within them (compare 2 Corinthians 13:3). So they rightly took courage to give their words of guidance with great authority, even where some matter of conduct was not laid down in the sacred writings.

The inspired Paul was such a man. “I say,” he writes, “to the unmarried and the widows, it is good for them if they remain as I am,” and so on (1 Corinthians 7:8). Where we have no divine law, he has of necessity put “I say”; but where Christ was the one giving the command, he says “I command,” adding at once, “not I, but the Lord” (1 Corinthians 7:10). Yet what necessary thing did Christ overlook when he gave the law? Do those who lead us into the mysteries devise something better? And how could it be anything but ignorant and utterly senseless to think that what comes from Christ is not complete? What, then, shall we say?
