The divine preaching of the Gospel did not forbid marriage, since God, I think, measures the commandment to human nature. For when the Pharisees, testing him, asked the Lord “whether it is lawful to put away his wife” (Matthew 19:3) for a cause other than fornication, he told them that whoever puts away “his wife, except on the ground of fornication, causes her to commit adultery” (Matthew 5:32; compare Matthew 19:9). At this the disciples said to him, “If this is how the case stands between a man and his wife, it is better not to marry.” And he said to them, “There are eunuchs who were born so from their mother’s womb, and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who is able to accept this accept it” (Matthew 19:10, 12). For he set it before those who wish to achieve it, but he did not bring it under law, since he knew that not all are able to master the impulses of the flesh.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul sometimes gives his own judgment and sometimes the Lord's command.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul presents his own state as a pattern of the undistracted life and ranks the unmarried state above the other.
comments.comment: Paul therefore does very well to say to the unmarried and the widows, “It is good for them if they remain as I am” (1 Corinthians 7:8), but, “To the married I give charge, not I but the Lord,” and so on (1 Corinthians 7:10). He brings forward his own case as a pattern of the chosen and undistracted life (compare 1 Corinthians 7:35), plainly ranking the unmarried state above the other. So if anyone has put off the yoke of the law, let him remain, he says, in self-control; for in this way he will inherit the kingdom of heaven. And the One who awards the crowns will confirm it, saying, “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: As many as keep my Sabbaths, and choose the things that I will, and hold fast to my covenant, to them I will give in my house and within my wall a renowned place, better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name, and it shall not fail” (Isaiah 56:4–5).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Married people may not leave one another, so that the message of salvation does not fill the world with turmoil.
comments.comment: But those already bound by marriage he does not permit to leave the wife once joined to them, so that the message of salvation may not fill the world under heaven with turmoil. For Christ, the Savior of us all, does not approve of this practice, even though the law, by way of concession, allowed the people of old to do it “because of their hardness of heart” (Matthew 19:8), as the Savior himself says.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul forbids those already married to separate, and why the law's allowance of divorce was a concession.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A yoking already bound is not to be loosed, and a separated wife must stay unmarried or be reconciled.
comments.comment: I charge, then—not I but the Lord—that a wife not be separated from a husband. The primary point is this: a yoking that has already been bound must not be loosed. But if she is also separated—for many causes of separation can arise; for example if fornication happens to the wife, it is a sin to keep the wife who has fornicated. If then she is also separated and some cause of separation arises, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to the husband. Likewise I also want a husband to be such that he not send away a wife.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul's 'to the married' means believers, and he does not count the unequally yoked as married in the same way.
comments.comment: From here he passes to another legislation: To the married I give charge, not I but the Lord; the legislation toward the married is not from me but from the Lord. At the same time he keeps a necessary observation: he named “married” when both are believers, both the husband and the wife. That he did not name among the married the others who are unequally yoked is clear from his adding: To the rest I say, I not the Lord. Are the rest then not married? He does not measure them as married; for on these a wife is not fitted to a husband from God; …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul's laws are second laws after the Lord's, as Moses gave second laws beside God's.
comments.comment: To the rest I say, I not the Lord. To those who have married I do not legislate, but the Lord; to those not married but unequally yoked with unbelievers I do not have a law to give from God; for they are not even worthy of God’s laws; but let them hear us. And I will use what is written in the law to make the matters of the place understood. The laws according to Moses—some are God’s, and some are Moses’. And knowing this difference of God’s laws and Moses’ laws, the Lord said concerning those legislated by God: For God said, Honor father and mother; and concerning those by Moses: Moses, because of your hardness of heart, allowed you to dismiss your wives (Matthew 19:8). If you keep the matters of the book of divorce you will find the law written not from a command of the Lord. Moses then, serving God, gave second laws beside the laws of God; Paul, serving the gospel, gave second laws to those of the church after the laws from God through Jesus Christ. And it is good to hear laws from the Lord rather than to hear laws of Paul the apostle. For even if he is holy, still he has laws far lesser than the laws of the Lord.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's 'I, not the Lord': his counsel is below the Lord's own commands.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Believers are steadier than the people of old, so they may live with unbelievers in hope of drawing them to godliness.
comments.comment: That those in Christ are steadier and stronger than the people of old, anyone who wishes can easily see from this as well. The law forbade the children of Israel to associate with foreigners and to be bound to them in marriage (compare Deuteronomy 7:3); but to us Paul says, “If any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever,” and so on (1 Corinthians 7:12). For their mind was unsound and unsteady, but we are not so; for we have been anointed with the Holy Spirit for adoption as sons, and Christ has come to dwell in us. Standing so firmly, then, toward every good thing, we are in no way afraid any longer to live with one of the unbelievers. Rather, we are confident that we will draw them as in a net into godliness, and that we will not become the prey of the ignorance that is in them. We bless those who have not yet believed rather than being defiled by them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul lets believers stay married to unbelievers though the law forbade it.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The believer and the unbeliever in marriage are blended like wine and water, and one of the two comes to prevail over the other.
comments.comment: As a kind of blending happens of the two, husband and wife, into one flesh, as of wine and water; and as the believer imparts holiness to the Gentile spouse, or the reverse—the believing woman to the unbelieving husband—so also the unbeliever imparts pollution to the believing wife, or the unbelieving wife to the believing husband. Why then does he say the unbeliever is made holy by receiving something from the believer, and is not also profaned by receiving something from the unbelieving part? For each, conversing from the abundance of the heart with the other, either imparts or receives, and in time the one entirely conquers the other. And what need, he says, of such a contest and danger? For either he will succeed or fail, and either he will lose his soul as well or, after much toil, scarcely be able to gain.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The holiness of the believer overcomes the filth of the unbeliever, and if the unbeliever separates the believer is blameless.
comments.comment: For “the unbelieving husband,” he says, “has been made holy in his wife,” and so “your children too are holy” (1 Corinthians 7:14), since the holiness in those who believe surely overcomes the filth of those who have not yet believed. “But if the unbeliever separates,” he says, “let him separate; in such cases the brother or the sister is not enslaved” (1 Corinthians 7:15). Let the defiled one go away, if he so decides, from the one who makes him holy, and take the loss that comes with it as the wages of his own choice. But the one who follows the divine commandments is wholly blameless; for he will be blessed as obedient by Christ, the Savior of us all.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's saying that the unbelieving spouse and the children are made holy, and what to do if the unbeliever leaves.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Believers from the circumcision wondered whether they must go back to uncircumcision to honor life in Christ.
comments.comment: Some of those from the circumcision, it seems, were reasoning among themselves: “How shall we be acceptable and honor the life in Christ, when we already have circumcision? Perhaps we shall have to draw the foreskin forward, that is, to go back to uncircumcision and do violence to the nature of the flesh.”
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Circumcision is in itself a matter of indifference, so it is neither required nor to be shamefully removed.
comments.comment: Yet it is not out of place sometimes to use the saying against those who think after the faith one must be circumcised from a reverence—yet a reverence not according to knowledge—because of what is written in the old covenant about circumcision. Again it is not good, because of certain ones from circumcision who believe and think circumcision brings them shame and wish to draw a foreskin, to use the saying that says: Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised. And there is reason to say to such that in itself circumcision is a matter of indifference.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul's words on circumcision and slavery may be taken as a picture of the married and the unmarried.
comments.comment: It will seem that he has unseasonably cast beside the word about marriage and chastity, since no inquiry had arisen about those from circumcision who believe not needing to draw the foreskin, and again those in uncircumcision not needing to be circumcised, and about “Were you called a slave? Do not be concerned,” and what follows. Perhaps then he took slavery and freedom as a paradigm of the married and the unmarried, calling circumcised the one who has put away the wife and uncircumcised the one who has married? For as the two will become one flesh and wife and husband are one flesh, and the circumcised has put away the things of the flesh, so the one who has put away the wife has as it were circumcised his own flesh; …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Celibacy and marriage are each indifferent in themselves, and what saves is keeping God's commandments.
comments.comment: So now it is neither about circumcision nor about uncircumcision, but about the unmarried and the married: Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised—as if he were saying: Let him not draw a wife; he has already been circumcised; he put away a wife; let him not marry another. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised—as if: You were called in marriage; do not put away your wife. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing. Since some think the unmarried has something more in this respect than the married, and the married something less than the unmarried by the very fact of having married, we wish, he says, to teach that in its own account celibacy is indifferent and in its own account marriage is indifferent. For the one who is unmarried and truly pure from every mixture, yet living badly in other ways, may gain no benefit from celibacy; and someone in marriage, doing the things of marriage in order and season, keeping the rest of the way of life, may be no less than the unmarried. That celibacy itself and purity itself are indifferent we will prove thus. If only those from the church practiced celibacy, one might say that celibacy in its own account is something pure and divine; but now one can find also those unmarried with a base intention. Those from Marcion also practice celibacy and purity, but not as the church’s people do; for these do so to please the God who created the world, those so as not to cooperate with the god of the world. Celibacy is adorned by an ecclesiastical life and word, by pure knowledge and truth. So also the unmarried is indifferent in his own account; and it is possible also for one in marriage to be without blame, as we have already given. Circumcision then is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing, both according to the wording and according to what is set before us. But what is it that saves? Keeping God’s commandments. For everyone who looses one of these least commandments and teaches people so—he did not say will not enter the kingdom of the heavens but will be called least in the kingdom of the heavens (Matthew 5:19). And if the one who loosed one of the least commandments will be called least in the kingdom of the heavens, where will the one who loosed two commandments be found? Let each therefore remain in the calling in which he was called. Were you called in marriage? Do not envy the unmarried. Were you called unmarried? Do not by all means draw a foreskin, if you are able to live more purely.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Circumcision is nothing without the other commandments, and uncircumcision nothing without a life worthy of the Gospel, so each stays in his calling.
comments.comment: So the way had to be opened wide for them [believers of Jewish and Gentile birth] by a clear and most vivid proclamation of the truth: that circumcision is nothing when it lacks the other commandments of God, and in the same way uncircumcision is nothing unless it is adorned with a life worthy of the Gospel (compare 1 Corinthians 7:19). It is fitting, then, that the one who has been called should remain in his calling, in whatever state he may be (compare 1 Corinthians 7:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's 'circumcision is nothing' and 'remain in the calling in which you were called'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The married man is a slave of necessity, and he may become free by agreement for prayer.
comments.comment: He named a slave of necessity the married man; for the husband is a slave of the wife, not having authority over his own body, and the wife of the husband; for she does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. Were you called a slave? Do not be concerned about it; but if you are also able to become free, rather use it—that is, if you are not transgressing according to the Word, you are able to be free; how? By agreement, that you may have leisure for prayer with all concord.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Even one called as a slave should rise above faint-heartedness, since greed spoiled the beauty of freedom that Christ is restoring.
comments.comment:
That is: even if you were called through faith into free sonship while you still bore the yoke of slavery according to the flesh, even if you have become a partaker of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4), rise above faint-heartedness; you will find that the toil you bear in slavery is not without its reward. For the Creator knows our nature as free, since it was made so by him; but a kind of greed, slipping in somehow over the course of time, has ruined the beauty of freedom.

Those who have suffered this must by all means throw off the burden of this evil, since Christ is refashioning all things to what they were in the beginning. For what is in him is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17), and there is neither slave nor free, but he himself is all and in all (Colossians 3:11). Indeed Isaiah cried out beforehand about the state of the life we await, the life that is to be, and about the equality that is found with God, saying, “And the people shall be as the priest, and the servant as his master, and the maidservant as her mistress” (Isaiah 24:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul tells slaves not to be troubled and to use freedom if they can.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The yoke of slavery is not without gain for those who have lived rightly under it, so long as freedom is kept for all alike.
comments.comment: So, he says, even if you could become free, rather make use of it; for, as I said, the yoke is not without gain for those who have shown good will and have lived rightly under it. That slavery according to the flesh has now been laid on some out of greed will do no wrong at all, so long as freedom is kept for all alike, in equal manner and measure, before God, who judges what is just and weighs our affairs in holiness.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: No one escapes the name of slavery, since all created things are slaves, so the slave is Christ's freedman and the free man Christ's slave.
comments.comment: Besides, he says, since we are human beings, it is not possible for us to escape the name of slavery. For everything that has been made is a slave, and all that has been called into being is subject to the divine scepter. So the slave is Christ’s freedman, and the one called to freedom is surely a slave as well (compare 1 Corinthians 7:22), as the psalm says, “for all things are your slaves” (Psalm 119:91).
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's saying that the slave is the Lord's freedman and the free man Christ's slave.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The freedman is neither purely free nor still a slave, and the free man is a slave of the Word and not of a wife.
comments.comment: Were you called a slave? Know this, that you are not only not a slave, but you also have something of freedom because of the Lord. For the freedman is neither purely free nor still a slave, so that the one wholly pure is free and the one in marriage a slave; but when he is a slave in the Lord, then we say he is the Lord's freedman. And the one called free is a slave not of a wife but of the Word of God. … With all your strength understand the one who bought us out, the Word of God; let us propitiate the blood poured out for us.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We were bought with Christ's blood, so we must not become slaves of men.
comments.comment: Yet the guide into the mysteries shows in another way too that those saved through Christ are helped by him. That is why he says, “You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men” (1 Corinthians 7:23). For we were, beyond dispute, bought with a price, since Christ, the Savior of us all, paid his own blood for us; we have been rescued from the greed of the devil and from the cruelty of the demons, and we have been called to freedom through Christ (compare Galatians 5:13). So, as those who have been bought and who owe their own life to the One who purchased them, “do not become,” he says, “slaves of men.” … We do not say that he is urging them to leap out of slavery according to the flesh …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Teachers who draw believers into the law bring in days and months, but the believers were bought with Christ's blood and should be subject to his laws.
comments.comment:
[Those who try to carry off] the believers into the observance of the law. These people pour the venom of the ancient deceit into the souls of the simpler; they persuade them to keep days and months (compare Galatians 4:10), they practice what is called self-made religion (compare Colossians 2:23), and they advise others to choose to fulfill it.

Since, then, he says, you were bought with a price (1 Corinthians 7:23), and were ransomed “not with perishable things, with silver or gold,” but rather “with precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot, Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19), let us rather be subject to his laws.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Some commandments are commanded and others left free, and virginity is a counsel and not a command.
comments.comment: Of the commandments some are commanded, and some are not commanded but left free and entrusted to choice by God. For those without which one cannot be saved—these are the ones commanded; but the greater ones than the commanded, which even if we do not do we are saved, are not a command of God. Hear, he says, the gospel of Jesus Christ teaching in it and saying: when you have done all that is commanded you, you ought to say we are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to do (Luke 17:10). And if, when I do all that is commanded, I am an unprofitable servant, when will I flee being an unprofitable servant? If being more ambitious you ascend from what is commanded; for example: if I keep "you shall not commit adultery" and not looking at a woman to desire her, I have done what I ought. But if I remain a virgin, not ordered and not commanded, I no longer say over the achievement of virginity: we are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought. So also on the remaining commandments: if I do not steal or overreach, we ought to say we are unprofitable servants. But if I sell all that I have and give to the poor, I no longer say I am unprofitable; I have done what I ought. Therefore the apostle says: Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give an opinion as one who by the Lord's mercy is trustworthy.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's 'no command of the Lord, but an opinion': he is offering counsel beyond what is commanded.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The present necessity is our time in the body, and four times Paul calls the unmarried state good but speaks of marriage as not sinning.
comments.comment: By necessity he means the sojourn in the body, as also elsewhere he says: but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake (Philippians 1:24). Four times in the place the apostle named the good; for he says first: it is good for a man not to touch a woman; second: it is good for them if they remain as I also am; third: I think therefore that this is good because of the present necessity; fourth: it is good for a person to be thus. You see how many things said about chastity are named with the good; but whatever is said about marriage, with the marrying person's not sinning.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'present necessity' and why Paul calls virginity good but marriage not a sin.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul tightens and loosens so that the hearer may judge what he can bear, and he says marriage is not a sin without calling it good.
comments.comment: Through the whole discourse, as has been said, he tightens and loosens, that the hearer, taking it in his own authority, may judge what he is able and to what exercise he can give himself. So also here he turned away from loosing marriage, and again exhorts to live purely. Therefore he called the married husband bound; and if to be bound is a circumstance, one must flee circumstances as far as possible. And do not seek to loose being bound to a wife; and the one not bound ought to guard himself lest he be bound; for truly you will find them bound by the marital love-charm. It is not permitted, then, for the one forestalled in marriage to seek untimely freedom, but to remain in the slavery; and if someone has been loosed, not to seek a wife. But if you also marry, he says, you have not sinned. He did not say: If you marry, it is good; but: If you marry, you have not sinned; keep the difference.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Married women have affliction in the flesh, as the pains of childbearing show, and the virgin is free of it.
comments.comment: For how will they not have affliction when what was said to the woman comes upon the married woman: In pain you will bear children, and your turning will be toward your husband, and he will rule over you (Genesis 3:16)? From all these the virgin is free, set free by purity, awaiting a bridegroom of blessing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by 'trouble in the flesh' for those who marry.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Corinthian believers knew idols were nothing and ate sacrificial meat freely, but this made weaker believers stumble, so Paul stops the feasts.
comments.comment: “Now concerning food offered to idols, we know that we all have knowledge” (1 Corinthians 8:1). The believers at Corinth were convinced that God is by nature one and only, and that idols are not gods. They laughed at those who sacrificed to them, saying that meat offered in sacrifice is nothing at all, and they ate it without distinction, reckoning that no defilement came from it. But they caused the weak to stumble, those who thought they gave no offense to God if they honored the feasts of the idols. For this reason Paul puts a stop to these feasts, wishing the believers to be single-minded, worshiping the all-holy God alone.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the situation behind Paul's words on food offered to idols.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To the mature there is one God and food offered to idols is nothing, while for those who think there are many gods such food will count.
comments.comment: … to those mature in mind, there is one God by nature and no other beside Him, and an idol is nothing in the world (1 Corinthians 8:4), and food offered to idols is counted as nothing (for how could one who does not know an idol know food offered to idols?), while to those who think there are many gods there will certainly be such a thing as food offered to idols (1 Corinthians 8:5–7), …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To those who know that idols are nothing, there is no idol in the world, and they believe in one God the Father and one Lord Jesus Christ.
comments.comment:
“We know that there is no idol in the world” (1 Corinthians 8:4). For those who do not know the idols at all, or who know precisely that they are mere wood and stone, there is no idol in the world, for they do not count them worth any account at all. Thinking in this way, they believe in one God, the Father, from whom are all things, and in one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things (1 Corinthians 8:6).

He [the Son] has the glory of the lordship of God the Father; and, as the One begotten of him, he has the pre-eminence of the One who begot him, since he exists, and is understood to be, God in his own nature, and not by that participation in the Spirit by which many have been called gods and lords. This knowledge few possess.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by "no idol in the world" and the one God and one Lord.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: People who share in the Holy Spirit are called gods and lords, while unbelievers and some believers still think there are many gods.
comments.comment: “As there are many gods and many lords” (1 Corinthians 8:5). It is by being counted worthy of a share in the Holy Spirit that many have been called gods and lords; and this mystical knowledge few possess. For unbelievers still think there are many gods, and some even of those who have believed in Christ do not wholly depart from the customs of idolatry.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in what sense Paul says there are "many gods and many lords".
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Scripture speaks of gods and lords, some only so called and some truly so, and Paul teaches the same about lords.
comments.comment: The word knows of gods, some of whom are so called, while others actually are gods, whether they are so called or not. Paul teaches the same about lords too, both those who are and those who are not, when he says: “For although there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, as indeed there are many gods and many lords” (1 Corinthians 8:5).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those called gods besides the Trinity are so called only by sharing in divinity.
comments.comment: …According to this, the meaning of divinity and angels and divine powers is said to be 'gods,' as the apostle says, 'As there are many gods and many lords in heaven and on earth' (1 Cor 8:6), so all those called gods with the Trinity are such by participation of divinity.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Some believers had not wholly left idolatry, so eating sacrificial meat defiled their weak conscience and they needed teaching instead.
comments.comment: “But some, being conscious of the idol until now, eat it as food offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled” (1 Corinthians 8:7). Some of those who have believed in Christ have not wholly turned away from idolatry, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. For out of a weak soul they perhaps even think it benefits them to be purified by sharing in sacred sacrifices, and to make a meal of the sacrificial meat. But the weak must be led on by spiritual teaching, not by eating without distinction and reclining at table with unbelievers.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the weak conscience is defiled.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By eating in the temples and treating it as indifferent, the strong made their firmness a cause of stumbling, and the right of faith must not be used out of season.
comments.comment: “But take care that this right of yours does not become a stumbling block to the weak” (1 Corinthians 8:9). By being indifferent about eating sacrificial meat and reclining with unbelievers in the temples, they made the display of their own firmness an occasion of stumbling for some. For we must not use the right that faith gives in every case, nor out of season and without discernment; rather, it would be fitting for everything to be done by us in a seemly way (compare 1 Corinthians 14:40).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how a right can become a stumbling block.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Eating idol meat so as to destroy the brothers is as bad as murder.
comments.comment: …He shows those who are able to understand what is said there that the one who partakes of things sacrificed to idols is doing nothing short of what a murderer does, since he destroys his own brothers, for whom “Christ died” (1 Corinthians 8:11). …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Causing the brothers to stumble is an offense against Christ, who died for all, and it turns knowledge into a pit for the weak.
comments.comment:
“Thus, sinning against the brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ” (1 Corinthians 8:12). By causing the brothers to stumble we shall offend against Christ himself, who died for the salvation of us all; and what wrong could weigh as much as that? For “the weak man is destroyed by your knowledge” (1 Corinthians 8:11); our good has become sin, the firmness of faith a stumbling block to the brothers, and knowledge a pit.

It is a very grievous thing, for it all but amounts to leaping on the weaknesses of the brothers, instead of taking pains to strengthen their weak conscience. For we must “not put a stumbling block or an occasion of falling before a brother” (Romans 14:13)
comments.selected_reason: Explains why harming a weak brother is a sin against Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "For an age" in Paul's words means "through life".
comments.comment: The phrase 'unto the age' is placed instead of 'through life,' which is similar to what is said by Paul: 'I will not eat meat for an age, so that I may not scandalize my brother' (1 Corinthians 8:13). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The command about oxen was written for the sake of human beings and, under its outward form, teaches about the nature of things.
comments.comment: For he would have seen that “God does not care for oxen” (1 Corinthians 9:9), even where He seems to be making laws about oxen or animals without reason (Deuteronomy 25:4), but that what was written for the sake of human beings (1 Corinthians 9:10), under the outward appearance of dealing with animals without reason, contains a teaching about the nature of things.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A teacher who has sown a soul and brought it to harvest may take food from it, yet he uses this authority in hope, as a farmer, to offer the produce to God.
comments.comment: …Break up your fallow ground, clearly for the reception of seeds, about which it is written: The sower went out to sow (Jeremiah 4:3; Matthew 13:3). And after sowing the newly broken ground he says: I watch the seeds, lest the birds of the heaven come and take the seed; and when it bears fruit and makes fruits of righteousness and when it is already white toward harvest, it is then permitted me to take. For he will not be scandalized when he remembers how much I have toiled that I may plow his soul, that I may sow, how I persisted up to the point his seed came finished to the threshing floor. And for this reason it is permitted me to take foods from him. But I have not by all means used the authority; yet I do this in hope, to present the produce to the master of the house; for I am a farmer; not that I may take into my own storehouses the things owed to be rendered to God. Then teaching something about the same the apostle says: If we sowed spiritual things for you, is it a great thing…
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who serve the altar share equally in the sacrifice, as Paul writes.
comments.comment: …This law too is preserved in the churches, and it secures equality for those who serve at the altar, giving each, without variation, his portion of the bloodless sacrifice. Knowing this, Paul writes: ‘So also the Lord commanded that those who attend the altar should live from the altar’ (1 Corinthians 9:13–14).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: What we do from necessity earns no boast, but what we do willingly by choice earns a reward, so the reward is in not using an authority we have.
comments.comment: For if I proclaim the gospel, it is no ground for me to boast; for necessity is laid upon me; and woe to me if I do not proclaim the gospel. For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship (1 Corinthians 9:16–17). We are taught that whatever we do from necessity has no boast; but whatever we do by choice, with no necessity laid on, these things have a boast. For example: the one who does not commit adultery or murder does not have a boast, but the one who lives as a virgin; for he did not come to virginity from necessity but from choice. And where "woe" stands beside if I do not do it, I have no boast. Therefore he says: If I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship. Again we are taught something catholic. Some things we do willingly with the whole soul; some things we do, yet not willingly nor with the whole soul, but from grief or from necessity. Of the things done by us willingly there is a reward; of the things done, yet as from grief, there is neither reward nor punishment. For example: I give alms; if willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I am not charged with those who hear: I was hungry and you did not give me to eat, and what follows (Matthew 25:42). This then is the reward: that where I have authority I may not do it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the difference between necessity and choice in Paul's words on boasting and reward.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Being free from all marks a perfect apostle, who is free from the law yet serves those under it.
comments.comment: …To be free from all is of a perfect apostle. For someone can be free from fornication but a slave of anger, free from love of money but a slave of empty glory; he can be free from one sin but a slave of another. But to say "being free from all" is of a perfect apostle—such as Paul was. And according to what is before us the sense is such: I became to the Jews as a Jew, that I might gain Jews—for being free from Judaism I enslaved myself to Jews, that I might gain Jews; being free from being under the law I made myself as under the law, that I might gain those under the law. For Paul would go down into synagogues of Jews, would go in to them, would do according to their customs without harm, not sharing their pretense but hunting some from them. Some have asked what the difference is of those under the law beside the Jews; we say then that those under the law are other than Jews, as Samaritans.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be free from all and yet a servant to all.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul offered at the altar to persuade the Jews he was no apostate from the law.
comments.comment: But why do I say that those who preached “to the circumcision” drew back and separated themselves from the Gentiles, when Paul himself also became “to the Jews a Jew, that he might win Jews” (1 Corinthians 9:20)? That is why, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles, he even brought an offering to the altar, to persuade the Jews that he was not an apostate from the law (Acts 21:21–26).
comments.selected_reason: Gives a concrete case of Paul becoming a Jew to the Jews.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul qualifies his words where needed: he is not himself under the law, since Christ redeemed us from it, and he is not lawless toward God but under Christ's law.
comments.comment: [Of Paul:] At the same time he keeps his own exactness. “I became to the Jews as a Jew”: he did not say here, “not being a Jew.” For he was a Jew in secret, no longer in the open. And again: “to those under law as under law, though not myself under law”—here he had to put “not myself under law,” for Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, becoming a curse for us; as if he said, “not being a Samaritan.” “To the lawless as lawless, not being lawless toward God.” Someone will suppose I have become an apostate from the law and lawless toward God; I say that even if I do not keep the law according to the letter, I am not lawless toward God but under Christ’s law, keeping the polity according to the gospel, that I may win the lawless.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul adds "not myself under the law" and "not being without God's law".
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul adapted his teaching to each hearer, being a Jew to Jews, lawless to the lawless and under law to those under law, to win them all.
comments.comment: …Or was not Paul a various horse, being a follower of the Christ speaking in him, when to the Jews he became a Jew to win these, and to the lawless as lawless, to turn them from the lawless disposition, and to those under law as under law, so that he might win them also, persuading them to transcend 'the law of shadow' (Heb 10:1)? After having said these things, he says: 'I have become all things to all, so that I might save all' (1 Cor 9:22).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: At Athens Paul used the Greek poets and the altar to an unknown god to reach those without law, without himself doing anything lawless.
comments.comment: To those without law as without law: he came to Athens; he found philosophers there; he used not prophetic words nor legal ones, but wherever there was a lesson from Greek preparatory education he, recalling it, spoke to Athenians; for he says: as also some of your own poets have said, for we too are his offspring (Acts 17:28). There to those without law he became as without law, that he might gain those without law. And again he says: going through and observing your objects of worship, I found also an altar on which was inscribed: To an unknown god. What therefore you worship in ignorance, this I proclaim to you (Acts 17:23). And through these he begins to hand on reverence for God. To those without law then as without law, not being without law toward God. Not in condescending to them did I do any lawlessness, but I kept myself under Christ's law…
comments.selected_reason: Shows concretely how Paul became as one without law, from Acts.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul boasted in weakness, so he became weak to the weak through his gentle rulings on marriage.
comments.comment: “I became to the weak as weak”: he did not say here “not myself being weak.” For it would have been boastful and arrogant, and not according to the apostle, to say “not myself being weak,” when he had heard from the Lord that my power is perfected in weakness and for that reason boasts in weaknesses. How then was he weak to the weak? When he permits those who burn to marry; when he sympathizes with women who have lost husbands; when he says, because of porneias let each man have his own wife and each woman her own husband, and the rest. In these he became weak to the weak, that he might win the weak.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Paul became weak to the weak.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Everyone is one of five kinds, and Paul became perfect to the perfect, who are the "all" he wins.
comments.comment: Then after this he says, “I have become all things to all, that I may save all or some.” Whichever person you take, he is one of the five: either Jew, or under law, or lawless, or weak, or “all.” The perfect is all; so to all—that is, to the perfect—I have become perfect, that I may win all. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Only the perfect can say that they do all for the gospel, since whoever sins becomes a partner of that sin instead.
comments.comment: Only the perfect can utter the perfect apostle’s word in the Lord: “I do all things for the sake of the gospel.” The one who sins cannot say this. If the one who does all for the gospel is a partner of the gospel, the one who commits porneia is a partner of the porneia of the spirit—and likewise with the other passions. Each becomes partner of that with which he shared.…
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Although many run, the one who receives the prize is the whole body of the saved, who are one in Christ.
comments.comment: Then do we all run and one receives the prize, and the rest perish? For he said one receives the prize while many run. All who are being saved are one and one body; for if we all share one bread and the same bread, we are all Christ’s body. So all the saved are the one who receives the prize. In the stadium, then, all run who order their life by a doctrine—those from the heresies who live by a doctrine, and perhaps Jews, and those who live by Greek doctrines while philosophizing. These are all who run in the stadium; the church also runs; but one receives the prize—the one man of whom the apostle says, until we all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The incorruptible crown is the one the self-controlled receive, in place of the corruptible crown of lower contests.
comments.comment: And this same is the incorruptible, about which the Apostle writes literally: 'He who struggles exercises self-control in all things' (1 Cor 9:25), but one who, having run the lower and human contests, competes 'so that he may receive a corruptible crown' (1 Cor 9:25), 'but we receive an incorruptible' (1 Cor 9:25), which has also been called unfading by the most supreme Apostle Peter (1 Pet 5:4).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devout run toward the end of the race and box against wickedness, not aimlessly and not beating the air but striking the powers of the air.
comments.comment: But those who are devout according to the teaching of Jesus also run, until, having reached the end of the race, they say in a strong and truthful frame of mind: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith; from now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness” (2 Timothy 4:7–8). And each of us runs in this way, “not aimlessly”, and boxes against wickedness in this way, “not as one beating the air” (1 Corinthians 9:26), but beating those who are under “the ruler of the power of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience” (Ephesians 2:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what running "not aimlessly" and boxing "not beating the air" mean for a Christian.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christians who abstain do so to discipline the body and bring it into subjection, and to put to death the deeds of the body.
comments.comment: …But if we do such a thing [abstain from animal food], we do it because we discipline “the body” and bring it into subjection (1 Corinthians 9:27), and wish to put to death “the members that are on the earth: fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness, passion, evil desire” (Colossians 3:5); and we do everything so that we may put to death “the deeds of the body” (Romans 8:13).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul beats and subdues his body.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul warns those who think their knowledge perfect from what befell Israel in the wilderness, since joining in meals with unbelievers is dangerous even for the firm.
comments.comment:
“I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud” (1 Corinthians 10:1). Having charged those who supposedly have perfect knowledge not to eat sacrificial meat, Paul now tries to persuade them, from what befell the people of old, that the practice is not profitable but rather dangerous, and that it is not without harm to rush in among those accustomed to doing wrong. For it carries one off to do what is not lawful, since the human mind is easily shaken, little by little, toward what is not fitting.

So he takes no unlovely image of the matter, indeed a very close likeness: what happened in the wilderness to those of the blood of Israel. And he shows very forcefully that wanting to live with unbelievers would not be without harm even for those who stand firm.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul turns to Israel's history in the middle of his argument about idol meat.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel promised to live by the laws of Moses, just as in baptism we promise to live by Christ's commandments.
comments.comment: The phrase “they were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:2) means this: just as those people, having obtained these things, promised to live by the Mosaic laws, so we too, receiving the Spirit of adoption in baptism, make covenants and confessions to live from then on according to Christ’s commandments.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what "baptized into Moses" means.
comments.author: Gennadius of Constantinople
comments.work: Fragments on the First and Second Epistles to the Corinthians

comments.capsule: The cloud and the pillar of fire portrayed Christ, the mystery of justification and sanctification in faith and baptism.
comments.comment: Indeed, the blessed Paul says that those of Israel's blood were baptized in the cloud and in the sea (1 Corinthians 10:2). As they crossed that deep desert, the cloud hung over them by day, and by night a pillar of fire went before them (Exodus 13:21). Through both of these Christ was being portrayed, that is, the mystery concerning him: justification and sanctification in faith and holy baptism.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The cloud, the sea, the bread from heaven and the water from the rock were prefigurings of a spiritual reality, Christ himself being the rock.
comments.comment: What he says is this: those who had been freed from slavery were made perfect through the cloud in the sea, with the cloud hanging over them in their midst and Moses acting as mediator (compare 1 Corinthians 10:2). They ate the bread from heaven; they drank the life-giving drink; for Christ gave them drink, being himself the rock (compare 1 Corinthians 10:3–4). For he is unbreakable as God, even though he willingly suffered the assault of death. We say that such things are prefigurings of a spiritual reality.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the meaning of the cloud, the sea, the spiritual food and the rock.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We too were slaves of Satan, but Christ led us across this life as across a sea and made us perfect through baptism.
comments.comment:
For we too, before our faith in Christ, were yoked under the greed of the demons and were slaves to the spiritual Pharaoh, that is, to Satan, the author of evil. We toiled for him in vain, standing in the works of the flesh as in clay and brickmaking (compare Exodus 1:14). But “the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:5–6), rescued us too. He brought us too across the surge of this present life, as across a kind of sea, and made us perfect through holy baptism.

For he is the cloud from above, the spiritual cloud, which supplies living water to those who love it; and the living water is the Spirit. Indeed Christ said, “He who believes in me, as the Scripture has said, out of his heart will flow rivers of living water” (John 7:38). And the inspired evangelist, making the saying plain, at once added to the words about it, “Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive” (John 7:39).

We too have eaten the truly life-giving bread, we have drunk the spiritual drink, just as they drank the water from the rock; and the rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4) …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel's baptism in the cloud and sea was a type of true baptism in the Spirit into Christ, and nothing they received came without it.
comments.comment: …That Israel was baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea (1 Corinthians 10:2), handing down to you the types and marking out the truth that would be shown in the last times. But you altogether shun baptism—not one prefigured in the sea, but one brought to completion in truth; not in the cloud, but in the Spirit; not into Moses, your fellow servant, but into Christ, the Maker. If Israel had not passed through the sea, they would not have been separated from Pharaoh; and you, if you do not pass through the water, will not be separated from the bitter tyranny of the devil. They would not have drunk from the spiritual rock if they had not been baptized in type (1 Corinthians 10:4); and no one will give you the true drink unless you are truly baptized. They ate the bread of angels after baptism (Psalm 78:25); how will you eat the living bread unless you first receive baptism? They entered the land of promise through baptism; how will you return to paradise unless you are sealed with baptism?
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Those baptized in the cloud and sea slipped because they ate with idolaters.
comments.comment: He brings forward the whole story in Numbers, teaching that those who had been baptized in the cloud and in the sea, and had been counted worthy of the spiritual food, slipped because they ate with the idolaters (1 Corinthians 10:2–5; Numbers 25:1–2).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel was not saved by the great benefits they received, because they proved unworthy of them, and God was not pleased with the many sinners.
comments.comment: …the sons of Israel, though benefited so greatly, were not saved when they proved unworthy of God’s benefaction. For God was not well pleased with most of them; they were struck down in the wilderness. And since the sinners were more and the righteous fewer, for that reason God was not well pleased with the many sinners rather than with the few righteous.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Receiving God's gift does not save unless one remains worthy of it.
comments.comment: The apostle wants to show us that it is not merely obtaining a gift of God that saves the one who obtained it, but that after obtaining the gift one must remain, having become worthy of it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says God was not pleased with most of them.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: These things were written as types so we do not fall into the same desires.
comments.comment: He says these things have become types for us, so that we should not be desirers of evils as they desired. Those things were written typologically with a view to us, so that when we read the sins for which they suffered these things, we may keep ourselves from falling into the same desires as theirs.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that these things were "types" for us.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who ate the bread from heaven and drank the spiritual drink still fell into idolatry by sharing meals with idolaters, so living among the wicked is dangerous.
comments.comment:
And what happened to the people of old after this? In what way did they stumble? They were defiled at Shittim, they served idols, they were initiated into the rites of Baal of Peor (Numbers 25:1–3; Psalm 106:28). See, then, how those baptized in the cloud and in the sea, though they had eaten the bread from heaven and drunk the spiritual drink, became entangled with the idolaters. Because they shared meals with them and touched the table of the idols, they were at once easily carried away and slid into apostasy, and they danced with women: “And the people who understood were entangled with a prostitute,” in the words of the prophet (Hosea 4:14). For this is what is meant by “they rose up to play” (1 Corinthians 10:7).

So it is dangerous to live in the company of the wicked and the unbelieving. Indeed Solomon said somewhere, “He who walks with the wise will be wise, but he who walks with fools will be known” (Proverbs 13:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what "they rose up to play" means and why Paul draws the warning.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "They rose up to play" stands for fornication.
comments.comment: And “they rose up to play” stands for committing fornication with the Midianite women (1 Corinthians 10:7–8; compare Numbers 25:6).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The stories of Israel were written for our good, so that we avoid the same faults and the same misfortunes.
comments.comment: So the prophetic word here seems to be looking for those who listen more fairly, that is, more wisely, since it tells what befell the people of old for the safety of those to come. As Paul says: 'These things happened to them as types, and they were written for our warning, on whom the ends of the ages have come' (1 Corinthians 10:11). For we must not read the accounts about Israel to no purpose, but receive them for the good of the soul, and firmly refuse to be caught in the same faults, so that we may not fall into the same misfortunes as they did.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says these things were written for our warning.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God does not grant freedom from being tempted but freedom from being tempted beyond power.
comments.comment: And Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says God grants not freedom from being tempted but freedom from being tempted beyond power: 'No temptation has taken you but human; but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted beyond what you can, but will make with the temptation also the way out, that you may be able to bear it.' (1 Corinthians 10:13)
comments.selected_reason: States clearly what Paul's promise about temptation does and does not mean.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's body and blood give life, which belongs to God alone.
comments.comment: Human flesh, as far as its own nature goes, would not be life-giving, nor would human blood if it were common and by itself; but Christ’s body and precious blood give life — and being able to give life belongs to God alone…
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Part of each offering was carried up to the altar and the rest fed the priests, who were therefore partners in the altar.
comments.comment: The offerings dedicated for a pleasing aroma, a calf, say, or a sheep, were carried up to the altar in part, once the entrails, the feet and head, the fat, and sometimes the kidneys too had been taken out; and with what remained they fed the priests. For ‘those who eat the sacrifices are partners in the altar’ (1 Corinthians 10:18)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: Demons grow strong on the smoke and blood of sacrifices, so to sacrifice is to feed them and submit to them.
comments.comment: Since some, not beholding the earthly intent of the hostile power's assault, suppose the idols nothing — hear: the demons, dwelling in earth's thick air, are fatted by sacrifice-smoke and blood, and by such food grow strong to deceive. 'He that sacrificeth to gods shall be uprooted' — save to the Lord alone. To sacrifice is to feed demons and subject oneself to them: 'the things the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons, and not to God; and I would not ye have fellowship with demons.' (1 Corinthians 10:20) Flee then the demons' table, lest, fed by you, they boast to have overcome God's soldiers (Exodus 22:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that sacrifices are offered to demons.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul sets a wise law of love: love looks also to the things of others and to how the brothers fare.
comments.comment: And Paul the divine also was setting for us a wise law of the love unto one another, saying thus: ‘Not seeking the things of themselves, but also the things of the others.’ (1 Corinthians 10:24) For love does not seek the things of itself; but it rather looks around also at the things of the others, and how the things of the brothers would hold well.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what seeking the good of the other means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 8

comments.capsule: The apostle tells Gentiles and Jews not to be superstitious about foods, since the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord.
comments.comment: The apostle instructs, advising those from the Gentiles and the Jews not to be superstitious about foods, saying: 'Whatever is sold in the market, eat, without examining anything (1 Cor 10:25); for the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord (Ps 24:1).' Meat is especially sold in the markets, but also other things contributing to nourishment.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says to eat whatever is sold in the market.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To a mind that knows idols are nothing, food offered to idols is nothing, yet he must not eat when another warns him, for the weaker one's conscience.
comments.comment: In the same way, of course, for the faithful mind, firmly set on true knowledge, an idol is nothing in the world (1 Corinthians 8:4), and neither is food offered to idols anything (1 Corinthians 10:19); yet such a person is not permitted to eat when another warns him, for the sake of the conscience of the weaker (1 Corinthians 10:28). ‘For why am I judged by another’s conscience? If I partake with thanks, why am I denounced over that for which I give thanks?’ (1 Corinthians 10:29–30).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Paul can say that idol meat is nothing and still forbid eating it.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: The conscience in question is not the strong man's own but the other's, lest the weaker one copy in ignorance what he does not understand.
comments.comment: So for conscience’ sake one must abstain from what one ought to abstain from. And by conscience I mean not one’s own, for one’s own is the conscience of the one with knowledge, but the other’s, so that he may not be built up in the wrong way (compare 1 Corinthians 8:10), copying in his ignorance what he does not understand, and so become a man who despises instead of a man of great soul.
comments.selected_reason: Explains whose conscience Paul means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We live by God's word when we do all to his glory.
comments.comment: We must indeed live, and we must live according to the word of God, so far as is possible and so far as it is granted to live according to it. And it is granted when, whether we eat or drink, we do “all things to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). We must not refuse to use, with thanksgiving to the Creator, the works he has made for our sake.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul added "as I am of Christ" to show he meant true imitation, not appearance.
comments.comment: But the blessed Paul does not act thus, but saying, 'Become imitators of me' (1 Cor 11:1), he did not simply command this, but further brought it forth, 'just as I am of Christ' (1 Cor 11:1), not in appearance but in truth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul uses the law of nature and the making of man to show that Christ, the archetype, is the head of man and shares our nature.
comments.comment:
Since it was right that he should put them to shame with compelling arguments, so that they would choose to think as they ought, and that he should make the law of nature a kind of umpire of what befits each, Paul tries to persuade them from the natural law to think as they ought, and he goes back to the making of man in the beginning.

By “head” he here means the archetypal beauty. Each of those named here, being enriched with its image, may rightly be understood to have received as a portion a kind of noble descent that in some way belongs to their very being, or, to put it another way, a sameness of nature.

For the first man, that is, Adam, came into being according to the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1:26), for so the Creator of all says somewhere: “For in the image of God I made man” (Genesis 9:6). So the head of man is Christ: the archetype as God, and also of the same form with us by the law of our nature when he appeared as man, although the Word is God. Indeed, everywhere he calls himself Son of Man, although his birth from God the Father is beyond words.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by calling Christ the head of every man.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Woman came into being in the image of man and is of one nature with him, as Adam confessed.
comments.comment: Then the woman came into being according to the image and likeness of man, that is, of Adam. She is in no way of a different stock, but rather of one nature and one form with him. And the forefather Adam himself plainly confessed this when he said, “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh,” and what follows (Genesis 2:23).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the man is the head of the woman.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: If counting the Son among creatures because he is the head of every man were right, the same would reach the Father.
comments.comment:
Some say that the Son has come into being, like the rest of the creatures, of which, they say, Christ is the head, “for the head of every man is Christ.” Before anything else they must consider that the force of their blasphemy will not touch only their teaching about the Son, but, rushing on as in an unchecked course, will drive right through to the Father himself. And how, I will tell.

For if they say that the Word who is from God the Father has come into being, and that it is right to count him among the creatures because he is the head of every man, how would the Father himself not be thought, in the same way, to be created and made, if indeed he is the head of a Son who is related by his very being to us, that is, to creatures (1 Corinthians 11:3)? For, as they themselves say, the head is in every way and altogether bound to the rest of the body by natural laws, so as to be one and the same with it. Then, by way of the Son, the kinship with every man will reach God the Father himself as well. How, then, does he still rise above the nature of things that have come into being? Or whom are we to seek as the Creator of all?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Word is uncreated, called head of every man as the archetype, and given as head to the Church because he appeared as man.
comments.comment: [Of those who say the Son is a creature:] But we shall not follow their foolishness. How could we? We believe that the Word who sprang from the Father is uncreated, as being from an uncreated Father. And we say that He has been called the head of every man (1 Corinthians 11:3), as the archetype, as I said; but since He appeared as man in the last times of the age, and as one of the same kind as men in His humanity, He was given as head to the Church, which is His body (Ephesians 1:22–23). For He holds the first place in all things, as Paul says (Colossians 1:18).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "Head" means "beginning": Christ is our head as man, and the man is head of the woman because she was taken from him.
comments.comment: So he is our beginning — that is, our head — insofar as he has appeared as human; yet as God by nature he himself has as head the Father in the heavens, for the Word, being God, has been begotten from him by nature. That “head” signifies “beginning” confirms, for minds that doubt, that the man became head of the woman (1 Corinthians 11:3): for she was taken from him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that "head" can mean "beginning".
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: God made man to rule the beasts, and just as Christ rules the man, so the man has the woman under him.
comments.comment: For God, having made all things and being both ruler and leader of all—for as Creator he is thus both ruler and king—having made man to rule over the beasts, cattle, and birds, shows that man is his image in respect of ruling. That it has this in such a way is to be learned from the apostolic word: 'But I want you to know that Christ is the head of every man, and the man is the head of the woman' (1 Cor 11:3). Just as the man is ruled by Christ, so the woman is ruled by the man, having him as head.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Nature judges what befits each: openness for men, a veil for women.
comments.comment: Do you see how he makes the law of nature the judge and arbiter of what befits each? For openness is most fitting for men, while for a woman being veiled is an adornment.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: New believers at Corinth prayed in an unseemly way, men covered and women uncovered, against what nature teaches.
comments.comment: Some of those in Corinth were newly established in the faith and did not know the right manner of prayer. They had given the faith a home in themselves, but they had not yet learned exactly how one ought to enter the house of God. They came to pray to God and to offer their petitions for themselves, and then Paul found this being done in a most unseemly form. For the men made their approach without uncovering their heads of their customary coverings, and the women likewise came before God with their hair unshaded and uncovered, while nature all but cried out against them both. For nature has given openness to the man, while by modesty it draws the woman in toward seemliness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the situation Paul is correcting.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because man is the image and glory of God, he should keep his head uncovered before God, as nature does not reproach him.
comments.comment: So the unseemliness of the image would quite reasonably be an insult to the archetype. For if man is the image and glory of God (1 Corinthians 11:7), as according to the Scriptures he was made (Genesis 1:27), let him keep before God the openness that befits him, with his head uncovered, since nature does not reproach him for having to go uncovered. For the Divine is free and beyond all blame, rich in its own glory and held in wonder.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says a man should not cover his head.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The "image of God" is the Word, while man is made after that image and is the image and glory of God.
comments.comment: …that the “image of God” is the “firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), the very Word, the very Truth, and also the very Wisdom, which is “the image of his goodness” (Wisdom of Solomon 7:26), while man has been made “after the image” of God (Genesis 1:27); and further, that every man of whom “Christ is the head” (1 Corinthians 11:3) is “the image and glory of God” (1 Corinthians 11:7). …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul softens his words about woman as the glory of man by adding that neither is woman without man nor man without woman.
comments.comment: The inspired Paul uses yet another skilful device. He said that man was made according to the image and likeness of God, and he plainly insisted that the female has been cast, as it were, behind his honor and glory, adding what follows: “For woman,” he says, “is the glory of man; for man was not created for the sake of woman, but woman for the sake of man” (1 Corinthians 11:7, 9). Then, gently covering over what would likely grieve women, he goes on to say, “Nevertheless, neither is woman without man, nor man without woman” (1 Corinthians 11:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul adds "neither is woman without man".
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The angels stationed in the churches are not harmed by seeing women but are grieved when what is fitting is neglected.
comments.comment: So, he says, let her be veiled because of the angels (1 Corinthians 11:10), clearly meaning those whom God has stationed in the churches. Not that they suffer anything in seeing women. Human beings, who have this coarse body taken from the earth and are pushed down toward baser things by inborn pleasures, might suffer harm, being stirred by the beauty of women toward what is not fitting. But as for the holy angels, what could anyone think or say of that kind? For they are holy and above all defilement, since they are outside the flesh and have bodies that are fine and spiritual, beyond the grasp of the human mind. Rather, it is because they are deeply grieved if anyone neglects the law of what is fitting.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what "because of the angels" means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Although woman came from man, she shares in bringing man into being, and both depend on each other and on God the Creator.
comments.comment: For woman admittedly came from man, and this is true (1 Corinthians 11:12); yet she has been found to have her share in bringing man into being. Nature, bringing both together into one, has made them need each other, wisely binding them together in love. And he further confirms that God is the Creator of all things, saying, “But all things are from God” (1 Corinthians 11:12); for all things were brought into being through Christ (John 1:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Paul balances "woman from man" with "man through woman".
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Woman is the image of an image, nature gives her long hair, and she is not blamed for covering herself modestly.
comments.comment: And if woman is in the likeness of man, an image of an image and a glory of a glory, and nature also lays it down for her to wear long hair (1 Corinthians 11:15), why should what comes second in grace contend with what is first? For she too is according to the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1:26), but as it were through the mediation of man, so that in some small respect she differs in nature. I will not bring a charge against her when she wraps her person in modesty as far as she can and crowns it with her hair; for to go openly uncovered is not without harm for women.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the point of "her hair is given to her for a covering".
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Nature itself shows that being veiled befits women, since her hair is given as a covering.
comments.comment: And being veiled befits women, and nature is witness to this: “for her hair,” he says, “has been given to her as a covering” (1 Corinthians 11:15). So let what is fitting be kept in this matter too, because of those who know the will of the Creator better than we do.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord allows these divisions so that the test of truth shows the proven and exposes the faithless.
comments.comment: The Lord permits and allows these things to happen while the choice of one's own freedom remains, so that when the test of truth examines our hearts and minds, the whole faith of the proven may shine with clear light. The Holy Spirit warns us beforehand through the apostle and says: "There must also be heresies, so that those who are proven may be evident among you" (1 Corinthians 11:19). In this way the faithful are tested, and in this way the faithless are exposed. Even before the day of judgment, the souls of the just and the unjust are already divided here, and the chaff is separated from the wheat.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says there must be divisions among them.
comments.author: Cyprian of Carthage
comments.work: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

comments.capsule: As the approved doctor or philosopher is the one who has examined the various schools, so one who studies the sects becomes the wisest Christian.
comments.comment: Of these, Paul seems to me to have spoken most admirably: “For there must also be sects among you, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Corinthians 11:19). For the man approved in medicine is the one who, having trained himself in various sects and fairly examined most of them, has chosen the best; and the man who makes great progress in philosophy is the one who, having come to know more of them, has trained himself in them and attached himself to the argument that prevailed. In the same way I would say that one who has looked carefully into the sects of Judaism and of Christianity becomes a most wise Christian.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We eat and drink to remember the Lord who died and rose, but we are told to discern his body, having put away defilement.
comments.comment: …What then are these words, and what benefit comes from them? It is so that, as we eat and drink, we may always remember the one who died and rose for us, and so be necessarily taught to keep that apostolic commandment given to us, which says: “For the love of Christ constrains us, because we have judged this: that if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose for them” (2 Corinthians 5:14-15). For the one who eats and drinks clearly does so for an indelible remembrance of the obedience unto death of the Master and Creator, who for my sake became what the formed thing was. But we are not commanded to eat simply; rather, we are urged to discern this body of the Lord—clearly, having put away defilement of flesh and spirit, and having prepared a vessel for the spiritual ointment, so to approach the pure sacrifice, in Christ Jesus our Lord
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Coming to the mystical blessing without cleansing is dangerous, so Paul tells us to examine ourselves lest we be judged.
comments.comment: …For it is a perilous and truly harmful thing to draw near to God without being cleansed. That is why the wise Paul charges us, if we wish to share in the mystical blessing, to examine ourselves and only then to come forward (1 Corinthians 11:28). And he reveals that carelessness in these matters is full of danger, when he says, ‘That is why many among you are weak and sick, and a good number have fallen asleep. For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged. But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined, so that we may not be condemned along with the world’ (1 Corinthians 11:30–32).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 9

comments.capsule: The Holy Spirit enlightens the prophet's soul, while an impure spirit darkens and drives the diviner, who does not know what he says.
comments.comment: … he [Paul] now speaks of the energies of the Holy Spirit, which he distributes to each according to his merit, such as to one to evangelize, and to another to prophesy, and to another something else. But through the phrase 'you are led toward the idols,' he demonstrates the greatest difference between prophecy and divination. For in the idols, the possessors do not act soberly by the impure spirit, but are carried up by an impure spirit, proceeding by a non-voluntary will; for this is made clear by the words 'you are led' and 'you are being brought along.' He says, therefore: you know the energy of the impure spirit from which you suffer, but the energy of the Holy Spirit possesses the pure energy. Consequently, the diviner darkens the soul and does not know what he says, but the prophet's soul becomes brighter, and having learned what he did not know, he speaks the things revealed to him. The demon, as an enemy, darkens the soul, but the Spirit, as a benefactor, enlightens the soul as it approaches, which he leads upward.
comments.selected_reason: Shows the difference between true prophecy and the possession the Corinthians knew from idol worship, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Even demons named the Lord Jesus, so saying the name is not by itself a perfect confession of his lordship.
comments.comment: … for all blasphemies against Christ are worked by the evil one who thunders at the soul.
