This, therefore, he says, to secure those who claim to be God-bearing and who speak against Christ. Since even the legion and the Pythia were naming the Lord Jesus, we do not say that he who says this speaks perfectly—for there are many lords called righteous—but rather he lacks the confession of the lordship and sovereignty of Christ over all. Perhaps they said this while being tested, as the devil had brought him to the mountain. Therefore, he does not receive their testimony as if they were unworthy and being tested.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Because the Spirit glorifies the Son, whoever speaks in the Spirit confesses Jesus as Lord, and those who confess him as God are brought by the Spirit into the knowledge of God.
comments.comment:
… And if his Spirit glorifies the Son, how could anyone speaking in the Spirit speak evil of him? He will rather say, “Jesus is Lord” (1 Corinthians 12:3).

… But those who devoutly confess that Jesus is God and Lord will have the fact itself as witness that they have been initiated through the Spirit into the knowledge of beholding God in him. “For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10). Knowing what is hidden in God, the Spirit carries it across to the souls of the saints and plants in them a knowledge free from error and beyond reproach.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why speaking in the Spirit leads to confessing Jesus as Lord.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Spirit glorifies Christ by making his people wise and by making Christ dwell in the saints.
comments.comment: … Our Lord Jesus Christ promised that when He had gone away He would send us the Comforter (John 16:7), and to this He added, “He will glorify Me” (John 16:14). And we understand, quite rightly, that His Spirit glorifies Christ both by making wise those in whom He comes to dwell and by making Christ dwell in the saints through Himself; for Christ is in us through the Holy Spirit. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because spirits differ and no one can judge them by sight alone, John teaches us to test them by whether they confess Jesus, neither believing nor rejecting rashly.
comments.comment: … There are many differences among spirits, which no one will know accurately unless he has the gift of discernment of spirits. And so that we may not too rashly either reject the spirits in those who speak or approve them, John says in the letter, Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits whether they are of God; every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ come in flesh is of God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not of God. He also teaches us that when we hear people speaking we should neither assent at random nor rashly deny that what is said is from a divine spirit, but that each hearer, knowing he risks in the very act of approving or rejecting, should attend carefully neither to trust the false nor to distrust the true.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a practical way to weigh what people say is from the Spirit.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Someone who knows the Scriptures yet curses Jesus lacks God's Spirit, so his Scripture-teaching should not puzzle us.
comments.comment: How do we who hear the divine word need to learn that no one speaking in God’s Spirit says “Jesus is anathema”? Let us see: some can be ambiguous to those who do not know the facts accurately—whether they speak by God’s Spirit or not—while they anathematize Jesus. If ever you see a Jew expounding the divine Scriptures and not contemptibly, to the many, prophetic words, you might perhaps be in doubt whether God’s Spirit is also in that one. So that you may not be pulled about over such a person—whether a holy spirit is in him or not—Paul teaches that since every Jew says Jesus is anathema, and no one speaking in God’s Spirit says Jesus is anathema, the one who claims to know the law and the prophets while anathematizing Jesus does not have God’s Spirit. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: As earthly rulers honor their more loyal guards with different honors, so the Trinity gives different gifts, from the Father through the Son in the Spirit.
comments.comment: … “Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of service, and the same Lord; and there are varieties of workings, but it is the same God who works all things in all” (1 Corinthians 12:4–6). For just as those who hold power over affairs on earth, and adorn the thrones of kingship, crown the more loyal of their own guards with different honors, so the holy and consubstantial Trinity distributes a rich possession of the good things from above to those who love it with a sound heart and a whole mind, through the one Spirit, as through Christ, from the Father. For all things are from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a plain picture of one giver and many different gifts.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: What God works, the Spirit works, so the Spirit is not to be brought down into slavery.
comments.comment: The Apostle says: “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit. And there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord. And there are varieties of workings, but the same God who works all things in all” (1 Corinthians 12:4-6). So then, what God works, the Spirit works. “The one and same Spirit works all things,” he says, “apportioning to each one as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11). Let no one bring the Spirit down into slavery when he hears that the Spirit works all the things of God just as he wills. …
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: The Son apportions ministries and the Holy Spirit carries them out, as in the setting apart of Barnabas and Saul.
comments.comment:
Both the one and the other [the word of wisdom and the word of knowledge] are supplied to the worthy through the one Spirit, from the Father through the Son, who is said to apportion the ministries (1 Corinthians 12:5). For some of the holy apostles he commanded to proclaim the word of faith to those of the blood of Israel, and others again he assigned to the lands of the Gentiles. And this too he brought about through the Holy Spirit. Indeed, in the Acts of the holy apostles we shall find it written: “While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them’ ” (Acts 13:2).

The inspired Paul was appointed to the apostleship of the Gentiles, and this ministry fell to him as his lot. He will confirm it himself when he writes, “Inasmuch then as I am an apostle of the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry” (Romans 11:13). So the Son apportions the ministries, and the Holy Spirit carries the matter out with authority, for he is the Spirit of the Son. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul begins from the Spirit and rises through the Son to the Father, to whom the working is ascribed.
comments.comment: … For all things, as I said, are from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, and in everything that is well done the holy and consubstantial Trinity is glorified. For see how he begins from the Spirit, as the one who is in us and works the distribution of the divine gifts; then, raising his account to the Son, who is Son by nature, he goes up at last to the Father, ascribing to him, by way of the Son, the working done through the Spirit.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The word of wisdom is ready and flowing speech, and the word of knowledge is knowing the sense of the divine oracles and unfolding it, even without eloquence.
comments.comment:
“To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for what is profitable. For to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom,” and so on (1 Corinthians 12:7–8).

… The word of wisdom, as it seems to me at least, is the word given “in the opening of the mouth” (Ephesians 6:19): ready and flowing, as if it came from a very nimble tongue.

“To another, the word of knowledge” (1 Corinthians 12:8). For there are some among us who lack readiness in speech and have not gained the freedom to express themselves with ease, yet they are very deep in understanding. They come to the sacred words most thoughtfully and with great subtlety, and they are able to lead others into the mysteries and readily lay open what they have contemplated. But both the word of wisdom and the word of knowledge are supplied through the one Spirit, from the Father through the Son, to those worthy to receive them. It is a word of knowledge when someone knows the sense of the divine oracles and is able to unfold their meaning, but cannot teach it eloquently.
comments.selected_reason: Distinguishes the word of wisdom from the word of knowledge in everyday terms.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Wisdom is the first of God's gifts, knowledge second, and faith third, as Paul's order shows.
comments.comment: Divine wisdom, then, which is different from faith, is the first of what are called the “gifts” of God (1 Corinthians 12:4). After it, second, for those who know how to be exact in such matters, comes what is called knowledge; and third, since the simpler people too, who come to godliness as best they can, must be saved, comes faith. That is why Paul says: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:8–9). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the order of the first three gifts in Paul's list.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The word of wisdom is understanding what God's wisdom spoke in the prophets and presenting it, faith is receiving the message faithfully, and discernment of spirits guards against imitation prophecy.
comments.comment: … the word of wisdom is to understand the things spoken in wisdom of God in prophets and evangelists and to present them to those hearing; … faith is merely to believe the proclamation; for it is not simply hearing this that constitutes faith, but to receive the things spoken with faithfulness. Discernment of spirits exists because divination has imitated prophecy in that the Holy Spirit seems to foretell in the same way, and He has granted the discernment of these things so as not to be led astray.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The later list keeps order, the earlier lists gifts as they occur, and powers rank below apostleship, prophecy and teaching.
comments.comment: … There [in 12:28] he kept the word more in order; here [in 12:8–10] he comes on as if by allotment and mentions the gifts as they occur to him. Yet even so, from the second saying it rings out that the gifts worked beside the powers are lesser than the gift according to apostleship and prophecy and teaching …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Faith here means steadfastness toward every good thing and toward whatever God wills, not only believing that there is one God.
comments.comment: “To another, faith by the same Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:9). Faith here would be, as I think, steadfastness toward every good thing whatever, and toward whatever God may will. For in this sense we say that Moses, the revealer of holy things, was faithful “in all his house” (Hebrews 3:2; Numbers 12:7). For faith would not be understood or spoken of as only the duty to believe that by nature and in truth there is one God of all, but as standing firm in soul, “and being ready to walk with the Lord God,” in the words of the prophet (Micah 6:8). And so the inspired disciples once came to Christ, saying plainly, “Increase our faith” (Luke 17:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by faith as a gift, in plain terms.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Healings and miracles are given in the one Spirit, yet it is Christ who gives them, as the miracles of Moses and the prophets show.
comments.comment:
Besides this, gifts of healing are also given by the one Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:9). And again, mark this closely, I ask you: though the Spirit is said to distribute the gifts of healing, it is Christ who gives them. For he gave the holy apostles “authority over unclean spirits, to cast them out” (Matthew 10:1); and indeed he said, “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You received without cost; give without cost” (Matthew 10:8).

The workings of miracles are certainly his as well, but in the one Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:10). For instance, Moses threw his staff on the ground and it became a serpent (Exodus 4:3); he turned the rivers into blood (Exodus 7:20); he brought water out of the rock (Exodus 17:6). And the blessed prophets performed a great many deeds beyond words and beyond wonder. These, we say, are the workings of miracles through the one Spirit. Another, again, prophesies, but not apart from the Spirit; and someone has the discernment of spirits, but in the Spirit himself (1 Corinthians 12:10). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the gifts of healing, miracles, prophecy and discernment with Bible examples.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Speaking in tongues was given to believers of that time as a sign, not counted among the gifts, as Isaiah foretold.
comments.comment: Paul also insists that to others it is given to know kinds of tongues, and indeed their interpretation (1 Corinthians 12:10). This we call a gift of its own kind, supplied to some in God’s plan, at a set time and for a need. But some spoke in the tongues though they had not known them before, while others understood and interpreted them, though some of them had never before had an ear trained in such languages or used to them. Yet the inspired Paul firmly states that speaking in tongues was given to the believers of that time not as counted among the gifts but as ranking as a sign. And he set beside it a prophetic oracle that runs thus: “By people of strange tongues and by the lips of others I will speak to this people, and not even so will they believe” (1 Corinthians 14:21; Isaiah 28:11–12).
comments.selected_reason: Says what tongues were for and why Paul ranks them as he does.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Tongues were a sign given to those preaching the Gospel to every nation.
comments.comment: Because, then, those who were to lead the world under the sun into the mysteries were to speak the saving proclamation of the Gospel to every tongue and every nation, he gave them the tongues as a sign. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who spoke in others' languages made the grace a display and boasted of it, neglecting their duty to argue the Gospel from the prophets.
comments.comment: But once they were speaking in the languages of others, they made the grace given through the Spirit into a kind of display and took the sign as an occasion for boasting. They grew careless about their duty to discuss with the crowds what comes from the holy prophets and to argue for the teachings of the Gospel as foretold from of old, long beforehand. Priding themselves on the mere ability to speak in tongues, they thought they should lay claim to this and this alone, and it ranked among their most pressing concerns.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Spirit distributes gifts differently to each so that Christ's body, the Church, has its perfect structure from a multitude of saints joined in spiritual unity.
comments.comment: The Spirit works the distribution of the gifts differently in each (1 Corinthians 12:11), so that, as he says, just as this coarse body from the earth is made up of parts, so too Christ, or rather his body, that is, the Church, has its most perfect structure through a great multitude of saints joined into a spiritual unity (1 Corinthians 12:12, 27). For this reason the inspired David too says that she is clothed “in a garment woven with gold,” embroidered in many colors (Psalm 45:9), signifying by this, I think, how many and how precious the gifts are.
comments.selected_reason: Compares the Church's many gifts to the many parts of a body.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul calls the church by Christ's own name, showing the lesser from the greater.
comments.comment: … he [Paul] depicts Christ as being composed of many members from the whole body, thereby showing the church through Christ; for since it has been said that Christ is the head of the church and the church is the body of Christ, and He named the church Christ, He shows the lesser from the greater. …
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Believers are one body in Christ through the one Holy Spirit, whom we were given to drink as a life-giving drink, so we should keep the bond of love unbroken.
comments.comment:
“For just as the body is one and has many members,” and so on (1 Corinthians 12:12). For we are united to one another and have become one body in Christ, since he has raised us up together and all but bound us into one through the one Holy Spirit, who is in all, and whom we have been given to drink as a life-giving drink (1 Corinthians 12:13). So it was that Christ, when he was speaking with the woman at Jacob’s well, said, “Whoever drinks of this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him, it will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John 4:13–14). And somewhere he also said to the Jews, “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, ‘Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.’ ” “Now this he said,” it says, “about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive” (John 7:38–39).

Do not be surprised. For if he himself is “the river of God,” in the words of the Psalmist, the one “full of waters” (Psalm 65:9), the torrent of delight whom God the Father is said to give as drink to those who love him (Psalm 36:8), how could his Spirit not have to be understood as the life-giving drink and water? Since, then, we have been called into unity through the Spirit and have become one body with Christ, let us keep the bond of love unbroken (Ephesians 4:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how many believers are one body through one Spirit.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Even the lesser member contributes to the church's common life.
comments.comment: … he [Paul] says this so that the more humble ones are not overlooked in the church; for even if someone is lesser by nature, he contributes to the commonality of the church. …
comments.selected_reason: A short, clear point on why Paul stresses that no member is unimportant.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Martyrs are members of our body, so their honor is shared, and the head cannot say to the feet that it has no need of them.
comments.comment: … Because the martyrs are our parts and members. If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; if one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it (1 Corinthians 12:26). … We are the feet, the martyrs are the head. But the head cannot say to the feet, “I have no need of you” (1 Corinthians 12:21). The members are glorious, but the surpassing glory does not make them strangers to their connection with the remaining parts. …
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Believers are many members from one member, Christ the head.
comments.comment: … he [Paul] did not say members from members, but many members from one member; for the head is a member of the whole body. … for the head is one member, who is Christ, the head of the church. …
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The whole Church is Christ's body given life by the Word, who moves each member, and they do nothing apart from him.
comments.comment: … The divine words say that the whole Church of God is the body of Christ, given its soul by the Son of God, and that individual believers are members of this body, taken as a whole (1 Corinthians 12:27; Ephesians 1:22–23). For just as the soul gives life to the body and moves it, though the body is not by nature able to move itself with the motion of life, so the Word, moving the whole body, the Church, to what is needful and working in it, moves it and each member of those who belong to the Church; and they do nothing apart from the Word.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The list begins with the apostles, then church prophets and teachers, and a teacher is set before healers because signs exist so that knowledge may be believed.
comments.comment: … Since he [Paul] mentions members and a body, he begins from the more honorable of the other members after the head, namely the apostles. And 'prophet' he says refers to those in the church, not those in the Law. Third, 'teachers'. Do not marvel if a teacher is set before those performing healings and powers; for the signs are so that knowledge may be believed, and knowledge is provided through the teachers. … 'Governments' refers to the ecclesiastical administrations.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the order of the list and why teachers come before healers.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The word 'prophecy' has two senses, so 'second prophets' is one sense and 'if you all prophesy' is another.
comments.comment: … See whether I can still show the saying more clearly: God set in the church first apostles—but not all are apostles; for if all were apostles, to whom would they minister the apostleship? Second, prophets—not all are prophets; yet according to the other prophecy, “if you all prophesy, and an unbeliever or ungifted person comes in,” it is spoken not as of an impossibility but as of a possibility that all prophesy in that way. So there are two significations from the name “prophecy.” Therefore here too the apostle’s order is kept that says first apostles, second prophets, and the rest. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Interpreting Scripture is better than merely loving tongues, which are empty sounds.
comments.comment: [Of speaking in tongues without understanding:] … For if I utter empty sounds, “I have become a noisy gong” (1 Corinthians 13:1). So it is better to prophesy, that is, to interpret the divine Scriptures in church, than to be fond of merely using tongues.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Without love even angelic speech would be unclear, for nothing makes human or angelic speech plain as love does.
comments.comment: [Of angels conversing with one another:] … do they converse in these same tongues humans use, so that some angels would happen to be Greek, some Hebrew, others Egyptian? Or is it absurd to say this about the upper angelic ranks? Then perhaps, just as there are many dialects among humans, so also among angels? … “If then I speak with the tongues of humans and of angels, but do not have love, I have become a sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal.” Just as sounding bronze gives an indistinct voice, and the clanging cymbal nothing clear, in the same way, without love, a tongue—even of angels among humans by hypothesis—is unclear; for nothing makes human or angelic speech clear and plain as love does; when love is absent, what is spoken is nothing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's picture of the tongues of angels and why speech without love is mere noise.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul speaks by hyperbole, which overshoots the truth for emphasis, so that gifts and love may be weighed and love pursued above all.
comments.comment:
… We ask here whether someone in this life can both have prophecy and know all the mysteries without love, and altogether whether it is given to anyone to know all mysteries; for Paul says, If anyone thinks he has come to know something, he does not yet know as he ought to know; and again, we know in part and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, the partial will be done away. Saying these things about himself and the apostles like him shows that it is not possible to know all mysteries and all knowledge. How then does he speak as if it were possible to know all knowledge and understand all mysteries?

If we look at the preface of the words, in which he says, “And I show you a still more excellent way,” and understand what “excellence” (hyperbole) is, all this will be clarified. Hyperbole, then, as even the Greeks defined it, is speech that for the sake of emphasis overshoots the truth; and they use the example that some are said to be whiter than snow—not that anything can be whiter than snow, but it is said by hyperbole. And again: some horses run like wind—not that such a thing is possible, but for emphasis, so that the horses’ speed may be shown, such a thing is said of them. And in the Scripture of the Psalms it is said of the sea, their waves go up to the heavens and go down to the abysses—which is impossible, but said for emphasis. And in the law you will find the manner of hyperbole written where it is written, We saw cities great and walled up to heaven. How can this be? Yet it is said hyperbolically, the speech not altogether presenting the thing signified itself but showing the greatness of the waves or the lowliness, and the greatness of the walls, or something near these.

So also here the apostle takes a hypothesis in order that the nature of gifts and the nature of love may be examined—not that it is possible for a gift, and so great a gift, to exist without love; or that it is possible in this life for someone to know all knowledge without love, or to have such faith as to move mountains; but wanting to show that if love were set in a balance—the word being spoken by hypothesis. He says, then, that one must especially zealously pursue love. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul can speak of knowing all mysteries or moving mountains without love.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Knowing the open things is knowledge, while knowing the more unspeakable divine things is knowing the mysteries.
comments.comment: What is the difference between knowledge and knowing the mysteries? For the apostle speaks about two things. I hold, then, that knowing about the open things is knowledge, more generic than the mysteries; for within a part of knowledge lies the science of the mysteries. But knowing about the more unspeakable and more divine things is knowing the mystery—so that there is a generic account of knowledge, yet not every grasp of knowledge is grasp of mysteries, about which it is said, But we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom which God predestined before the ages for our glory. When I know these things, then I have the knowledge of the mysteries. “And if I have all faith so as to move mountains”: it is written in the gospel, If you have faith as a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and thrown into the sea,’ and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you. For the one who has faith as a mustard seed has the whole of faith.
comments.selected_reason: Says what Paul means by knowing all mysteries and by faith that moves mountains.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul speaks by hyperbole, so claims like moving mountains exaggerate without lying.
comments.comment: When the height of the cities constructed by those before Israel who possessed the land is spoken of, saying, 'we saw cities there with walls, whose walls reached even to the heaven', it was spoken hyperbolically. And the apostle also knew the logic of hyperbole and the use of the name. 'And still, by way of hyperbole, I say to you: if I have all knowledge and know all the mysteries, but do not have love, I benefit nothing' (1 Cor 13:2). For it is not profitable to know knowledge and all the mysteries without divine love. 'If we have all the faith so as to remove mountains, not having love, the greatness of the faith is nothing' (Matt 17:20). He says love is greater and that it is faith; and he gives it the power to say the mountains are removed; this is not lying, even if it exaggerates.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Love is the fulfillment of the law and better than faith and hope, and Paul weaves it a crown.
comments.comment: … The love then is a fulfillment of law, and better than faith and hope. For thus the divine Paul writes for us. Therefore as it were weaving together for it some many-formed crown from spring flowers, he says again: ‘And if I feed out all my belongings, and if I hand over my body in order that I be burned, yet do not have love, I am benefited nothing. …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 7

comments.capsule: One can give away goods or die as a martyr for empty glory instead of love.
comments.comment: … “If I feed people with all my goods” not because of love; “if I hand over my body that I may boast”—as if it were possible to give away goods not for love but for empty glory, and as if it were possible also to bear witness for the sake of boasting and the glory with which martyrs are glorified in the churches.
comments.selected_reason: Shows how even great sacrifices can come from boasting instead of love.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Not even martyrdom equals love, for love without martyrdom makes disciples of Christ, but martyrdom without love does not.
comments.comment: A man caught up to the third heaven and carried away into paradise, who shared in secret mysteries and enjoyed such boldness before God, did not receive strong perception of those good things unless he also saw his brothers being saved along with him. For Paul knows—Paul knows clearly—that of love nothing is either greater or equal, not even martyrdom itself, which is the chief point of all good things. And how is this so? Listen. Love, even without martyrdom, makes disciples of Christ, but martyrdom without love would not be able to accomplish this. From where is this clear? From the very words of Christ. For he said to his disciples, “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another” (John 13:35). See, love without martyrdom makes disciples. And that martyrdom without love not only does not make disciples but does not even benefit the one enduring it, listen to Paul saying, “If I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have love, I gain nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3).
comments.selected_reason: Shows plainly, from Christ's own words, why even martyrdom gains nothing without love.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Each phrase of Paul's praise of love is a test: patience, kindness, freedom from envy, boasting and indecency, and not seeking one's own all show whether a person has love.
comments.comment: … He [Paul] goes through the praises of the love that surpasses the gifts. For he had to teach both what love is and how the one who has love is. “Love is patient”: if you have patience that is a fruit of the Spirit, you have it because of love. “Is kind”: what is opposite to kindness? Wickedness. If you act wickedly against anyone, you do not have love. If you are kind and sweet toward all humans, you have love. “Love does not envy”: if there is envy in you like Cain’s toward Abel or like Joseph’s brothers toward Joseph, you do not have love. Loving and envying are fighting things. “Love does not brag”: when someone is rash, professing to know about a craft or a science or knowledge, that one is the braggart because he does not have love. “Does not behave indecently”: no one who has love does anything indecent; so if ever a brother and sister claiming to love one another according to God fall through weakness under the pretext of love, let us tell them they do not have love; for love does not behave indecently. “Does not seek its own”: no one who has love seeks his own things; for example a mother loving her son, or a father, does not seek his own as he seeks the son’s; for having love is not self-loving. …
comments.selected_reason: Goes through the qualities of love one by one with plain examples.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Each trait Paul gives to love is learned from patience, so love is patient, kind, free from envy and pride, and endures all things.
comments.comment: Now love, the highest sacrament of faith, the treasure of the Christian name, which the apostle commends with all the strength of the Holy Spirit—by what training is it taught if not the disciplines of patience? Love, he says, is patient: it takes this from patience. It is kind: patience does no evil. It does not envy: that is patience's own property. It is not arrogant: it has drawn its modesty from patience. It is not puffed up, not rude: those things have nothing to do with patience. It does not seek its own: it endures its own while benefiting another. It is not provoked: otherwise what would be left for impatience? Therefore, he says, love bears all things, endures all things (1 Corinthians 13:4-8)—precisely because it is patient. Rightly, then, it will never fail. For the rest will be emptied, completed, exhausted: tongues, knowledge, prophecies. But faith, hope, and love remain (1 Corinthians 13:8-13): faith, which Christ's patience brought in; hope, which human patience waits for; love, which patience accompanies under God as its teacher.
comments.author: Tertullian

comments.capsule: Moses and Paul show love that seeks others' good, Moses asking to be blotted out and Paul wishing to be cut off from Christ for his kinsmen.
comments.comment: [Examples of love that does not seek its own:] … Come also to the saints; see Moses’ love: If you forgive them their sin, forgive; if not, blot me out of your book which you have written. And the apostle also says, just as I also please all in all things, not seeking my own advantage but that of the many, that they may be saved, and I could wish to be anathema from Christ for my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh. He prays to be anathema from Christ for the salvation of others.
comments.selected_reason: Shows by the examples of Moses and Paul what love that does not seek its own looks like.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Love pours itself out on the brother and does not seek its own.
comments.comment: But you, learn the way according to excess that Paul points to for salvation. "Love does not seek its own things," but is poured out upon the brother. It is frantic for him, and soberly raves for him. …
comments.author: Clement of Alexandria
comments.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?

comments.capsule: Tongues cease once minds speak directly.
comments.comment: … Tongues will cease when I converse with mind to the one with whom I wish to speak.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Our progress now is a child's, but the perfect brings full knowledge and the vision of God.
comments.comment: … The one who seems to advance here advances as among children; but when the perfect comes and we attain to a perfect man, then we will contain the things of men—knowledge and prophecy and the vision of God which the blessed will see because of purity of heart.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms the contrast between our partial knowledge now and the perfect to come.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The 'face' in 'face to face' is not a face of the senses but is understood figuratively, like the eyes and ears of God.
comments.comment: … Now, to use Paul’s words, it is “through a mirror and in a riddle, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12). And if I say “face,” let no one misrepresent, because of the word, the sense it conveys. Let him learn instead from the words “with unveiled face, beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, we are being transformed into the same image, from glory to glory” (2 Corinthians 3:18), that in such places it is not a face of the senses that is meant, but one understood figuratively, like the eyes and ears and all the other things we showed above to share their names with the members of the body.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'face to face' does and does not mean.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Faith ends in sight and hope in possession, but love only grows when perfection comes.
comments.comment: [That love is greatest:] … And rightly so. For faith departs when we are persuaded by seeing God with our own eyes, and hope vanishes when the things hoped for are handed over. But love comes together into fullness and grows all the more when the perfect things are handed over. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why love is the greatest of the three.
comments.author: Clement of Alexandria
comments.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?

comments.capsule: Speaking in tongues must not outrank interpreting the prophets, for prophesying now means explaining the prophets' writings, and a tongue speaker speaks to God because no one hears.
comments.comment:
“For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God,” and so on (1 Corinthians 14:2). He weans them from thinking that speaking in tongues does more for one’s good name than interpreting the writings of the prophets. For once faith and hope have first been laid down in us and given first place, and indeed love toward God and the brothers, which holds the fulfillment of the whole Law (Romans 13:10), let the rest be added. For then, then indeed and at the right time, we shall be filled with the very gifts that come from God and grow rich in the gifts given through the Spirit. I mean the ability to prophesy, that is, to interpret the writings of the prophets.

For once the Only-begotten had become man, had suffered and been raised, and his saving plan for us had been carried to completion, what time was there still for prophecy, or what events were still left to foretell? So here “to prophesy” would be nothing other than simply being able to interpret prophecies. And when we make them as clear as we can to our hearers, and then from them firmly establish our own teaching in the truth, we shall be right and unerring interpreters of the noblest things.

So, he says, one who speaks in a tongue speaks to God rather than to men. But how, or in what way? “For no one hears,” he says (1 Corinthians 14:2). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul prefers prophesying to speaking in tongues, and what prophesying means here.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because no one understands a tongue except God, the one speaking in a tongue speaks to God, while the prophet speaks to people to build them up.
comments.comment: … For no one will understand except God alone, who knows all things. “For he speaks mysteries in the Spirit,” he says (1 Corinthians 14:2). Notice how the one who speaks to God speaks in the Spirit: so the Spirit is God. Therefore the one who speaks in a tongue, he says, speaks to God rather than to men; “but the one who prophesies speaks to men for building up, encouragement and consolation” (1 Corinthians 14:3).
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly why a tongue speaks to God and prophecy to men.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Interpreting the prophets ranks higher than speaking in a tongue, because the tongue speaker builds up only himself while the interpreter builds up the church.
comments.comment: Knowing, then, that “to prophesy” here means interpreting the writings of the prophets, through which the word of encouragement is made sure and the mind of those being instructed in the mysteries is led by the hand to the truth concerning Christ, he shows in another way as well that interpreting the prophets ranks incomparably higher than speaking in a tongue. “The one who speaks in a tongue,” he says, “builds up himself” (1 Corinthians 14:4), for he understands, but no one else at all does. But the one who uses the words and predictions of the holy prophets as testimony builds up the church (1 Corinthians 14:4). So prophesying is the greater thing and belongs among the highest grounds for boasting and among bright hopes, if indeed it is admittedly better to build up the church than to speak in a tongue to oneself alone.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by building up oneself and building up the church.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul welcomes tongues as a sign given to believers but turns eagerness toward prophesying, which is greater unless the tongue is interpreted.
comments.comment: “Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more to prophesy,” and so on (1 Corinthians 14:5). It was something wonderful and truly God-given that men who were Hebrews could speak the languages of others. So that no one would think the apostle was rashly passing judgment on what had happened, by calling worthless what had been bestowed through the working of the Spirit (for it was given as a sign to believers), he welcomes the thing and says, “I want you all to speak in tongues.” But at once he plainly cuts short their eagerness for it and turns them to what is better, adding immediately, “but even more to prophesy,” and stating most clearly that the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in a tongue (1 Corinthians 14:5). Yet he shows that the gift is not altogether useless either to those who have it or to those who hear, when he adds, “unless he interprets” (1 Corinthians 14:5), that is, unless he has someone always at his side to interpret for those being instructed in the mysteries.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul both welcomes tongues and ranks prophecy higher.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The one with the building gift is greater as more useful, but a tongue speaker who also interprets is no longer lesser.
comments.comment: … The one who has the building gift is greater than the one who does not, inasmuch as the one with the building gift is more useful to the common good; but if the one speaking in tongues also has interpretation for building the church, the prophet is no longer greater. For sometimes he speaks high things, speaking to himself and to God, so that the church cannot hear.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Prophecy is knowledge that signifies the unseen, teaching is the word given to many, and revelation is the mind going outside earthly things.
comments.comment: … Prophecy is knowledge that signifies the unseen through speech—knowledge of the world’s constitution and of the working of elements and times. Teaching is the instructional word distributed to the many. Revelation is when the mind goes outside earthly things and puts away every fleshly practice by God’s power; the one who obtains this has come into revelation. Perhaps also knowledge about future things can be called revelation; and one who has understood each term’s proper sense may use the names more loosely.
comments.selected_reason: Defines the four ways Paul says he could profit the Corinthians.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who speak in a tongue without interpretation should be silent in church, like a lifeless flute or a trumpet giving no clear call.
comments.comment: … He [Paul] wants to shame those who speak in a tongue into silence in church if there is no interpreter. Lifeless flute and lyre that give no distinction of musical notes are not known by what rhythm they played; the soldier does not arm for war unless the trumpet utters the voice that rouses to war; and those who speak in a tongue and do not interpret ought not to speak, as giving no distinction to the words for understanding. He called the doctrines of contemplation flute and lyre as showing nothing ethical, and those who urge toward virtue a trumpet. Hence one may say that the unclear parts of Scripture—such as the sacrifices in Leviticus and the tent in Exodus—should not be read unless someone clarifies their mind by exposition.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's musical pictures of unclear speech.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Though humans do not understand, the powers hear.
comments.comment: … The one who speaks in a tongue speaks in God; even if humans do not understand, still the powers about the air hear.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who prided themselves on tongues did not pray in the hearers' language, yet where hearers do not know the language nothing is gained, and teachers must use familiar speech.
comments.comment:
“And none of them is voiceless” (1 Corinthians 14:10). Some people used to come into the churches who had been enriched, by the working of the Spirit, with the ability to speak in tongues. Then, when they ought to have offered the prayers in the churches, and before these the litanies or the psalmody, using the language of those present, which they were able to do, they did not do it. Priding themselves only on the gift of tongues, they offered neither prayers nor psalmody. Paul teaches this: if the hearers do not know the language in which the one who has the gift is speaking, nothing is gained from it. For there are countless nations and many human languages, and none of those once counted among rational beings, or among men, is voiceless.

He says that none of those counted among rational beings, that is, among men, is altogether voiceless. But if someone does not know the meaning of another’s speech, and the others in turn do not know his language, they will be foreigners to one another (1 Corinthians 14:11), even though each speaks correctly in his own tongue. So those who wish to teach others must utter speech familiar to their hearers. But if the sound has no clear meaning and the speech is unfamiliar, he has labored in vain, merely striking the learner’s ear with an empty noise (1 Corinthians 14:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the point of Paul's examples about languages and unclear sounds.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Even lifeless bodies give voice when one strikes another.
comments.comment: … So even the lifeless give voice, some with this distinction of notes, some without it; for every body has a property of voice when it strikes another body.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Speech a hearer cannot understand makes each a barbarian to the other, and gifts grow only when used for the common good.
comments.comment: … Everyone who speaks to someone what that one does not understand seems a barbarian to the hearer, and that one to him. … Abounding happens by the superiority of gifts from seeking what builds the church, inasmuch as the one who does not seek the common good does not abound in the gifts. For likely the working of the gift is idle when it does not shine before humans. Therefore if we want the gifts to grow, we will give ourselves over to the benefit of the many.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the barbarian image and why gifts must serve the common good.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A tongue speaker without interpretation understands what moves him to speak, but the fruit comes when others understand.
comments.comment: … If the tongue speaker does not have the gift of interpreting, even if others do not understand, he himself understands what is cast into him from the spirit so that he is moved to speak. But when what is spoken is understood by others, then that seems to be fruit of the speaker toward those who understand.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: When praying in a tongue one must still engage the mind and understand the psalmody, or the mind becomes unfruitful and gains nothing.
comments.comment:
… So if, he says, I offer the prayers in the churches “in the spirit,” that is, using the tongue given through the Spirit, my mind will be unfruitful (1 Corinthians 14:14). For in prayer one must be intent and seek from God what leads to salvation, not pride oneself on a tongue and give oneself over merely to speaking in a tongue, since then the mind becomes unfruitful and gains no benefit from such display.

“I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind also” (1 Corinthians 14:15). So, he says, if I choose to pray in a tongue, that is, to win esteem by speaking in a tongue, I must take earnest care not to have an unfruitful mind, and not to give myself over only to speaking in the tongue, but to rouse my mind within me. And if I happen to sing in a tongue, I must sing no less with the mind as well, by understanding the meaning of the psalmody and of the prophecy, and not leave such words unexamined (1 Corinthians 14:15). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to pray with the spirit and with the mind.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Our mind cannot pray or sing to the Father unless the Spirit first prays and hymns him.
comments.comment: [Of praying with the spirit and with the mind:] … For our mind cannot pray unless the Spirit first prays, as in accompaniment of it — just as it cannot sing and hymn the Father in Christ rhythmically, melodiously, metrically, harmoniously, unless the Spirit who searches all things, even the depths of God, first praises and hymns him whose depths it has searched and, as far as it could, grasped.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: These words teach the common good.
comments.comment: … Through these [verses] too we are taught to seek the common good of the church.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Without understanding the language, the listener cannot answer Amen to the prayer, so the tongue speaker may do well himself but the other is not built up.
comments.comment: “Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit, how will the one who fills the place of the uninstructed say the ‘Amen’?” (1 Corinthians 14:16). When you speak in a tongue, he says, how will the one who stands in the rank of the layman, if he does not know your language, answer “Amen” at your thanksgivings, that is, your prayers? For it is plain to everyone that in the churches the custom is for the prayers of those in the leaders’ charge to end together with the prayers of the leaders. They answer “Amen,” closing their own supplications to God at the priest’s words, so that whatever seems lacking in the people’s measure may be made up by the perfection of the priests, and so that God may receive, as it were, “the small together with the great” (Psalm 115:13) as in unity of spirit. For the people in their charge, joining their own prayers to the prayers of the priests, have believed that these will be accepted. … You yourself will do well, at least by the understanding that is in you, but the other is not built up (1 Corinthians 14:16–17). Yet everything we do must be done for building up and for the benefit of the brothers (1 Corinthians 14:26).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the Amen of the people and why unclear prayer does not build them up.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Speaking sense words aims at the common good of the five senses, and hearing only the bare sound of Scripture marks catechumens, not the faithful.
comments.comment: … Even speaking the sense words spiritually is seeking the common good of the five senses; and the word of catechesis through the five senses is set for the hearers in church, as they too are catechized by the five words. For those who do not know the clarity of what is said, but attend only to the bare sound of the Scriptures, are called catechumens; but those who hear the distinction of the notes from Scripture are not catechumens but faithful.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since Paul's command is possible, we can be perfect in mind and infants in evil.
comments.comment: … Since what he commands is possible, it is possible for us to become perfect in our minds. This nearly interprets, Unless you turn and become as the children; for the one who is an infant in evil, having turned, becomes as a child.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul calls prophecy 'law', quoting wording found in Aquila.
comments.comment: … He also called the prophetic word “law”; and we found these words in Aquila and the other editions, not indeed in the Seventy.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Prophecy has a more universal kind like Isaiah's and a last-ranked kind that convicts an unbeliever by laying bare his heart.
comments.comment: … He [Paul] will call the more catholic [universal] sort, imitating the prophecies of Isaiah and Jeremiah, second rank after the apostleship; but this last-ranked sort after the gifts already named is such as: if you prophesy, and an unbeliever or ungifted person comes in, he is convicted by all, examined by all, the secrets of his heart become plain, and so falling on his face he will worship God and announce that God is truly among you. For this is not far from the working of powers and the gift of healings that happen for the amazement of those who see, so that the one prophesying may say, “You have this in your heart; from this sin you have come to the church.” This prophecy can also be later in rank than the former ones, while that more divine and greater one is second, of which he says, God set in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophetic gift lays bare an unbeliever's heart, and that convicting and examining shows that God is in the spirit of such people.
comments.comment: … Since the prophetic gift makes known the secrets of the unbeliever’s and ungifted person’s heart when he draws near them, clearly when the perfect comes they will know perfectly every ungifted and unbeliever’s secrets—and likely then also the holy person’s secrets become plain to the prophets, perhaps the greater knowing the lesser’s. And the one benefited is cautious to look into God’s face; therefore imagining God he falls on his face, giving him the superiority and glory, and so worships God. Convicting and examining the heart’s secrets—that is, making them plain—marks that God is in the spirit of such people. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: All who can teach may speak.
comments.comment: … When we come together, all who have gifts and are able to teach must be allowed to speak.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Prophets need others with the gift of discernment to judge their words, and not everyone knows the things of God unless he is a prophet or spiritual.
comments.comment: … By “others” he [Paul] means those who have the gift of clarifying the prophets’ spiritual words, if indeed the prophesying ones themselves did not have the gift of discernment; for in what they lack this, they may well have been deceived by some wicked spirit transforming itself into an angel of light, as if they had obtained prophetic rank. … There is danger for those who read to declare simply, and likewise for those who hear. Hear Paul saying, If anyone thinks he is a prophet or spiritual among you, let him acknowledge that what I write is of God, as if not everyone knows the things of God unless he is prophet or spiritual. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the others are who discern, and why discernment is needed.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Prophets were not beside themselves, since they had power to stay silent, and the spirits are subject to the prophets.
comments.comment: … Therefore the prophets were not beside themselves; for in them was the power to be silent and to hold back the spirit upon them. … For this reason the subjection shows willingly in silence; that the spirits are subject to the prophets, but it is the prophets’ souls that prophesy.
comments.selected_reason: Shows that the prophets stayed in control of themselves.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A gift of discerning prophets lay among the people and many were permitted to speak, which is why Paul allowed all to speak.
comments.comment: … there was a gift among the people, as of prophesying, so also of discerning prophets. “For you can all prophesy one by one”: there was then abundance of speakers and of those permitted to speak. For this reason the apostle allowed all to speak in church; he almost allowed even the women to speak, if he had not said what follows.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: From the beginning men had authority to speak and women asked about what they were unsure of, and the law means Genesis.
comments.comment: … Since from the beginning the men had authority to speak and benefit the hearers, and the women asked about what they were unsure of. And by “law” he means what is said in Genesis, Your turning shall be to your husband. … As if all speak and can speak when a revelation comes to them, he says women are to be silent in the churches. The women’s disciples—those discipled by Priscilla and Maximilla—were not of this commandment …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Even if women prophesied, as Philip's daughters did, they are not shown speaking in church, and a woman is still not permitted to speak there.
comments.comment:
… But still let us be fair and meet even their plausible points. They [the disciples of Priscilla and Maximilla] say Philip the evangelist had four daughters and they prophesied. If they prophesied, what is absurd, as those people say, if our women also prophesy as prophetesses? We will solve this. First by saying: our women prophesied—show the signs of prophecy in them. Second: even if Philip’s daughters prophesied, they did not speak in the churches; for we do not have this in the Acts of the Apostles. Nor in the old: Deborah is attested a prophetess, and Miriam sister of Aaron took the tambourine and led the women. But you would not find that Deborah harangued the people like Jeremiah and Isaiah; you would not find that Huldah, being a prophetess, spoke to the people but to one who came to her. And in the gospel Anna is recorded a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel of Asher’s tribe; but she did not speak in church. So even if a woman is granted to be a prophetess from a prophetic sign, she is still not permitted to speak in church. When Miriam the prophetess spoke she was leader of certain women; for it is shameful for a woman to speak in church, and I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man.

I will also show this from elsewhere, even if that was said more securely about the woman not becoming leader by the man’s word: an older woman in a deportment sacred, a good teacher, that she may train the young women—not simply that they teach. For let women also be good teachers, not so that men sit and hear women as if men able to be ambassadors of God’s word were lacking. “If they wish to learn something, let them ask their own husbands at home; for it is shameful for women to speak in church.” It seems to me “their own husbands” does not refer only to married men; for virgins would either speak in church or have no teachers, and widows likewise; but perhaps “own men” such as brother and household member and son? Once for all let a woman inquire of her own man according to the generic name “man” over against “woman”; for it is shameful for a woman to speak in church, whatever she may say, even if she says wonders, even if holy things, only because it comes from a woman’s mouth. …
comments.selected_reason: Gives this early reader's reasons for how he read the command to be silent.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul asks if God's word and the church's rule came only to the Corinthians.
comments.comment: … “Or did the word of God go out from you, or did it come to you alone?” As if this disorder was in Corinth along with the other sins. So he says God sent his word into the world. Did the truth and the church rule then come only to you Corinthians?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Only a prophet or spiritual person can know that Paul's writing is the Lord's, and one who does not know it has not yet arrived at being God's.
comments.comment: … Spiritual is the one able to test every word and every mind, and through great depth of mind hard to diagnose so as not to be examined. It is not for just anyone to know that what Paul writes is the Lord’s, but for a prophet or spiritual; therefore the one who does not know it is the Lord’s is neither prophet nor spiritual. Believing is one thing and knowing another; therefore the one ignorant that it is the Lord’s is ignorant, not yet having arrived at truly being God’s; for the one known is somehow mixed into the one who knows him.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We should ask the Giver of gifts for a prophetic gift so as to judge what is God's, since one deprived of this grace cannot understand.
comments.comment: … So that we may know the things of God, let us ask the Giver of gifts to give us a prophetic gift and make us spiritual from the ruling spirit; and so be ready to judge which things are God’s and which are not. For the one deprived of this grace cannot understand; hence he added, “If anyone is ignorant, let him be ignorant.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul teaches that every person, whether in the faith or outside it, has a spirit from God besides his own human spirit.
comments.comment: … If anyone thinks he is a prophet or spiritual, let him acknowledge that what I write is of God; but if anyone is ignorant, he is ignored. So not only is the one who ignores the apostle’s things ignored by God, but if someone ignores while speaking by a divine spirit—and were to say that he does not speak by a divine spirit—he is ignored by God. Through these things the apostle seems to teach that there is no human who does not have another spirit in him besides the spirit of the human that is in him. Whether he is alien to the faith or belonging to it, he has a spirit belonging to him from God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The gospel Paul preached is that the dead rise, beginning with Christ, who would have become man in vain if death were not abolished.
comments.comment:
I say not something foreign, he says, but what I preached. And not only did I preach, but you did not receive, but what also you received. And you did not receive in vain or without foundation, but in which you are being saved. He says that he is about to say that he made known to you that the Lord Jesus died for us; by what word is this gospel, so that the resurrection may be believed; for Jesus is the firstfruits of the resurrection, having died for us. For if death were not to be abolished, the Savior would not have become man, unless in vain he returned. …

The word of the gospel is the resurrection from the dead, the beginning of which is Christ. For if God did not intend for death to be taken away, He would not have become human. Therefore, if you do not hold fast to what you heard but have rejected it, it is clear that you believed in vain.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul rightly calls the preaching of the resurrection a gospel, because it announces every good thing, and to stand in it is to be firm in hope and well established in glory.
comments.comment: “Now I make known to you, brothers, the gospel that I preached to you” (1 Corinthians 15:1). Very aptly and wisely he calls the preaching about the resurrection of the dead, and surely also about the resurrection of Christ himself, a gospel, for it truly is the announcement of every good thing to those who have received the faith. And he says that they stand in it and are being saved (1 Corinthians 15:1–2). “To stand” signifies that believers are firm in hope and well established in glory …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To stand in the gospel is to rest one's soul on it as on a boat; the Jews, those who take it their own way, and those who sin have not stood in it, but those who live by it have.
comments.comment: “I make known to you, brothers, the gospel which I gospelled to you, which also you received, in which also you stand, through which also you are saved, by what word I gospelled to you, if you hold it fast—unless you believed in vain.” [Origen:] He calls gospel what he gospels, for this he also handed on; and this one stands in the gospel who has his soul mounted on it as on a boat, through which he is also saved. And he says the one who does not hold the gospel’s word has believed in vain—having heard irrationally and by chance and not by examination. [Origen:] Jews have not stood in the gospel, not receiving Jesus; those from the heresies stand badly, not understanding the gospel but taking it in their own way; those who sin have not stood, not living according to the gospel. Who then have stood in the gospel but those who received it and accepted it and live according to it?
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'in which you stand' and 'believed in vain'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who believe too early and fall away under trial have believed in vain, because they did not believe firmly.
comments.comment: Those who believe before the time and fall away in a time of trial believe in vain; and yet they have not believed false things but the true—yet because they have not believed firmly, for that reason they fall away in a time of trial. For one who believes well will not fall.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'believed in vain' means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul's gospel came from Christ himself, and Christ's burial proves his death was real while his rising proves he is God by nature.
comments.comment:
“For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received” (1 Corinthians 15:3).

He says that he delivered to them, not something that had simply come into his mind and been accepted without testing, but the gospel that he received, since the one who became man for our sake put the knowledge of it into him. For the same apostle says again of the gospel, “For I did not receive it from any man, nor was I taught it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (Galatians 1:12). If, then, the one who hands it on is taught by God, how can what he preaches not be true: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3), that is, both the Old and the New?

For the witnesses of Christ’s death and resurrection are very many, so that it can no longer be doubted in any way that Christ Jesus died for us according to the flesh, to take away the sin of the world (John 1:29), and that he rose again, trampling on death, so that we too might gain this. Here he necessarily says not only that he died but also that he was buried (1 Corinthians 15:4). For Emmanuel was laid in a tomb to confirm that he had truly died; yet he came back to life, as I said just now. By dying in the flesh he gave full assurance that the Word, though he is God, had become flesh (John 1:14); and by trampling on death he showed plainly that he is God by nature.
comments.selected_reason: States plainly what Paul handed on and why Christ's burial matters.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul handed on first of all not his own argument but what he received from Scripture and eyewitnesses.
comments.comment: 'In the first place' means 'before all things'; I delivered this to you. … I did not deliver a mere argument of my own, but what I received from the Scriptures. It was confirmed by eyewitnesses, that Christ, having died, rose and called him from heaven.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the plain sense of 'first of importance' and where Paul's message came from.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Christ gave life to his own body, and through it the whole of human nature was raised with him, as the Scriptures foretold and the apostles saw.
comments.comment:
Yet the Word who is from God the Father does not give life to a temple foreign to him, nor simply to that of someone else, but rather to his own body, through which he is also said to have died for us, so that the good of the resurrection too might be found to have truly come about for us. For the whole of human nature was in him, trampling on death; this is how we are said to have been buried with him and raised with him (Colossians 2:12), and seated with him “in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 2:6).

So he says that he was raised in accordance with the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:4), and that he appeared to the holy apostles, to some of them separately, as chosen ones, and also to a great number at once (1 Corinthians 15:5–7).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Twelve probably included Matthias, who replaced Judas.
comments.comment: “And that he appeared to Cephas, then to the Twelve.” [Origen:] He says the Lord appeared to the Twelve after the resurrection; for it is likely that Matthias also was present, who was set as apostle in Judas’s place.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The risen Christ appeared in order, to Peter, the Twelve with Matthias, the five hundred, James, the other apostles, and last to Paul.
comments.comment: Cephas, that is Peter, as it were the “firstfruits” of the apostles, was able to see it [his divinity]; after him the Twelve, Matthias having been appointed in place of Judas (Acts 1:26); and after them “five hundred brothers at one time.” “Then he appeared to James, then to all the” other “apostles” besides the Twelve, perhaps to the Seventy (Luke 10:1); “and last of all” to Paul, as to “one untimely born” (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). Paul knew well in what sense he said, “To me, less than the least of all the saints, this grace was given” (Ephesians 3:8); and perhaps “less than the least” means the same as “untimely born.”
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul calls himself untimely born because, as a persecutor, he had not been formed in the Law toward perfection, as infants are formed in the womb.
comments.comment: [On “one untimely born”:] an abortion [a miscarriage] is that which is cast out in the womb before being formed and receiving the time due to it, which also cannot live. Just as in the womb infants are being formed, so in the Law souls were being pre-formed toward piety, and were born of water and Spirit. But Paul persecuted the church without being formed in the Law toward perfection—for he did persecute—therefore he called himself an abortion, and he brings this forth further: because I persecuted the church of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul uses the unusual phrase 'untimely born'.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul humbly names himself last and untimely born among the apostles, yet by mercy he was called, and the resurrection was foretold and witnessed.
comments.comment: “And he appeared also to me,” as to the one untimely born among the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:8). He speaks very humbly: he insists that he persecuted the church, but that he received mercy from Christ and was called to be an apostle (1 Corinthians 15:9–10). And he shows that the great mystery of the resurrection was not unknown either to the saints of old, for it had been foretold, or to those chosen for apostleship, who also “became eyewitnesses and ministers of the word” (Luke 1:2).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul, though a persecutor, received grace by God's foreknowledge and used it in his labors.
comments.comment: Being a persecutor, he happened to receive such grace according to the foreknowledge of God, so that he labored more than the others. … 'not in vain did I receive much grace', but I used it for the sake of the preaching, laboring more than all of them.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul confesses his unworthiness, and says his labor was God's grace working with him, a grace that those who live unworthily receive in vain.
comments.comment:
“For I am the least of the apostles, who am not fit to be called apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.” [Origen:] Conscious of the sins from which he was freed, he says, “I am not fit to be called apostle.” …

“But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not empty, but I labored more abundantly than they all—yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me.” [Origen:] Having said that his grace toward me was not empty, he taught that those who live unworthily of the grace received it empty. It is not that grace labors, but it must be understood thus: “I did not do these things, but the grace that is with me.”
comments.selected_reason: Shows in plain terms what Paul means by 'not I, but the grace of God'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The apostles all agree about Christ's resurrection, so the proof is firm.
comments.comment: “Whether then I or they, so we preach and so you believed.” [Origen:] All the apostles having been fully persuaded about Christ’s resurrection from the dead, the proof is firm; therefore we say the same things; for you also believed thus.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since Christ died to open a way for human nature to overcome death, denying the resurrection of the dead makes no sense.
comments.comment: “Now if Christ is preached as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?” (1 Corinthians 15:12). He is astonished at those who, I do not know how, have been persuaded to set themselves against the holy and divine Scriptures and dare to think something other than this. For if Christ died, not to remain dead, but so that, proving stronger than death and corruption, he might become a kind of way and door for human nature (John 14:6; John 10:9), so that it could prevail over corruption and run back to life, then how, now that he who for our sake was among the dead has been raised, so that we too might rise with him to life, can they still bind in the snares of death those for whose sake Emmanuel, who is God by nature, is said to have died and come back to life?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Anyone who admits Christ rose but denies the resurrection of the dead ignores why the Only-begotten became man: to destroy death, redeem our bodies and change them.
comments.comment:
So if some agree that Christ has been raised, yet do not accept the mystery of the resurrection from the dead, they are wholly ignorant of the purpose for which the Only-begotten became man. For God the Word did not become man for his own sake; and “for the joy that was set before him he endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2). For what reason? The most wise Paul himself will teach us, saying, “Since the children share in blood and flesh, he himself likewise partook of the same, so that through death he might destroy him who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and set free those who through fear of death were subject to slavery all their lives” (Hebrews 2:14–15).

So if death is not destroyed, his design was in vain, and the mystery of the dispensation in the flesh is of no profit to us either; and we have missed the hope of life as well. And how have we been called to adoption, and how are we children of God, as the wise John says (1 John 3:1)? If it is true that “we wait for adoption, the redemption of our body” (Romans 8:23), what redemption is there at all, unless Christ has made us stronger than death? Or how “will he change the body of our lowliness to be conformed to the body of his glory” (Philippians 3:21)? For what time will there be for this at all, unless death is made idle? Or what change will there be for those who will stay as they were, or rather end in a worse state?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul argues that since Christ died for us and rose as the firstfruits of renewed humanity, no one should say the dead will not rise.
comments.comment: See how skillfully he brings them round to the necessary admission that we must say our earthly bodies will come to life again in due time. For if, he says, Christ has been proclaimed through the whole of inspired Scripture as raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead (1 Corinthians 15:12)? For he died, as we have said already, not for himself but rather for us, so that, since he is Life by nature as God, he might destroy death by the death of his own flesh, since human nature would follow him. For he came to life again and became, as it were, the firstfruits of humanity as it passes over into life, is created anew for incorruption, and conquers death. For what is in Christ is a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17). Since the thing has made its beginning, how shall we remain in the earth? Or how do some among you dare to say that the dead will not come to life again?
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christ's rising leads to ours.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those at Corinth who denied the resurrection were likely Sadducees; Hymenaeus and Alexander also slandered it.
comments.comment: These [who deny the resurrection], it seems likely, were Sadducees; for they used to say “that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit” (Acts 23:8). Hymenaeus and Alexander also slandered the mystery of the resurrection, “saying that the resurrection has already taken place” (2 Timothy 2:18).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To deny the resurrection of the dead, even only in the heart, is to deny Christ's resurrection too, and it is no more impossible than the making of the body, heaven or the sun.
comments.comment: Some shamelessly admit that Christ has been raised from the dead, yet say there is no resurrection of the dead. Therefore the apostle says, If Christ is preached that he has been raised from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?. Even if someone does not say it with the mouth, but says in the heart “there is no resurrection of the dead,” he effectively rejects also Jesus Christ’s resurrection. For if the universal is false, clearly the one who rose from the dead is also contained in the universal. For if the dead are not raised, and Jesus also was among the dead, then Jesus has not been raised either; but if he has been raised, through him the resurrection of the dead is shown—unless we disbelieve the thing as impossible in itself, forgetting who promised. For what, among impossibles so to speak, is more impossible: that the body be made alive, or that heaven come to be from things that are not, or the sun, or the rest of the creatures?
comments.selected_reason: Plain argument that Christ's rising and ours go together.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ's rising and ours stand or fall together.
comments.comment: it is not possible that Christ rose and the rest do not; but, to speak in agreement, if for nothing Christ died and rose, then through nothing is our resurrection.
