comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Christ rose in his own flesh; those who allegorize human resurrection should allegorize his too.
comments.comment: if Christ is preached raised, how do some say there is no resurrection of the dead? [Origen:] Christ’s resurrection with the flesh he had is clear from the text before us. But some, or rather the heterodox, want to allegorize humans’ resurrection; let them allegorize the Savior’s too, badly rejecting the wording.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: If Christ were not raised, the apostles' preaching and the believers' faith would be empty, and the apostles would be false witnesses against God.
comments.comment: “If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is empty” (1 Corinthians 15:14). For the second follows on the first, and with the second the first is taken away too. If that happened, that is, if we accepted it as our belief, the preaching of the holy apostles would be empty and powerless, and faith too would be empty (1 Corinthians 15:14). For this is what the word of faith holds, the word that through the saints has taught the mysteries to the initiated throughout the whole earth. How then shall we still believe, if, as some say, he did not come to life again? For, he says, we are even found to be false witnesses against God, claiming that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if the dead are not raised (1 Corinthians 15:15). Then how could so great a multitude of saints escape an indictment for slander? They would not even be saints. How could they be, when their offense would be slander against God? But that is not how things stand; for the teachers of the mysteries do not lie when they say that Christ has been raised.
comments.selected_reason: Shows in plain steps what hangs on Christ's resurrection.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since the preaching and faith are not empty, Christ has been raised, and since he is the firstfruits, the dead are raised too.
comments.comment: “If Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is empty, and your faith is empty.” [Origen:] Since neither the preaching nor the faith is empty, it is clear Christ has been raised. … If the one who says Christ rose bears false witness against God, then also everyone who says there is a resurrection of the dead; but if Christ rose as firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, it is clear the dead are raised.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Faith justifies, so if Christ has not been raised, faith is useless.
comments.comment: “If Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). Most truly and very rightly he adds this as well to the rest. For faith justifies; but if one declares it futile, on the ground that Christ has not been raised, what difference does it make any more?
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Without the resurrection the psalmists' words on forgiveness would be in vain, since we are justified in Christ, who was raised for our justification.
comments.comment: In vain, too, did the inspired singer say, “Lord, you were pleased with your land; you forgave your people their iniquities; you covered all their sins” (Psalm 85:1–2); and again, “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered; blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not reckon sin” (Psalm 32:1–2). And yet the blessed Paul says, in his Letter to the Romans, that the blessing spoken in these words reaches both the circumcision and those from the Gentiles (Romans 4:9). For we have been justified in Christ, “who was handed over for our trespasses and raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Without the resurrection the saints' labors and deaths would be for nothing, but the dead will rise, and God will judge each as he deserves.
comments.comment: “Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished” (1 Corinthians 15:18). For it seems they have been deceived and have laid down their lives for him without reward, if Christ has not been raised. If the hope of the saints is not full of immortality, if they do not look to reign with him, then perhaps they have perished; and since they endured even death itself for nothing of use, their labors have brought them only loss. Away with such dreadful ignorance! For “the dead shall rise, and those in the tombs shall be raised,” as the prophet says (Isaiah 26:19); and he who hands out the crowns weighs out to each the one most fitting for him, and he will surely bring punishment on the ungodly; for as God he is the judge of all.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says those who died in Christ would have perished.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Unbelief in the resurrection amounts to not believing in any life after death, which would make Christians most pitiable.
comments.comment: And the apostle took unbelief in the resurrection from the dead as equal to not believing that we shall exist at all after departure. Therefore to those who do not believe there will be a resurrection of the dead he says, as if according to them there is no other life besides the present, If in this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are of all humans most pitiable.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because Christ is the firstfruits and firstborn from the dead, the rest of humanity must follow him.
comments.comment: Why do they [who deny the resurrection] rob the human race of the good things that come from the resurrection, and slander the goal of his saving work in the flesh? For if Christ has become “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20) and “the firstborn from the dead” (Colossians 1:18), then surely what remains will follow its own firstfruits and will go along with the firstborn, and with good reason, in keeping with what a firstborn is understood to be.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is the firstfruits of the dead, the first to trample down death, as Adam was the first to enter it, and the resurrection of the dead follows his.
comments.comment: “But now Christ has been raised from the dead, and has become the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,” and so on (1 Corinthians 15:20). From here he takes it as agreed that we must believe that Christ came to life again and became the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, the first of those on earth to trample down death, just as our forefather Adam was the first to step into it and became the firstfruits of those who slipped into corruption. And that the resurrection of the dead will follow the resurrection of our Savior he adds when he says, “For as death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead also came through a man” (1 Corinthians 15:21).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'firstfruits' and why the resurrection comes through a man.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul here means not the general rising, which even the ungodly will have, but the blessed resurrection of those to be transferred into glory.
comments.comment: ‘But now,’ he says, ‘Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep. Since death came through a human being, resurrection of the dead also comes through a human being’ (1 Corinthians 15:20–21). Here the apostle speaks not of the general resurrection, which even criminals and impious people will experience, but only of those to be transferred into glory. He indicates blessed resurrection by the unqualified name ‘resurrection,’ passing over the ungodly’s rising as though, compared with it, it were no resurrection at all.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Christ rose with a body, so if he is the firstborn from the dead, those who rise must rise as he did.
comments.comment: … If then Jesus also is firstborn from the dead, the resurrection of those who rise must be of the same kind. And if he wore a body, and his resurrection was with a body so that he even ate, as is written in the Gospel according to John, while those who rise among believers in Christ rise otherwise, as those from the heresies think, they cannot show how Jesus is firstborn from the dead. For if we have become conformed to the death of Christ, we shall also be conformed to his resurrection; and how does Paul teach saying, who will transform the body of our humiliation conformed to the body of Christ’s glory?
comments.selected_reason: Explains in familiar terms why our rising is like his.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since firstfruits means the first part of many, Christ is the firstfruits of all who have died, and Paul says that all, not only the righteous, will be made alive in Christ.
comments.comment: “But now Christ has been raised from the dead; he became firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.” Firstfruits is firstfruits of many. As we saw in the law’s examples: firstfruits of wheat is offered by those who harvested wheat; and say of wine by those who gathered wine; and of oil from those who crushed olive; so if our Lord Jesus Christ is firstfruits of those fallen asleep, there must be many of whom he is firstfruits; and we ask whether he is firstfruits of all or of many? For Christ, it says, is firstfruits of those fallen asleep. If we did not have a wording from the start, we might even say—thinking it somehow ill-omened here to call him firstfruits of all—that he is firstfruits of the righteous fallen asleep only, not of the rest. But now the apostle himself also says, For since through a human came death, through a human also resurrection of the dead; how then does he say of some what he says of all? For as in Adam all die, so in Christ—he did not say “the righteous will be made alive” but all will be made alive.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'firstfruits' implies and who is made alive.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ rose first, and the others will follow in due time, not in a confused mass but in order, rank by rank.
comments.comment: Christ, as all agree, has been raised as the firstfruits, “so that he himself might have first place in all things” (Colossians 1:18), as it is written. Yet in due time the others will follow in coming to life again, though, as is fitting, not in a confused mass, but in order, rank by rank, and as at a word of command (compare 1 Thessalonians 4:16). For after the firstfruits, that is, Christ, he says, those who are his will be raised (1 Corinthians 15:23).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A man had to conquer death for us, so the Word became man, healing what had fallen and overcoming death through obedience.
comments.comment: See how he shows once more that the mystery of the dispensation in the flesh is full of a skill worthy of God. For it was needful, truly needful, he says, that a man should conquer death for us. For this reason God the Word, who shone forth from God, did not take hold of angels, as Paul himself says, but of the seed of Abraham, so that he might be made like his brothers in every way (Hebrews 2:16–17). For, as I said, what had fallen sick had to be healed, and what had fallen had to rise. What had come under death through transgression and sin had to overcome death through obedience and righteousness. That is why the Only-begotten Word of God, who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21), became man: so that, as in Adam we have all been condemned, when human nature suffered death, so also, justified in Christ, we might strip off, together with sin, the death that sprang from it. The inspired Paul himself will bear witness, saying, “For as by the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners” (Romans 5:19).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: As the first Adam brought us down into corruption, Christ brought us up into life, as God in the flesh raising his own temple so that we might be raised with him.
comments.comment: “For since through a human comes death, through a human also comes resurrection of the dead; for as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.” (1 Corinthians 15:21–22) Christ has been named second Adam; and just as the first Adam brought us down into corruption, so also Christ brought us back up into life — not as a bare human who died for us, lest we also remain dead in him, but as God in flesh, having suffered in it humanly, so that when he raised his own temple divinely we might be raised with him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: As human nature was condemned in Adam, so in Christ it is blessed again, for the Word, who is Life, passes his life on to the whole of human nature.
comments.comment: So, as in Adam all die (1 Corinthians 15:22), since, as I said, human nature was condemned in him because of the transgression, so in Christ they will be made alive, since in him human nature is blessed again in the same way because of the justification. The second, then, is the undoing of the first. For “he was handed over for our trespasses and raised for our justification” (Romans 4:25). So when he was raised, we too were raised with him. For the Word who is from God is Life by nature; and he surely does not give the good that belongs to his nature, I mean life, to his own flesh alone, but passes it on to the whole of human nature.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how all die in Adam and are made alive in Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: All are raised by the power that created them, but only believers are made alive in Christ's faith.
comments.comment: It follows: ‘As all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ’ (1 Corinthians 15:22). Does ‘All will be made alive in Christ’ include the ungodly, or refer only to believers? If to the ungodly, because everyone is made alive in Christ, no one is punished. If to believers, then not everyone is made alive in Christ’s faith, but only believers, although absolutely everyone is raised by the same power through which they were created.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: That all will be made alive does not make the toil of the righteous vain, for each rises in his own order, and Christ took up the death of the dead to become the firstfruits of life.
comments.comment: Then so that you not be disturbed and say, “Was so much toil poured out for me in vain, if Christ raised from the dead is firstfruits of all who have fallen asleep and in Christ all will be made alive?” he says, But each in his own order. So all died in Adam, and all will be made alive in Christ; yet even though all died in Adam, Abraham was no less righteous, Isaac was a patriarch, Jacob who fathered the twelve patriarchs was Israel; and so one will come also to the other righteous. I dare say that while the apostle said Christ Jesus is firstfruits of those fallen asleep, I would put beside that: this one is firstfruits unto life of those who will live, while Adam has become firstfruits of humans’ death; for in Adam all die, he having taken the firstfruits of death; but the Savior, wanting to take up the firstfruits of life, first took up the death of the dead, that having abolished death he might become firstfruits of those fallen asleep and of the living.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who belong to Christ after his coming are better than the saints under the law, so they rise first, as the master of the vineyard paid the last first.
comments.comment:
[Those who belong to Christ at his coming are] those who lived after he became man, and who have fallen asleep in faith. For there were, admittedly, saints from time to time in Israel, while the life under the law was praised and still held sway. But those in Christ are better: they have been justified through faith, have become partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4), and have been made rich with the Spirit of adoption (Romans 8:15). They have also been called by grace into brotherhood with him who is Son by nature and in truth. Among those under the law there was a spirit of slavery, but we cry, “Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15). So, as I said, those in Christ are better than those of older times.

That is why he says that they will be the first to come to life again, following, as it were, in the footsteps of him who is the beginning of all, because they are closer to him and for this reason have been honored above the others. Our Lord Jesus Christ himself also hints at something of this kind in the parables of the Gospel. For he said that the one who hired the workers for the vineyard (he was the master of the house), “when evening came, said to his steward, ‘Call the workers and pay them their wages, beginning from the last up to the first’” (Matthew 20:8).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Son hands the kingdom to the Father when every rule of unclean spirits is destroyed and death is wholly idle.
comments.comment: “Then comes the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, when he has destroyed every rule and every authority and power” (1 Corinthians 15:24). He says that the kingdom will be handed over by the Son to God the Father when every rule of the unclean spirits has been destroyed and death itself is at last wholly idle.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: When the Son has destroyed death and sin and finished the whole plan of salvation, he presents to the Father the kingdom that had been plundered.
comments.comment: The sense of the words is this. Since man sinned and came under corruption, and through the devil and the demons fell away from him who is God by nature, the Only-begotten became man for our sake and destroyed the power of death; he also removed sin, the root of death, and cast out the ruler of this age (compare John 12:31). Having done all this, when the whole dispensation has been brought to completion, he hands over, that is, he will present, to the Father the kingdom that had long ago been plundered and had passed under the power of others…
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the Son hands over the kingdom.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Son's subjection to the Father does not make him lesser in nature, since subjection describes a way of acting, and he is subject by way of the plan of salvation for our sake.
comments.comment:
“When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28). Since some try, as far as lies with them, to belittle the Son, saying that he hands over the kingdom to the Father and is subject to him as to one greater, we must say that the Son underwent the voluntary self-emptying when he became like us, and humbled himself, as it were, from the heights, though he was of the same form as the Father and equal to him (compare Philippians 2:6–8). Now seated at the right hand of the Father, he is hidden in God (compare Colossians 3:3), but he will be revealed in glory at the time of the end of the present age.

If he is brought down from the honor he now has, does he then undergo a second self-emptying? And if he also hands over the kingdom, how does he come “with the holy angels in the glory of his Father” (Mark 8:38)? So it would be unwelcome to the Son that “his enemies should be put under his feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25), if now he reigns with the Father but then falls from the kingdom. Yet even if the Son is subject to the Father, he is not for that reason less than the Father. For subjection is not a defining mark of nature and essence; it points rather to a way of acting. Even among us, when it happens, it does not show that we are of different essence from one another. How so? A son is subject to a father, a slave to a master, a pupil to a teacher, and one of those under a ruler’s hand and yoke to the ruler. Yet in none of these cases is the principle of sameness of essence harmed; for they are of one kind with one another, even if they stand in this relation, yielding to one another and being subject, and not counting it a dishonor, for the sake of what is beneficial.

How then can they make an argument that is weak even in our case hold good in the case of God? For if, as they say, being subject is a property or measure of nature in the Son, then his not being subject is the property of another nature in him, a nature perhaps better than that one, if subjection belongs to lesser beings. For he is subject by way of the dispensation, for our sake.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: When all are subjected to the Son, we are found to be his members, and he is then subjected to the Father on our behalf, as head for his members, handing over the restored human kingdom.
comments.comment: But when all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:28). This is what it means: when we all are subjected to the Son, we are found to be his members, and we become sons of God in him. “For you,” he says, “are one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28). Then he himself will be subjected to the Father on our behalf, as head for his own members. For as long as all his members have not yet been subjected, he, their head, has not yet been subjected to the Father, but is awaiting his own members. If he were one of those who are subjected, he would have been subjected to the Father from the beginning, and would not be doing this at the end. For we are the ones who are subjected to the Father in him, and we are the ones who reign in him, until our enemies are placed under our feet. For because of our enemies the Master of the heavens came in our likeness, and took the human throne of David, his father according to the flesh, in order to rebuild it and set it upright. So that when it is set upright, we all might reign in him, and he might hand over the human kingdom, set upright, to the Father, so that God may be all in all, reigning through him as through the Word of God, after he has reigned through him as through a human savior.
comments.author: Marcellus of Ancyra
comments.work: On the Incarnation and against the Arians

comments.capsule: Paul's questions about danger and dying daily presume that there is no life beyond this one for those who deny the resurrection.
comments.comment: And in what follows also, as according to those who say there is no resurrection of the dead, nor life existing beyond this life, he says, Why are we also in danger every hour? I die daily, and the rest. And the heresy of the Sadducees who reject the resurrection of the dead also shows that it follows for them that you do not even live after the present life.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A martyr is made not by death alone but by intention, and Paul's 'I die every day' means he was ready and prepared for death, as Abraham completed his sacrifice in will.
comments.comment: I have often said to your love that it is not death alone that makes a martyr, but also the intention. For the crown of martyrdom is often woven not only from the outcome, but also from the will. And it is not I who give this definition of martyrdom, but Paul, who says, “I die every day” (1 Corinthians 15:31). How do you die every day? How is it possible for one mortal body to receive ten thousand deaths? By the readiness, he says, and by being prepared for death. So also God declares. For Abraham did not stain the knife with blood, did not redden the altar, did not sacrifice Isaac, yet he completed the sacrifice. Who says this? The very one who received the sacrifice: “You have not spared your beloved son for my sake” (Genesis 22:16).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by dying every day.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Paul's words on dying daily raise the question of the command not to swear, and beasts can also be intelligible ones.
comments.comment:
“I die daily, by your boasting which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord.” [Origen:] One must inquire whether he did not transgress the gospel command that says Do not swear at all. …

“If according to man I fought with beasts at Ephesus, what is the profit to me?” [Origen:] There are also intelligible beasts.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Love of sins makes people doubt future things and suppose there is no judgment; denying the resurrection means not knowing God's power.
comments.comment: ‘Do not be deceived: bad conversations corrupt good morals. Some have ignorance of God; I say this to your shame’ (1 Corinthians 15:33–34) (1 Corinthians 15:33). Love of sins, he says, persuades you to distrust future things. People suppose there is no judgment so that they may sin more boldly. Those denying resurrection, he says, completely fail to understand God. You therefore deny not only reward but divine power, and should be deeply ashamed. I say it to your shame that such people can be found among you.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul warns and shames them.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: The right teaching of the faith is that this very flesh will rise, as Christ's did.
comments.comment:
But perhaps you will say this: “Yes, you are right; and from now on I give up the need to ask, ‘How are the dead raised?’ Yet it is necessary to know clearly ‘with what kind of body they come’ (1 Corinthians 15:35). For will this very body that comes from the earth and is held fast by corruption come back to life, or some other body beside it, though made from it?”

To this I would say at once that the right teaching of the faith brings us to the resurrection of this very flesh. For so Christ came back to life, “the firstborn from the dead” (Colossians 1:18), “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20). …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The resurrection was foretold by Isaiah and the Psalms, and we are being reshaped and created anew by the Word and the Spirit, as God refashions life from death by his unspeakable power.
comments.comment:
“But someone will say, ‘How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?’” and so on (1 Corinthians 15:35). The prophet Isaiah cried out long beforehand the mystery of the resurrection from the dead, that it will take place in due time, as God grants it and by his unspeakable power refashions into life what death held fast. He said, “The dead shall rise, and those in the tombs shall be raised, and those in the earth shall rejoice; for the dew that comes from you is healing to them” (Isaiah 26:19). By dew, I think, he means figuratively the life-giving working of God, by which he gives being to things that are not, and grants well-being to things already brought into existence. For all things hold together in him (Colossians 1:17), just as they were also brought into being through him (compare John 1:3).

And somewhere the inspired David sings of the creatures on earth to God, the Savior of all: “When you open your hand, all things will be filled with goodness; when you turn away your face, they will be troubled; you will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust; you will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth” (Psalm 104:28–30). For in Adam, because of the transgression, human nature suffered the turning away of the divine face; and so it was all but thrown into confusion and troubled, went back to its own dust, and was brought down into death and corruption. But since the Only-begotten Word of God has become like us, and we have been enriched with a share in the Holy Spirit, we are being reshaped to what we were in the beginning and, as it were, created anew. For we have been called to newness of life (Romans 6:4), escaping the power of death.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Since Christ has risen, it is folly to keep asking 'How?', for we cannot explain how God made anything, and the dead rise with the same body, as the Lord raised his own flesh.
comments.comment:
The most wise Paul will bear witness, saying, “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will give life to your mortal bodies also through his Spirit who dwells in you” (Romans 8:11). Since, then, Christ came to life again, trampling down the power of death, and became the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, who will surely follow in his footsteps, how is it not utter madness still to doubt the mystery of the resurrection in any way at all?

If anyone chose to turn the eye of his mind too curiously on the works of the Godhead, and tried to look closely into the manner in which each thing was brought forth and the beginning of its coming to be, he would never stop uttering that senseless “How?” For how did the heaven come to be, from what matter, or from where? What foundation does it have? And the earth, how or from where did it come, and on what does it rest firm? How were the orb of the sun, the moon, the stars, and the other created things brought forth? How did the Maker of all take dust from the earth and form man (Genesis 2:7)? How was earth refashioned into bones and sinews and flesh? If, because we shall not be able to give an account of each thing that has been made, we shall for that reason deny that they came to be at all, where would these notions, or rather these perverse arguments, finally end?

After Christ’s resurrection, to doubt the resurrection, to say “How?” of the works of God, is a mark of bad judgment, ignorance, and arrogance. And indeed to ask, “With what body are the dead raised?” is also foolish; for it is quite plain that it is with the same body. For the Lord too raised his own flesh just as it was.
comments.selected_reason: Shows why 'How?' is the wrong question and that the same body rises.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God raises the dead as he brings fruit from every seed in its season, and the one time for the human body is the consummation of the age.
comments.comment: Then is the human seed useless to the Craftsman beside all those bodies, so that one hopes for a resurrection of the dead, if one may say so, in olive fashion and vine fashion and wheat fashion, and from the fig’s pip so great a fig rises, and you do not laugh at what you see by experience? And if someone tells you that from this small thing a fruit-bearing fig rises, having learned by experience you do not mock; but because the time has not yet come for what will rise from the human body according to the resurrection from the dead to spring up, you will not wait to see this too? Or do you not know that for all other seeds not every season is fit for seeds to spring? But a wheat grain rises at this time of year; the grape-stone at this hour of year; the olive pit in this month, not at every time. And do you want, for the human body, so that you may believe, the dead to rise yearly like the grape-stone, like the olive, and not see one paradoxical time that you may know the resurrection of the dead? What is the one time? At the consummation of the age, so that after the resurrection from the dead you may no longer be in the present evil age. For Jesus Christ suffered that he might deliver us from the present evil age; and we redeem the time because the days are evil. So God well stewarded this too with the rest.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A human seed, small and cheap, becomes a full human being, and the body is to the risen body what that seed is to the present body, as the grain falls, dies and yields an ear.
comments.comment: Come also to the human’s very beginning; recall his beginning. A human seed is shown you. If someone said, “This seed will be a human; it will be formed; there will be bones from it, flesh, sinews, veins; he will walk; from this small, cheap seed a human raised on earth will use organs”—would we not call the one preaching this to us mindless, if we had not taken experience of it? So then let me dare also to show you the resurrection, and you will rather accept it, trusting God’s perfection. What that seed was toward this present body—now the present, the generic, the sowing, the organ of words and works according to righteousness—this body becomes toward that: Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it falls into the earth and dies and decays, from the decay of the wheat grain a hundredfold ear comes.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul compares the body to a grain, which falls into the earth and rises not bare but clothed, as God gives each seed its own body.
comments.comment: The inspired Paul uses an excellent example. He says that the body falls into the earth like a grain, and that it will not rise just as it was sown, bare, but as if in a garment and covering of the things that usually grow on it, I mean stalk and leaves (1 Corinthians 15:36–37). For “God gives,” he says, “to each of the seeds its own body” (1 Corinthians 15:38).
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's grain illustration.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: All the dead will rise in incorruption, but God will give them different glory according to what each deserves, as Paul's two examples, the grain and the heavenly bodies, show.
comments.comment:
Since he says that not all who have fallen asleep will come back to life in glory, even if all will in incorruption (for surely it is not fitting that the unrighteous and those who work wicked deeds should be crowned with the renown that comes from God), he usefully mentions different seeds for this reason, to which God also assigns, in whatever way He Himself may choose, a difference in this form, it may be, or in another. For he says, “And what you sow is not the body that is to be” (1 Corinthians 15:37), and, “There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies” (1 Corinthians 15:40).

The account is one, in that each is and is called a body; but in another respect it is divided into different kinds. The bodies of all will come back to life in incorruption, yet there will be some difference in the glory and in the covering that God may provide, as He assigns to each what each deserves. “But the glory of the heavenly is one, and the glory of the earthly is another” (1 Corinthians 15:40).

It should be known that two examples have just been set before us, I mean that of the grain and that which shows the difference in glory among the heavenly bodies; for the present he relates the likeness of the resurrection of the dead to the force of the first, and says next, “It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:42).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: As an ear rises from a grain, a principle in the body that does not corrupt gives the body raised in incorruption.
comments.comment: We, then, do not say that the corrupted body returns “to its original nature,” any more than the corrupted grain of wheat returns to being a grain of wheat (1 Corinthians 15:37; John 12:24). For we say that, just as an ear rises from the grain of wheat, so a certain principle lies within the body; and from this principle, which is not corrupted, the body “is raised in incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:42).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christians know that bodies differ in glory, so the resurrection brings changes in the qualities of bodies: from corruption to incorruption, dishonour to glory, weakness to power, natural to spiritual.
comments.comment: For we too know that there are “both heavenly bodies and earthly bodies,” and that the “glory” of “heavenly” bodies is one thing and that of “earthly” bodies another (1 Corinthians 15:40); nor is it the same even among the “heavenly” ones, for “the glory of the sun is one thing, and the glory of the stars another,” and among the stars themselves “star differs from star in glory” (1 Corinthians 15:41). That is why, since we accept the resurrection “of the dead,” we say that changes take place in the qualities that are in bodies. For some of them, sown “in corruption, are raised in incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:42); sown “in dishonour, are raised in glory”; and sown “in weakness, are raised in power” (1 Corinthians 15:43); and bodies sown natural are raised spiritual (1 Corinthians 15:44).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God will renew creation and man with it, raising man in incorruption, strength and honor, clothed with divine glory, though this honor is for those chosen out from the rest.
comments.comment:
For He [God] is also the giver of the good things we expect to come. He will refashion creation and renew the whole universe, and He will set it free from slavery into the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Romans 8:21). And if this is true, how could it not be wholly necessary that the one for whose sake creation exists, I mean man, should be renewed together with creation?

Man too had to be seen as new: not tyrannized by the first corruption, not overpowered by fleshly pleasures into sins, but raised instead in incorruption, in strength and in honor, and clothed with a divine glory (1 Corinthians 15:42–43). For the inspired Isaiah also says somewhere, “Your righteousness shall go before you, and the glory of God shall clothe you” (Isaiah 58:8).

And indeed our Lord Jesus Himself plainly affirmed that at the time of the end of this age the dead will come back to life (Matthew 13:40–43; Daniel 12:2), but “those who understand will shine like the brightness of the firmament” (Daniel 12:3). Yet the grace of such honor and glory will not be set before all without distinction. It would rather befit those who have been chosen out from the rest, who have also been conformed to the image of His Son (Romans 8:29).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The body is seed of what will rise: sown in corruption, dishonor and weakness, it is raised in incorruption, glory and power, as God makes an ear from a grain.
comments.comment: That your body is seed of what will rise, hear Paul saying: It is sown in corruption, raised in incorruption; sown in dishonor, raised in glory; sown in weakness, raised in power; sown a soulish body, raised a spiritual body. You see how there, upon the seed, something cheap and of no account was sown, and a fair and beautiful human was raised; in the same way this dead thing is a grain of wheat to God as what is about to rise. Just as God had means from the wheat grain to make an ear—not outside the starting points in the small seed; for from that he raised the ear, and from each seed he raises what potentially exists in the seed—so from a human seed according to the beginning this human came to be. And if his body dies, it becomes seed of the one who will rise from the dead in glory in Christ Jesus.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Like a grain, the body is sown in corruption, weakness and dishonor, but will come back to life clothed in incorruption, glory and power, and renewed to a spiritual mind.
comments.comment:
… so in this same way the human body too is sown in corruption, in weakness and in dishonor, but will come back to life clothed in honor and incorruption, and in power as well (1 Corinthians 15:42–43). …

For his faith is firmly grounded, and he is confident that the body will come back to life in every way and without fail; so he likens the body's corruption to sowing, and with great skill and wisdom makes the nature of the thing match the example at every point. So, he says, like the grain, the body will not come back to life bare, but richly clothed with incorruption and glory, and with strength besides, and enriched also with this: that it comes to be of a spiritual mind, since the grace from above and the incomparable power of the Creator of all in a way refashion what is in it into the very opposite.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's pairs in terms of the grain illustration.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Corruption, weakness and a natural mind entered through the transgression, and in Christ God renews us and gives back glory, incorruption, power and a spiritual mind.
comments.comment:
For corruption and weakness and lack of beauty dwell in the body that has fallen and been sown, as it were, in the earth, and a natural mind as well, which we say is the same as the fleshly and more earthly mind. But it was not so by nature when it was brought into being in the beginning; these things crept in through the transgression and the sentence of death. Since our nature is being called back to what it was in the beginning, the putting off of what came in between is necessarily brought about by the power and working of God, and in exchange there is brought in a share in the good things that were ours first, in the beginning.

For we have been renewed in Christ, as the Scriptures say. A holy prophet said, “Take courage, Zion; do not let your hands grow slack. The Lord your God is in you, mighty to save you, and He will renew you in His love” (Zephaniah 3:16–17). For when God the Father loved us, then, at that very time, He renewed us in Christ. And indeed it is true that all things in Him are “a new creation; the old things have passed away, and new things have come” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

What old things does he mean? Those that have gone by. And what new things? Those that have been brought in. The old are corruption, and weakness, and dishonor besides, and the faults of the natural mind; the new, through Christ, are glory and incorruption and power and the spiritual mind. For our body will be spiritual (1 Corinthians 15:44).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A spiritual body does not mean a thin shadow-like body without flesh, since then it would not be the very thing that fell into the earth; it means a body freed from the fleshly, earthly mind.
comments.comment:
What would “spiritual” mean, O teacher of the mysteries? Does he mean that it will no longer be flesh, and will in no way be composed, as it is now, of bones and sinews, through which the nature of our body is made complete, but will rather be thin and airy, hardly more solid than a shadow? Not at all. For if some think this is how things stand, then surely it will not be the very thing that falls into the earth that comes back to life, but something else beside it, in no way like the first.

I would say that “spiritual” means not what has the form of a shadow, that is, of a bodiless spirit, but rather what has stood apart from, and indeed been wholly set free from, the fleshly and more earthly mind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'spiritual body' means and does not mean.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Natural' does not give the body the form of a soul but describes a fleshly mind, as Paul shows when he calls living people natural or spiritual.
comments.comment: For suppose someone chooses to call our body from the earth “natural.” One would reasonably not attach to it the form of a soul, but would rather turn the force of the word to the natural, that is, the fleshly, mind, just as we understand our own human wisdom to be “natural” and “earthly” (James 3:15). So too, even if it is called a natural body, one who attaches to it the form of a soul would not, I think, escape the charge of going astray. Otherwise, in what sense are some people, while still alive and still in these very bodies from the earth, called natural and others spiritual? For it is written, “The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him; but the spiritual man judges all things, yet he himself is judged by no one” (1 Corinthians 2:14–15).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A spiritual body is not a body turned into spirit but one so subjected to the spirit that it suits a heavenly dwelling, with all fragility and earthly stain changed into heavenly purity.
comments.comment: The Gentiles, for the most part, try to deal with us by the arguments of the philosophers, saying that nothing earthly can exist in heaven. They do not know our Scriptures, and they do not know how it was said, “A natural body is sown; a spiritual body rises” (1 Corinthians 15:44). It was not said as if the body is turned into spirit and becomes spirit, because even now our body, which is called natural, has not been turned into soul and become soul. Rather, a spiritual body is understood as one so subjected to the spirit that it is suited to a heavenly dwelling, with all fragility and earthly stain changed and converted into heavenly purity and stability.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what a 'spiritual body' is.
comments.author: Augustine of Hippo

comments.capsule: Adam, made a living soul, was not wholly free from fleshly desires, and even blameless desire for children is fleshly, or natural, in the nature of the act.
comments.comment:
Since it followed that he should confirm his argument on this point by facts as well, he adds, “The first man Adam became a living soul; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit” (1 Corinthians 15:45). So he called Adam natural; for this, I think, is what being made “a living soul” means: that he was not wholly free from fleshly desires. For the appetites that look and turn toward the passions of the flesh, even if they have the law to speak in their defense, would still in truth be charges against fleshly weakness, if one looks at the nature of what is done.

I mean something like this: “Marriage is honorable, and the bed undefiled” (Hebrews 13:4). For the Maker of all has planted in the nature of the body a movement of appetite that stirs the living creature to the desire for children. For it was said to man, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28); and, he says, “He who formed them in the beginning made them male and female” (Matthew 19:4; Genesis 1:27). So the desire that looks only to having children is blameless; yet as far as the nature of the act goes, the passion would be fleshly, that is, natural. And so it is with the other blameless passions as well.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Adam became a living soul, but Christ, God the Word united to a human, lived a divine, blameless life and as God was a life-giving spirit.
comments.comment: So the first man Adam became a living soul; but the second, the one from heaven, that is, Christ, became not a soul but rather a life-giving spirit. For God the Word, who came forth from God the Father and is God by nature, united the human to Himself and lived not a human life like ours, but a life divine, fitting for God, and wholly blameless. For “He committed no sin” (1 Peter 2:22): He kept His mind untouched by unseemly pleasures, and it could not be caught by desires for food. For even though He is seen to have taken food and drink, so that He might be believed to be truly a man like us, still He partook of them freely. For He was in the flesh for our sake, in keeping with the plan of salvation, and yet again above the flesh; for He was a life-giving spirit as God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'living soul' and 'life-giving spirit'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord became man from the Virgin, so Christ is the second Adam, the Savior of the first, said to be from heaven because the Word came down from heaven.
comments.comment: For how can it be said that a perfect man was taken up by the Lord like one of the prophets, when the Lord himself became man through incarnation from the Virgin? That is why it is written, “The first man was from the earth, earthly” (1 Corinthians 15:47). But after the one who had been formed from the earth went back into the earth, the one who became the second man ascended into the heavens. And it is said that there is a first Adam and a last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45). Just as it is acknowledged that the second comes from the first as far as the flesh is concerned, which is why Christ is both man and Son of Man, so it is also testified that the second is the Savior of the first, for whose sake he even came down from heaven. And since the Word came down from heaven and, having become man, ascended into the heavens, for this reason the second Adam is also said to be from heaven (1 Corinthians 15:47).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Adam, as a creature, needed the God who gives life, while Christ as God became a life-giving spirit; we who bore the dusty one's image will wear the heavenly one's when we put on incorruption.
comments.comment: The first human became a living soul; for as a creature he needed the God who gives life. But the last Adam — that is, Christ — because he did not need life as God, became a life-giving spirit for us, which is a proper advantage of the divine nature. And the first is the dusty one from earth; but the second is from heaven, though born through a woman — for the Word from above and from heaven and from God the Father, even if he has become human, is no less from heaven. And if, held by corruption and death, we are for that reason said to have worn the dusty one’s image, when we put on incorruption we will wear the heavenly one’s image. And incorruption again is a proper good of the deity by nature.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: 'Natural' does not mean a difference of nature but a quality of life, as Adam and Christ show, and the natural comes before the spiritual.
comments.comment:
That the word “natural,” then, would suggest to us not a difference of nature, but rather a quality of life, of character and of ways, by which one person is held fast by the more earthly and fleshly mind, and another shines out in the freedom of the Spirit, he shows clearly from Adam, the first and the second. For both came to be in earthly bodies; but the quality, so to speak, of the mind, and indeed the choice to live in a different way, showed the one to be natural, and the other to be incomparably better, that is, spiritual.

“But the spiritual is not first, but the natural, and then the spiritual” (1 Corinthians 15:46). In a way he takes hold of the times in which they came to be, and says, “But the spiritual is not first, but the natural, and then the spiritual.” Since he said that the body is sown in the earth natural, he shows plainly that it is not foreign to human nature to pass from a natural mind to a spiritual one, and that the natural would be older than the spiritual.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'natural' and 'spiritual' mean in Paul's wording.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul turns to our conduct, wanting the change between past and present to be as great as between mortality and immortality, using the names of substances to mark a difference of purpose.
comments.comment: ‘But the spiritual did not come first,’ (1 Corinthians 15:46) he says; ‘the animate came first, and then the spiritual. The first human is from earth, earthly; the second human from heaven, heavenly. As we have borne the earthly one’s (1 Corinthians 15:49) image, let us also bear the heavenly one’s image’ (1 Corinthians 15:46–47, 49). He plainly turns to our pursuits, wanting the difference between our past and present conduct to be as great as that between mortality and immortality. ‘The first human is from earth, earthly; the second human from heaven, heavenly.’ (1 Corinthians 15:47) He uses the names of substances to indicate a difference of purpose.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Adam was earthly and fleshly, but Christ, though also in an earthly body, is from heaven, and differed in his way of life.
comments.comment: The first man, he says, that is, Adam, had been made a living soul, that is, earthly and fleshly; but the second is from heaven. For even though the Word of God became flesh, as the Scriptures say (John 1:14), yet He was … also the One from heaven and “above all,” in the words of John (John 3:31). So both, as I said, were in earthly bodies, but they were not also equal in disposition, that is, in their way of life. For the first was of a fleshly mind, while the second, the One from heaven, was a life-giving spirit.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the contrast between the first man and the second.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Bearing the image of Adam means being weak toward sins and under corruption; bearing the image of Christ means rising above love of the flesh, sin, and death.
comments.comment: “And just as we have borne the image of the man of dust,” that is, the likeness to Adam, being overcome by passions and weak toward sins, and brought besides under the yokes of corruption, “so let us also bear the image of the man of heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:49), that is, of Christ: becoming superior to love of the flesh and to any wish to go on sinning, and having already conquered death itself, which of old was terrible and hard to face and ruled savagely over us as a tyrant.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what bearing an image means in everyday terms.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The image of the man of dust is a life of disobedience and sin, and the image of the heavenly one, Christ, is holiness, justification and obedience.
comments.comment: “For just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, let us also bear the image of the heavenly one” (1 Corinthians 15:49). For those who have paid no heed to fleshly desires are the ones who have imitated the image of Christ, that is, the way of life and conduct that is in holiness. For just as we say that the image of the man of dust, that is, of Adam, is the life lived in disobedience and sins, so too the image of the heavenly one, that is, of Christ, is holiness, justification and obedience.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: While the body is mortal flesh and blood it cannot inherit the kingdom, so it must be refashioned into incorruption and made radiant with divine glory.
comments.comment: “Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 15:50). By this too he establishes the mystery of the resurrection. For as long as the human body is flesh and blood, that is, mortal and corruptible, it could not inherit the kingdom of God, that is, unending existence. So it is wholly necessary that corruption be swallowed up and what readily withers be done away, and that the body itself be refashioned into incorruption and made radiant with a divine and unspeakable glory; for then it will inherit the kingdom of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Heavenly bodies are bodies without flesh, which Paul calls spiritual, so when he says flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom he is foretelling what flesh and blood will become, not denying the resurrection of the body.
comments.comment: For at that time of angelic change it will no longer be flesh and blood, but only body. When the apostle was speaking about flesh, he said: “There is one kind of flesh of cattle, another of birds, another of fish, another of snakes. And there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies” (1 Corinthians 15:39–40). He did not say “and heavenly flesh”; he said “heavenly and earthly bodies.” For every flesh is also a body, but not every body is also flesh. First, among these earthly things, wood is a body but not flesh; but a human being or a cow is both body and flesh. In heavenly things, however, there is no flesh, but simple and bright bodies, which the apostle calls spiritual, though some call them ethereal. And so what he says does not contradict the resurrection of the body: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 15:50). Rather, he foretells what that which is now flesh and blood will become.
comments.author: Augustine of Hippo

comments.capsule: Flesh and blood cannot possess God's kingdom because Scripture uses the words for vices, not for the substance of the body.
comments.comment: Following the course of his exhortation, he adds something that, unless understood, will seem to overthrow all he has said: ‘I say this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot possess God’s kingdom (1 Corinthians 15:50), nor will decay possess everlasting life’ (1 Corinthians 15:50). In these very passages he has labored only to establish flesh’s resurrection, saying it would be placed in the kingdom’s glory. Now he pronounces that flesh and blood cannot possess God’s kingdom. If flesh cannot possess it and blood cannot possess it, where is the resurrection of the dead whose splendor he has been setting forth above? But, following Scripture’s usage, he calls vices, not substance, ‘flesh and blood.’
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: All will rise incorruptible but only the righteous will be changed and glorified, and the change will not turn us into another nature but make us what we are, only better.
comments.comment:
For admittedly the bodies of all will come back to life clothed with the grace of incorruption, but not all will be changed (1 Corinthians 15:51). The wicked will remain in the form of dishonor, only so that they may be punished; but the righteous alone will be changed, and, besides the good of incorruption, they will be enriched with the covering of divine glory.

So He Himself, by His own power and a working fitting for God, “will transform the body of our lowliness to be conformed to the body of His glory” (Philippians 3:21). And what is the body of our lowliness? This body from the earth, held fast by death because of that ancient curse (Genesis 3:17–19), which Christ undid by “becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

The transformation will not carry us off into some other nature. For we shall be what we are, that is, human beings, but incomparably better: incorruptible and imperishable, and glorified besides.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'we shall all be changed' means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The trumpet is the archangel's voice and divine command, but it is Christ's voice that raises the dead, by his own power.
comments.comment:
“And the dead will be raised incorruptible” (1 Corinthians 15:52).

So he likens to a trumpet the voice of the archangel and that divine and most awe-inspiring command. And even if it is the archangel who cries out and gives the signal of resurrection to those who lie in the earth, still the voice will be Christ’s. For it is He who raises the dead by His own power, and certainly not the archangel’s voice; for every rational creature is yoked under the Master’s commands.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the trumpet in plain terms.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: At the last trumpet the dead will be raised whole in a moment, and those found alive will be changed into glory.
comments.comment: ‘In a moment,’ he says, ‘in the blink of an eye, at the last trumpet, the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed’ (1 Corinthians 15:52). Here again he turns to the saints whom that day will find in the flesh. He says that in a moment as brief as the final ending of a sound, those who had died will be raised incorruptible—that is, whole—and those found alive will be changed into glory.
comments.author: Julian of Eclanum

comments.capsule: Paul points as with a finger at this visible flesh when he says 'this corruptible' and 'this mortal', so the flesh itself must rise.
comments.comment: This visible flesh, then, which is properly called flesh, must without doubt be believed to rise. For the apostle Paul seems to point at it as with a finger when he says: “This corruptible must put on incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:53). For when he says “this,” he points his finger, as it were, at it. Now what is visible can be pointed at with a finger, since the soul can also be called corruptible; for it is corrupted by the vices of morals. And when we read, “and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53), the same visible flesh is meant, because the finger is again, as it were, pointed at it. For the soul can also be called mortal, just as it can be called corruptible because of the vices of morals.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'this corruptible' and 'this mortal' point to.
comments.author: Augustine of Hippo

comments.capsule: Since every bodily nature is corruptible and mortal, it must put on incorruption and immortality, and then death's victory and its sting will be overthrown as the prophets foretold.
comments.comment: “For,” since every bodily nature is corruptible, “this corruptible” tent “must put on incorruption,” and its other aspect, which is “mortal” and liable to the death that follows on sin, must “put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53); so that when “the corruptible puts on incorruption and the mortal immortality, then” there “will come to pass” (1 Corinthians 15:54) what the prophets foretold long ago: the overthrow of the victory death won when it conquered us and made us subject to itself (Isaiah 25:8), and of the sting that comes from it, with which it stings the soul that is not guarded on every side and inflicts on it the wounds that come from sin (Hosea 13:14; 1 Corinthians 15:55–56).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Unless the very thing held by death comes back to life, there would be no true resurrection and no triumph over corruption.
comments.comment: What true resurrection will there be at all, then, unless we say that the very thing held fast by death will come back to life? Or how shall we say, all but dancing in triumph over corruption, “Death is swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54; Isaiah 25:8), and what follows? “O death, where is your sting? O Hades, where is your victory?” (1 Corinthians 15:55).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul quoted the passage from the Hebrew text, not the Septuagint, which reads differently in Hosea.
comments.comment: It should be known that the blessed Paul cited the passage before us according to the Hebrew text. The Septuagint [the Greek Old Testament] does not read this way, for it is written in the Prophets, “Where is your penalty, O death? Where is your sting, O Hades?” (Hosea 13:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul's wording differs from the Greek Old Testament.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law gives power to sin because it can be either guarded or transgressed, so by it we are in the capacity of sin, not yet in its operation.
comments.comment: And again: 'the power of sin is the law' (1 Corinthians 15:56). The law is able and to be transgressed. It does not have it by actual operation. And well and timely the apostle has used this expression: 'the power of sin is the law'; for he wants us to be in the capacity of sin and not in the operation. If it had been said: 'the power of righteousness is the law', we would not have been righteous by operation, but in capacity. And being in capacity, we were unjust by operation. Thus the apostle set down the auspicious word; since it also has the power equally for both, for guarding and for transgressing; but because of what is advantageous.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Satan strikes with the sting of sin, and the Law made sin powerful by condemning sinners, but Christ undid this, and God gives us the victory through him.
comments.comment:
“But the sting of death,” he says, “is sin, and the power of sin is the Law” (1 Corinthians 15:56). For the one who holds the sting of death, that is, Satan (Hebrews 2:14), strikes like a scorpion. And he strikes in no other way than through sin. But the Savior has granted us “to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19).

For the sting of death has been destroyed, since sin has been taken away and no longer has the Law as its power. For the Law condemns those who sin; that is why the inspired Paul says that the Law is the power of sin. But this too has been undone in Christ: for sin will not be master over us, because we are not under the Law but under grace (Romans 6:14); and apart from the Law sin is dead (Romans 7:8).

Who, then, supplies us with all these things? Who is the dispenser of righteousness, the giver of freedom, the spring and cause of every good? We shall learn it from the blessed Paul, who says, “But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:57).
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's 'sting of death' and 'power of sin'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A great and effective door of the word brings many opponents, and it is effective when hearers turn the teaching into works; the opponents act out of envy, even attacking teachers to death.
comments.comment: For indeed the apostle says: 'A great and effective door has been opened to me, and there are many who oppose me' (1 Cor 16:9). If the 'great door' of the word is 'opened' and 'effective', then 'many who oppose' are present. And it is 'effective' when those who hear convert the teachings into works. And 'many' become 'opposing' … For, envying, they 'oppose' and attempt to contradict the truth, attempting to contradict those who teach well, sometimes even attacking them and leading them to death.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why a great open door goes with many opponents.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul sent Timothy in his place to set things right, and asks that he be without fear, because Paul himself came in weakness and fear among the weaker, and Timothy comes to make peace.
comments.comment:
Paul was doing the work of the apostleship; it was not fitting for him, spending time then in Asia, to leave the things in Asia and come to Corinth; but instead of himself he chose Timothy and sent him to set right the things in Corinth, and necessarily sending him with the letter entrusted him to the church.

For when the saints visited benefiting the hearers, they did not arrive in weakness or in fear or in trembling; but when they came to the weaker, they visited in weakness and in fear and in trembling. Such were the Corinthians, so that not the great Paul visited them but the weak one, inasmuch as he said, I became to the weak as weak, that I might win the weak. And for this reason he said, I also was with you in weakness; for this reason he also came in fear and much trembling, so that he might prevail with the hearers. Since then arriving in fear and trembling for the one about to benefit concerns the hearers, he now asks the Corinthians that Timothy be with them without fear; for he works the Lord’s work as I also do; what I would have done if I had visited you, Timothy does for you. So let no one despise him; for if you despise this one, you despise me also; for he works the Lord’s work as I also do. And send him on in peace, that he may come to me; now he comes to you to make peace. For he finds your faction in the church; but having agreed and been set right by what he says and taken up peace, send him on in your concord and peace, that he may come to me. For I await him with the brothers—which brothers? those of whom he said earlier, Whomever you approve by letters, these I will send. So I await hearing him return, announcing to me your affairs.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul asks that Timothy be received without fear and sent on in peace.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Apollos, seeing faction in the church, yielded rather than come, and will come when there is opportunity, that is, when they are at peace and do not despise Timothy.
comments.comment: About brother Apollos I urged him to come to you; and it was not at all will that he come now. He was a human, as is likely, holy, a friend of peace, and seeing faction and turmoil in the church under him, he did not claim this but yielded. Then the apostle asks him, having been patient, to return to his sojourning. And this one did not see Corinth at all, not disobeying the apostle; for he would not thus have recommended his seeming, if not subject; for he says, “It was not at all will that he come now”—that is, not without God’s will did he do the not coming to you; but he will come when he has opportunity. And when does he have opportunity? If you are at peace, if you do not despise Timothy.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Each command is explained: watch against the soul's sleep, stand firm in faith, act as soldiers, be strong in Christ, and act in love rather than fear.
comments.comment: “Watch, stand in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all your things be done in love.” [Origen:] For there is a sleep of soul and a watching; therefore the word, turning the soul from sleeping, says through Solomon, Give no sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids, that you may be saved like a doe from snares and like a bird from a snare. And the Savior says, Watch at every time and pray that you may be able to escape the trials that are about to come. “Stand”: do not be shaken but become firm. The double-souled has not stood in the faith, or the one doubting about the things according to the faith. “Act like men”: he speaks as to soldiers; for put on the panoply of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil. “Be strong”: that is, take up the strength, that having been strengthened you may be able to say, I can do all things in Christ Jesus who strengthens me. “Let all your things be done in love”: for beginners, doing in fear; for the perfect, doing in love.
comments.selected_reason: Takes each of Paul's short commands in turn in plain terms.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
